title: Critical--localized reentry under periodic spacer control
summary: Tracking a fixed fraction of a quasiperiodic spectrum tests whether repeated critical--localized alternation extends over a nonzero spectral weight. We find such alternation in a matched-dimer chain by varying only the spacer on-site energies and following a fixed interval of integrated-density-of-states (IDS) labels. An exact Bloch-determinant identity links the physical transfer discriminant to the bands of a periodic reference operator. For the golden cell frequency, we prove that, on a common full-measure set of phases and for every finite value of the spacer control, the physical spectrum in the open reference bands is critical, with purely singular-continuous spectrum and zero Lyapunov exponent, while the spectrum strictly outside the bands is pure point, with exponentially decaying eigenfunctions. Validated IDS bounds certify repeated critical--localized alternation of the same fixed spectral fraction at successive spacer controls. Spacer shifts move the physical levels and reference-band edges at different rates, allowing us to reshape finite-chain return windows and place their endpoints at prescribed controls. An affine recalibration relocates the control family exactly.

AI.tldr: In a matched-dimer chain, varying only spacer on-site energies produces repeated critical–localized alternation over a fixed nonzero spectral fraction, certified by IDS bounds for successive spacer controls.
AI.motivation: Tracking a fixed fraction of a quasiperiodic spectrum tests whether the repeated critical–localized alternation persists over nonzero spectral weight, rather than being confined to isolated points or measure-zero sets.
AI.method: Study a matched-dimer chain while varying only the spacer on-site energies, following a fixed interval of IDS labels. Use an exact Bloch-determinant identity relating the physical transfer discriminant to the bands of a periodic reference operator; prove spectral statements for golden-cell frequency on a full-measure set of phases and all finite spacer controls; use validated IDS bounds and spacer-shift-driven differential motion of physical levels versus reference-band edges, plus an affine recalibration of the control family.
AI.result: For the golden cell frequency, on a common full-measure set of phases and every finite spacer control: the physical spectrum inside open reference bands is critical, with purely singular-continuous spectrum and zero Lyapunov exponent; spectrum strictly outside the bands is pure point with exponentially decaying eigenfunctions. IDS bounds certify repeated critical–localized alternation of the same fixed spectral fraction at successive spacer controls. Spacer shifts reshape finite-chain return windows and place endpoints at prescribed controls; an affine recalibration relocates the control family exactly.
AI.conclusion: Repeated critical–localized alternation of a fixed spectral fraction is realized and certified in a matched-dimer chain by tuning spacer on-site energies alone, with an exact Bloch-determinant identity and IDS bounds providing the analytical and numerical control.

title: Wegner model in high dimension: singular continuous spectrum from U(1) symmetry breaking and AAT self-consistency
summary: We analyze the energy-spectral decomposition of the Wegner one-orbital model in high lattice dimension using ideas from field theory and statistical mechanics. Most notably, we identify a local spectral measure of singular continuous type for the disordered model at the Anderson transition. The key mechanism that leads to a singular continuous spectrum is a novel scenario of spontaneous symmetry breaking, intimately connected to the non-compactness of the global symmetry group of the field theory. While that symmetry breaks down to a compact subgroup in the metallic phase, it spontaneously breaks down to a nilpotent subgroup at criticality. We describe the symmetry-breaking extremal states approximately, by applying the self-consistent theory of localization due to Abou-Chacra, Anderson, and Thouless. The thrust of our work is to provide a field-theoretical foundation for disorder phenomena associated with singular continuous spectra.

AI.tldr: The authors analyze the energy-spectral decomposition of the Wegner one-orbital model in high lattice dimension using field-theoretic and statistical-mechanical methods, and identify a singular-continuous local spectral measure at the Anderson transition, tracing its origin to a spontaneous symmetry breaking in which the non-compact global symmetry of the field theory breaks to a nilpotent subgroup at criticality.
AI.motivation: Singular continuous spectra in disordered systems lack a solid field-theoretical underpinning; the authors aim to supply one and to explain which spectral type emerges at the Anderson transition in the Wegner one-orbital model.
AI.method: Energy-spectral decomposition of the Wegner one-orbital model at high lattice dimension, combined with field theory and statistical mechanics. The central tool is a novel spontaneous-symmetry-breaking scenario tied to the non-compactness of the global symmetry group: the symmetry breaks to a compact subgroup in the metallic phase but to a nilpotent subgroup at criticality. The symmetry-breaking extremal states are described approximately via the self-consistent theory of localization of Abou-Chacra, Anderson, and Thouless.
AI.result: A local spectral measure of singular continuous type is identified for the disordered model at the Anderson transition. The metallic phase exhibits breaking to a compact subgroup, whereas criticality shows breaking to a nilpotent subgroup.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a field-theoretical foundation for disorder phenomena associated with singular continuous spectra, linking the spectral type at criticality to a symmetry-breaking pattern governed by the non-compactness of the field theory's symmetry group.

title: Quantum resources and the onset of the quantum Monte Carlo sign problem
summary: The Monte Carlo sign problem poses a fundamental obstacle to classical simulation of quantum many-body systems, yet its connection to quantum resources remains poorly understood. We probe this connection by systematically tuning the degree of nonstoquasticity in random k-local Hamiltonians. In numerical tensor-network studies, we find the sign complexity and the quantum resources of entanglement and nonstabilizerness of the ground state to be strongly suppressed in a broad regime up to substantial nonstoquasticity. As nonstoquasticity is further increased, the considered quantum resources experience sharp crossovers into a regime where they are strongly enhanced. Surprisingly, numerical quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations drastically deteriorate in the same region, even though the Hamiltonian is already considerably nonstoquastic well before it, indicating that the failure of ground-state QMC is correlated more with the resource content of the state than the sign structure of the Hamiltonian. We corroborate these findings analytically by constructing an approximate ground state of k-local Hamiltonians in the stoquastic limit. Moreover, we identify a distinct behaviour in graph states. Their nonstabilizerness always vanishes, but, as we demonstrate analytically, on bipartite graphs the sign can be easily cured while in multipartite graph states it cannot. Our results thus shed light on the highly subtle interplay between quantum resources and the computational difficulty encountered by QMC methods.

AI.tldr: By tuning nonstoquasticity in random k-local Hamiltonians, the authors show that ground-state QMC failure correlates with entanglement and nonstabilizerness rather than the Hamiltonian's sign structure.
AI.motivation: The Monte Carlo sign problem is a fundamental barrier to classical simulation of quantum many-body systems, but how it relates to quantum resources (entanglement, nonstabilizerness) is poorly understood. The paper aims to probe this connection.
AI.method: Systematically tune the degree of nonstoquasticity in random k-local Hamiltonians. Use tensor-network numerical studies to compute sign complexity and quantum resources (entanglement, nonstabilizerness) of ground states; compare with numerical QMC performance. Support findings analytically by constructing an approximate ground state in the stoquastic limit, and analyze graph states (bipartite vs. multipartite) for sign-curing behavior.
AI.result: Sign complexity and quantum resources are strongly suppressed over a broad regime up to substantial nonstoquasticity, then undergo sharp crossovers to strong enhancement. QMC deteriorates sharply in the same region, despite the Hamiltonian being considerably nonstoquastic well before it, indicating QMC failure tracks state resource content more than Hamiltonian sign structure. Graph states: nonstabilizerness always vanishes; sign is easily cured on bipartite graphs but not on multipartite ones.
AI.conclusion: Ground-state QMC difficulty is governed more by the quantum resources of the state than by the Hamiltonian's sign structure, revealing a subtle interplay between quantum resources and computational hardness for QMC.

title: Parisi Energy before Parisi Geometry in the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures, supplemental material included (45 pages, 10 figures)
summary: The fractured low-energy landscape of spin glasses presents a notorious barrier to optimization. While high-depth calculations indicate that the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) can approach the Parisi ground-state energy of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass, how it does so remains elusive. Here, we treat the QAOA distribution as a statistical-physics object and probe its geometry directly in the thermodynamic limit. We draw two independent bitstrings from the same problem instance and couple them through their macroscopic similarity. We find that typical QAOA samples remain macroscopically uncorrelated, even as their sensitivity to this coupling grows with circuit depth $p$. By contrast, the low-energy tail shows a much stronger tendency to overlap and reveals a Parisi-like phase with the same critical behavior as the thermal spin-glass transition. The onset of this organization moves toward the typical output as the circuit deepens, consistent with the separation vanishing only as $p\to\infty$. Together, these findings suggest a route distinct from structure-exploiting classical algorithms and thermal sampling, one in which the QAOA approaches the Parisi energy before Parisi geometry becomes typical.

AI.tldr: Treating the QAOA output distribution as a statistical-physics object, the authors probe its geometry in the thermodynamic limit by coupling two bitstrings through their macroscopic overlap. Typical QAOA samples stay macroscopically uncorrelated, while the low-energy tail develops a Parisi-like phase with the thermal spin-glass critical behavior; this organization spreads toward typical outputs only as depth p→∞.
AI.motivation: Deep QAOA can approach the Parisi ground-state energy of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass, but the mechanism—how the algorithm exploits the fractured low-energy landscape—remains unclear. Understanding this could distinguish QAOA from classical structure-exploiting heuristics and thermal annealing.
AI.method: The QAOA distribution is analyzed as a statistical-physics object in the thermodynamic limit. Two independent bitstrings are drawn from the same instance and coupled via their macroscopic similarity (overlap), and the resulting geometry—typical-sample overlap, low-energy-tail behavior, and dependence on circuit depth p—is characterized.
AI.result: Typical QAOA samples remain macroscopically uncorrelated, even though their sensitivity to the coupling increases with p. In contrast, the low-energy tail shows a much stronger tendency to overlap and exhibits a Parisi-like phase sharing the critical behavior of the thermal spin-glass transition. The onset of this organization moves toward the typical output as p grows, consistent with the typical/low-energy separation vanishing only as p→∞.
AI.conclusion: QAOA appears to reach the Parisi energy before Parisi geometry becomes typical, suggesting a route to optimization distinct from structure-exploiting classical algorithms and thermal sampling.

title: The Bapat-Sunder eigenvalue conjecture fails over the reals
comment: 7 pages. Originally submitted as submit/7962729 in August 2026; resubmitted following a successful appeal. Certificate data and exact verification code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21543697
summary: In 1986 Bapat and Sunder asked whether $\operatorname{per}(A)$ is the largest eigenvalue of $F_A=[a_{i,j}\operatorname{per}(A(i,j))]$ for every positive semidefinite Hermitian $A$, where $A(i,j)$ deletes row $i$ and column $j$. Drury disproved this over the complex field in 2018 and conjectured that the property holds for real positive semidefinite matrices. We disprove Drury's conjecture with a rank-$4$, $32\times32$ integer Gram matrix and an integer vector whose Rayleigh quotient exceeds $\operatorname{per}(A)$; verification uses integer arithmetic. Together, the two counterexamples resolve the Bapat-Sunder eigenvalue conjecture negatively over both fields. Counterexamples exist of every order $n\ge32$. As an application to quantum optics, the violation yields a $36$-mode orthogonal interferometer and a direction of relative arrival-time delays among $32$ photons with identical-variance Gaussian wave packets along which every sufficiently small nonzero delay increases the probability that all photons are detected within four designated output modes.

AI.tldr: The Bapat–Sunder conjecture that per(A) is the largest eigenvalue of F_A is disproved for real positive semidefinite matrices via a rank-4, 32×32 integer Gram matrix counterexample, resolving the question negatively over both real and complex fields.
AI.motivation: Bapat and Sunder (1986) asked whether the permanent of a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix A is the largest eigenvalue of the matrix F_A = [a_{i,j} per(A(i,j))]. Drury (2018) disproved this over the complex field and conjectured it holds for real positive semidefinite matrices. The paper aims to settle the remaining real case of this long-standing open problem.
AI.method: Construct an explicit counterexample: a rank-4, 32×32 integer Gram matrix A together with an integer vector whose Rayleigh quotient for F_A strictly exceeds per(A). All verification is carried out in exact integer arithmetic. The construction is shown to extend to all orders n ≥ 32.
AI.result: The Rayleigh quotient of the constructed vector exceeds per(A), so per(A) is not the largest eigenvalue of F_A. Combined with Drury's complex counterexample, this resolves the Bapat–Sunder eigenvalue conjecture negatively over both reals and complex numbers, with counterexamples existing for every n ≥ 32.
AI.conclusion: The Bapat–Sunder conjecture fails for real positive semidefinite matrices. As an application to quantum optics, the violation yields a 36-mode orthogonal interferometer and a direction of relative arrival-time delays among 32 photons with identical-variance Gaussian wave packets such that every sufficiently small nonzero delay increases the probability that all photons are detected in four designated output modes.

title: Quantum Annealing with a Quantum Neural Network: Width of Annealing Matters
summary: Quantum annealing is a promising quantum algorithm for dealing with computationally hard optimization problems. Currently available hardware can implement the algorithm for a significant class of Hamiltonian problems. However, its performance is especially limited in discontinuous quantum phase transitions, where the energy gap shrinks exponentially with system size. In this paper, we introduce an extension of quantum annealing to a quantum neural network and study its performance in a number of prototypical optimization problems. In particular, we observe that already a random quantum annealing network of width W = 2 can exponentially reduce the number of evolution layers or depth of the annealing process in the quantum search problem. By tuning the network parameters the search problem can be solved with exponentially small errors by a quantum perceptron of depth L = 1 and width W = 2. The findings show that width of a quantum annealing network is critical to enhance the success probability of the algorithm by providing a larger and learnable evolution space for the annealing process.

AI.tldr: Extends quantum annealing into a quantum neural network, showing that even a width-2 random network exponentially reduces annealing depth, and a trained depth-1, width-2 quantum perceptron solves the search problem with exponentially small error.
AI.motivation: Current quantum annealers handle many Hamiltonian problems but suffer exponentially shrinking energy gaps at discontinuous (first-order) quantum phase transitions, degrading performance with system size. The authors aim to overcome this gap-closing bottleneck by broadening the annealing process into a learnable, network-structured evolution.
AI.method: The authors generalize standard quantum annealing to a quantum neural network: the annealing evolution is decomposed into layers with a tunable width W (parallel qubit/parameter channels) and depth L, and network parameters are optimized. They benchmark this framework on prototypical optimization problems, notably quantum search, comparing random versus parameter-tuned networks across widths and depths.
AI.result: A random annealing network of width W = 2 already exponentially reduces the number of evolution layers (depth) required for quantum search. Tuning parameters allows a quantum perceptron with depth L = 1 and width W = 2 to solve the search problem with exponentially small error. Width is identified as the critical resource that enlarges the learnable evolution space and boosts success probability.
AI.conclusion: Network width, not depth alone, is key to enhancing annealing success probability by furnishing a larger learnable evolution space. Quantum neural annealing offers a viable route around gap-limited phase transitions, with even minimal width (W = 2) yielding exponential gains in the studied search setting.

title: Scrambling leads to entanglement cost in NLQC
summary: In a non-local quantum computation (NLQC), shared entanglement along with a single simultaneous round of quantum communication is used to implement a joint channel. NLQC has many applications, most of which benefit from an understanding of lower bounds on the entanglement needed to implement a given channel as an NLQC. However, the properties of a channel that lead to it having an entanglement cost in NLQC have remained unclear, with most lower bounds only applying to specially constructed examples. Here, we give a new lower bound technique for unitaries based on scrambling: we find that a unitary has zero entanglement cost if and only if it does not scramble. Further, we find that the tripartite mutual information, an entropic object that quantifies the degree of scrambling, provides a quantitative lower bound on entanglement cost in NLQC. This is the first known lower bound on entanglement cost for unitaries in NLQC which is faithful. Our results also relate scrambling and NLQC for the first time. Leveraging the faithful scrambling based bound, we then show that the controllable correlation, an earlier studied quantity, is also a faithful lower bound, resolving an earlier conjecture of Cleve and May.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a scrambling-based lower bound on the entanglement cost for implementing unitaries via non-local quantum computation (NLQC), showing that zero entanglement cost holds if and only if the unitary does not scramble, and that tripartite mutual information yields a faithful quantitative bound.
AI.motivation: NLQC has many applications that benefit from lower bounds on the entanglement required to implement a channel, but the channel properties governing entanglement cost were poorly understood, with most known lower bounds applying only to specially constructed examples.
AI.method: The authors develop a new lower-bound technique for unitaries based on the notion of scrambling, linking the presence of scrambling to nonzero entanglement cost, and use tripartite mutual information as an entropic measure that quantifies the degree of scrambling to bound entanglement cost. They then apply this faithful scrambling-based bound to analyze the controllable correlation quantity.
AI.result: A unitary has zero entanglement cost if and only if it does not scramble. The tripartite mutual information provides a quantitative and faithful lower bound on entanglement cost in NLQC—the first known faithful lower bound for unitaries. Using this bound, the controllable correlation is shown to also be a faithful lower bound, resolving a conjecture of Cleve and May.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes the first faithful lower bound on entanglement cost for unitaries in NLQC, connects scrambling and NLQC for the first time, and confirms the faithfullness of the controllable correlation as a lower bound, resolving an earlier conjecture.

title: Look Mum, No Hands! Quantum State Preparation without Time-Dependent Control
summary: How much can be prepared with a quantum system whose Hamiltonian cannot be modulated in time? Common intuition suggests that the answer is not much. Without a knob to turn during the evolution, a system seems confined to a fixed trajectory through its state space, while time-dependent control can steer it almost anywhere. We put this intuition to the test by studying autonomous control, i.e., state preparation with a time-invariant Hamiltonian, where the only freedom lies in the static coupling strengths and the evolution time. We characterize basic mathematical properties of the autonomously reachable set and introduce two criteria of unreachability: a certificate that is cheap to evaluate and rigorously excludes that a target state can be reached for any choice of control parameters, and a stronger criterion based on exhaustive numerical optimization. With these tools we estimate the probability that a typical state in Hilbert space is unreachable under randomly drawn control terms. The dimensionality of the reachable set turns out to be independent of the system, yet the fraction of Hilbert space lying close to it depends strongly on the choice of control Hamiltonians. Strikingly, for sufficiently random controls and long enough evolution times, almost every state can become approximately reachable, even with the fewest generators that permit full controllability with time-dependent couplings. Autonomous control can approach the expressivity of time-dependent control, at the cost of longer evolution times.

AI.tldr: Autonomous control with a time-invariant Hamiltonian can nearly match time-dependent control's expressivity, though at the cost of longer evolution times.
AI.motivation: Common intuition holds that without a time-varying knob, a quantum system is confined to a fixed trajectory and can prepare little. The authors test whether this intuition is correct by studying state preparation with time-invariant Hamiltonians.
AI.method: They formalize autonomous control, where only static coupling strengths and evolution time are free. They characterize mathematical properties of the autonomously reachable set and introduce two unreachability criteria: a cheap-to-evaluate certificate that rigorously excludes reachability for any control parameters, and a stronger exhaustive numerical-optimization criterion. Using these, they estimate the probability that typical Hilbert-space states are unreachable under randomly drawn control terms.
AI.result: The dimension of the reachable set is system-independent, but the fraction of Hilbert space near it depends strongly on the control Hamiltonians. For sufficiently random controls and long evolution times, almost every state becomes approximately reachable—even with the minimal number of generators allowing full controllability under time-dependent couplings.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous control can approach the expressivity of time-dependent control, trading shorter control sequences for longer evolution times.

title: Collective Superconducting-Qubit Interfaces for Microwave-to-Optical Quantum Transduction
summary: Microwave-to-optical quantum transduction is essential for connecting superconducting quantum processors through optical networks. Mechanically mediated transducers, however, remain limited by weak electromechanical coupling, dissipation, and added noise. In this work, we study a transducer in which an ensemble of superconducting qubits couples collectively to a shared optomechanical resonator. For weak signals, we show that ensemble size and optical pump strength together set the conversion efficiency, added noise, and bandwidth, with pump heating limiting efficiency to a finite optimal pump strength. Near half excitation, the collective coupling grows nearly linearly with ensemble size, accelerating transfer of an excitation into the mechanics. We show that this speedup is offset by relaxation of the additional excited qubits, so the single-qubit coupling and lifetime still set the coherence requirement. Transferring exactly one excitation also requires an anharmonic mechanical mode, which an auxiliary qubit coupled to the mechanics can provide. In a lossless prescribed-Kerr benchmark with four qubits and $g_{\rm sm}/(2π)=3.81\,\mathrm{kHz}$, a mechanical anharmonicity of $100\,\mathrm{kHz}$ raises the final joint single-photon intracavity target probability from $19.6\%$ to $99.7\%$. Finally, we quantify the effects of decoherence, disorder, residual qubit--qubit interactions, and pump-induced qubit noise, finding that pair-dependent interactions reduce the optical retrieval efficiency from 58\% to 35\%. These results establish the coherence and selectivity requirements for collective quantum transduction.

AI.tldr: Collective coupling of a superconducting-qubit ensemble to a shared optomechanical resonator sets transduction efficiency, noise, and bandwidth by ensemble size and pump strength, but pump heating caps efficiency at a finite optimal pump; near half excitation the speedup from collective coupling is offset by relaxation of extra excited qubits, and faithful single-excitation transfer requires mechanical anharmonicity.
AI.motivation: Microwave-to-optical transduction is needed to link superconducting quantum processors via optical networks, but mechanically mediated transducers are limited by weak electromechanical coupling, dissipation, and added noise. The authors ask whether collectively coupling many qubits to one optomechanical resonator can overcome these limits, and what coherence and selectivity requirements such a scheme imposes.
AI.method: Analytical modeling of an ensemble of superconducting qubits coupled collectively to a shared optomechanical resonator. For weak signals, efficiency, added noise, and bandwidth are derived as functions of ensemble size and optical pump strength, including pump-induced heating. Near half excitation, the scaling of collective coupling with ensemble size and the transfer rate of an excitation into the mechanics are analyzed, accounting for relaxation of excited qubits. An auxiliary qubit coupled to the mechanics supplies the mechanical anharmonicity needed for single-excitation transfer, benchmarked against a lossless prescribed-Kerr model (four qubits, g_sm/2π = 3.81 kHz, mechanical anharmonicity 100 kHz). Decoherence, disorder, residual qubit–qubit interactions, and pump-induced qubit noise are quantified numerically.
AI.result: For weak signals, ensemble size and pump strength jointly determine efficiency, added noise, and bandwidth, with pump heating limiting efficiency to a finite optimal pump strength. Near half excitation the collective coupling grows nearly linearly with ensemble size, but the resulting speedup is offset by relaxation of the additional excited qubits, so single-qubit coupling and lifetime still govern the coherence requirement. In the lossless prescribed-Kerr benchmark, 100 kHz mechanical anharmonicity raises the final joint single-photon intracavity target probability from 19.6% to 99.7%. Pair-dependent residual qubit–qubit interactions reduce optical retrieval efficiency from 58% to 35%.
AI.conclusion: Collective qubit–optomechanics does not relax the underlying coherence requirement—single-qubit coupling and lifetime remain the limiting factors—and faithful single-excitation transduction additionally demands mechanical anharmonicity (selectivity). Residual pair-dependent qubit interactions are a dominant decoherence channel for retrieval. These results delineate the coherence and selectivity requirements for collective quantum transduction.

title: Optimal Joint Bounds for Sparse Ground-State Energy Estimation and Ground-State Preparation
summary: Ground-state energy estimation (GSEE) and ground-state preparation (GSP) are fundamental problems in quantum computing. Given a Hamiltonian $H$ with $\|H\|\le1$ and a guiding state $|ψ\rangle$ with overlap at least $γ>0$ with the ground space of $H$, the goal in GSEE is to estimate the ground-state energy of $H$ to additive error $δ$ with failure probability at most $\varepsilon$, while in GSP it is to prepare a state with ground-space weight at least $1-\varepsilon$, given a gap lower bound $Δ$. Their costs are measured by quantum query complexity, i.e., the number of oracle calls needed to access $H$. Recent work proved optimal bounds $Θ(\log(1/\varepsilon)/(γδ))$ for GSEE and $Θ(\log(1/\varepsilon)/(γΔ))$ for GSP in the time-evolution and block-encoding models. However, these models do not directly account for the sparsity of $H$, measured by the maximum number $s$ of nonzero entries in any row or column. In the sparse-access model, oracles instead return the locations and values of these entries. This introduces the additional parameter $s$, and it remained open how query complexity depends jointly on $s$, $γ$, $δ$ or $Δ$, and $\varepsilon$. We resolve this by proving sparse-query lower bounds $Ω(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(γδ))$ for GSEE and $Ω(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(γΔ))$ for GSP, even for stoquastic Hamiltonians. We also show that these constructions recover the earlier time-evolution and block-encoding lower-bound scalings. We then give matching upper-bound algorithms in the reversible in-place sparse-location model. Thus, we obtain $Θ(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(γδ))$ for GSEE and $Θ(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(γΔ))$ for GSP, showing that $\sqrt{s}$ is necessary and sufficient and completing the joint dependence on all problem parameters.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves the sparse-access quantum query complexity of ground-state energy estimation (GSEE) and ground-state preparation (GSP), proving tight Θ(√s·log(1/ε)/(γδ)) and Θ(√s·log(1/ε)/(γΔ)) bounds that complete the joint dependence on sparsity s, overlap γ, precision δ or gap Δ, and failure probability ε.
AI.motivation: Prior optimal bounds for GSEE and GSP were established in the time-evolution and block-encoding models, but these models do not directly capture the sparsity s of the Hamiltonian. In the sparse-access model, where oracles return entry locations and values, the dependence of query complexity on s jointly with γ, δ (or Δ), and ε remained open.
AI.method: The authors prove sparse-query lower bounds of Ω(√s·log(1/ε)/(γδ)) for GSEE and Ω(√s·log(1/ε)/(γΔ)) for GSP, holding even for stoquastic Hamiltonians, and show these constructions recover the earlier time-evolution and block-encoding scalings. They then construct matching upper-bound algorithms in the reversible in-place sparse-location model.
AI.result: Tight query complexities Θ(√s·log(1/ε)/(γδ)) for GSEE and Θ(√s·log(1/ε)/(γΔ)) for GSP are obtained, demonstrating that the √s factor is both necessary and sufficient and completing the joint dependence on all problem parameters.
AI.conclusion: Sparsity contributes a √s factor to the quantum query complexity of GSEE and GSP, and the matching lower and upper bounds yield optimal algorithms that fully characterize the dependence on s, γ, δ or Δ, and ε.

title: Symmetry classification of hyperfine rovibrational molecular phase space
summary: Symmetry-based structures have advanced molecular spectroscopy and quantum information science, yet connections between these fields remain largely unexplored. We construct a phase space theory of a molecule by jointly treating rotational, vibrational, and nuclear-spin degrees of freedom as the quotient of orientations and normal coordinates by the molecule's point group. The various combinations of how these three degrees of freedom transform under symmetries organize a molecule's states into molecular species, and we show that each species is defined by a particular absolutely maximally entangled (AME) carrier state, or, for 45 species, by a two-dimensional space of them. Up to local unitaries and the order of the sectors, molecular species realize 21 AME states across 75 point groups: a product state, four maximally entangled pairs, and 16 genuinely tripartite states. A Fourier transform on the quotient relates orientation and angular-momentum descriptions while preserving these carrier states. We propose an example experimental protocol for preparing and driving symmetry-adapted bend states of $\mathrm{CaOCH_3}$.

AI.tldr: The authors build a phase-space theory of molecules that treats rotational, vibrational, and nuclear-spin degrees of freedom as a quotient of orientations and normal coordinates by the molecular point group, showing that each "molecular species" corresponds to an absolutely maximally entangled (AME) carrier state, thereby linking molecular spectroscopy to quantum information.
AI.motivation: Molecular spectroscopy and quantum information science have both benefited from symmetry-based structures, but connections between the two fields remain largely unexplored. The authors aim to bridge them.
AI.method: They construct a phase-space theory by jointly treating rotational, vibrational, and nuclear-spin degrees of freedom as the quotient of orientations and normal coordinates by the molecule's point group. The transformation properties of the three degrees of freedom under symmetries organize states into molecular species, each defined by a particular AME carrier state (or, for 45 species, a two-dimensional space of them). A Fourier transform on the quotient links orientation and angular-momentum descriptions. An experimental protocol is proposed for preparing and driving symmetry-adapted bend states of CaOCH3.
AI.result: Up to local unitaries and the order of sectors, molecular species realize 21 AME states across 75 point groups: a product state, four maximally entangled pairs, and 16 genuinely tripartite states. The Fourier transform preserves these carrier states. A concrete protocol is proposed for CaOCH3.
AI.conclusion: Molecular species are in one-to-one correspondence with AME carrier states, establishing a rigorous link between molecular symmetry, spectroscopy, and quantum entanglement, and offering experimentally realizable symmetry-adapted states.

title: Qubit-qumode simulation of molecular torsion in photoisomerization
summary: Photochemical reactions driven by large nuclear motion, such as the photoisomerization of retinal, depend strongly on both the global anharmonic forces of the potential and the periodic topology of molecular torsion. In this work, we develop a hybrid discrete (qubit) and continuous variable (qumode) quantum simulation framework for photochemical reactions that maps electronic states to qubits, vibrations to qumodes, and the periodic torsion to a compact qumode encoding. Applying this approach to the two-mode Hahn-Stock and three-mode PSB3 models of retinal photoisomerization, we compare i) local vibronic approximations, ii) the full trigonometric potential on the noncompact line, and iii) the same potential on the compact circle, which matches the molecular torsion topology. We numerically show that the topological description can significantly alter relevant observables. We realize the compact torsion via both a wrapped Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) encoding and a two-qumode circle encoding and introduce two methods that reduce the hardware resources of both encodings. Spreading an encoded coordinate over several qumodes lowers the average occupation number of each mode, and adding counterterms to the Hamiltonian reduces the required squeezing amount. We expect that these methods make percent-level simulations of the considered molecules promising targets for hybrid qubit-qumode hardware. For more complex molecules, each additional nuclear coordinate is represented directly as a single qumode or an encoded register using the same native operations, so the framework extends naturally to larger systems.

AI.tldr: The authors develop a hybrid qubit-qumode quantum simulation framework for photochemical reactions with large nuclear motion, mapping electronic states to qubits, vibrations to qumodes, and periodic torsion to a compact qumode encoding, and show for retinal photoisomerization models that respecting torsion topology changes observables and can be made hardware-efficient.
AI.motivation: Photochemical reactions like retinal photoisomerization are driven by large nuclear motion and depend both on global anharmonic forces and on the periodic (circular) topology of molecular torsion. Existing simulations often ignore this topology or are resource-intensive, so a quantum framework that faithfully encodes periodic torsion while remaining hardware-feasible is needed.
AI.method: A hybrid discrete-continuous quantum simulation framework: electronic states mapped to qubits, vibrations to qumodes, and periodic torsion to a compact qumode encoding. Applied to the two-mode Hahn-Stock and three-mode PSB3 retinal models, comparing (i) local vibronic approximations, (ii) the full trigonometric potential on the noncompact line, and (iii) the same potential on the compact circle matching torsion topology. Compact torsion is realized via a wrapped GKP encoding and a two-qumode circle encoding, with two resource-reduction methods: spreading an encoded coordinate over several qumodes to lower average occupation, and adding counterterms to reduce required squeezing.
AI.result: Numerical results show that the topological (compact-circle) description can significantly alter relevant observables relative to vibronic approximations and the noncompact-line treatment. The resource-reduction methods lower per-mode average occupation (via multi-qumode spreading) and required squeezing (via counterterms) for both encodings.
AI.conclusion: Encoding molecular torsion topology matters for accurate photochemical observables, and the proposed resource-reduction techniques make percent-level simulations of the considered molecules promising targets for hybrid qubit-qumode hardware. The framework extends naturally to larger systems, with each additional nuclear coordinate represented as a single qumode or an encoded register using the same native operations.

title: Experimental constraints on gauge hidden-variable models in Bell tests
summary: Quantum mechanics assigns identical statistics to measurement procedures that realize the same final effect, irrespective of the transformations used to reach it. We test this operational equivalence with polarization-entangled photons by implementing one of Bob's analyzer settings either directly or through closed wave-plate trajectories $C_γ$ calibrated to produce the same measurement operator. Motivated by ontological descriptions in which a hidden frame is transported between contexts, we formulate a local path-memory model and derive the mixed-context bound $|S_γ^{\rm mix}|\leq 2+2p_γ$. The quantity $p_γ$ is a coupling-dependent counterfactual mismatch probability: it bounds a contextual Bell expression, but neither generates nor predicts the quantum Bell correlation. We therefore test path memory through the observable difference between direct and looped implementations, using a no-signaling phenomenological response in which a hidden holonomy $δ_γ$ modifies one correlation term in $S_γ^{\rm mix}$. The direct reference violates the Bell inequality, while the looped mixed-context curves remain indistinguishable from it within the experimental precision. Our results support the quantum equivalence of calibrated measurement implementations and constrain path-sensitive hidden-variable extensions that predict an observable memory of the optical history.

AI.tldr: The authors experimentally test whether quantum measurement statistics are invariant under the transformations used to realize a measurement, by comparing direct versus looped (closed wave-plate trajectory) implementations of Bob's analyzer setting on polarization-entangled photons; the looped curves are indistinguishable from the direct Bell-violating reference within precision, supporting operational equivalence and constraining path-sensitive hidden-variable models.
AI.motivation: Quantum mechanics assigns identical statistics to measurement procedures yielding the same final effect, regardless of the transformations used. Ontological/hidden-variable descriptions that transport a hidden frame between contexts predict a path-dependent (memory) signature, motivating an experimental test of this operational equivalence using calibrated implementations that should produce the same measurement operator.
AI.method: A polarization-entangled photon experiment implements one of Bob's analyzer settings either directly or via closed wave-plate trajectories C_γ calibrated to yield the same measurement operator. A local path-memory model yields the mixed-context bound |S_γ^mix| ≤ 2 + 2p_γ, where p_γ is a coupling-dependent counterfactual mismatch probability bounding a contextual Bell expression. Path memory is tested via a no-signaling phenomenological response in which a hidden holonomy δ_γ modifies one correlation term in S_γ^mix, comparing direct and looped mixed-context curves.
AI.result: The direct reference violates the Bell inequality, while the looped mixed-context curves remain indistinguishable from it within experimental precision. The hidden holonomy δ_γ does not produce an observable modification of the correlation term.
AI.conclusion: The results support the quantum equivalence of calibrated measurement implementations and constrain path-sensitive hidden-variable extensions that predict an observable memory of the optical history.

title: High-rate low-distance color codes
summary: Experimental implementations of two-dimensional color codes encoding a single logical qubit have surpassed the fidelity of physical qubits. A natural next step is to investigate higher-rate codes that encode multiple logical qubits. Here we propose small, high-rate 2D color codes for this purpose. We design distance-$3$ codes with encoding rates up to $1/3$ and distance-$4$ codes with encoding rates up to $1/4$. We prove that these rates are optimal for color codes with only color boundaries on surfaces with non-negative Euler characteristic. We benchmark the codes by simulating Steane-style error correction with real-time feedback and no post-selection in a linear trapped-ion chain model with all-to-all connectivity. The two best-performing codes have parameters $[[20,4,4]]$ and $[[16,4,4]]$ and achieve break-even at two-qubit gate infidelities of $0.22\%$ and $0.26\%$, respectively. These results match the performance of Shor-style error correction with bivariate bicycle codes that use weight-$5$ measurements.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes small high-rate 2D color codes for encoding multiple logical qubits, proves rate optimality for color-boundary color codes, and benchmarks Steane-style error correction on trapped-ion hardware, showing break-even at low gate infidelities.
AI.motivation: Two-dimensional color codes encoding a single logical qubit have already exceeded physical qubit fidelity, motivating the search for higher-rate codes that encode multiple logical qubits to scale quantum error correction efficiently.
AI.method: The authors design distance-3 codes with encoding rates up to 1/3 and distance-4 codes with rates up to 1/4, prove these rates are optimal for color codes with only color boundaries on surfaces with non-negative Euler characteristic, and benchmark by simulating Steane-style error correction with real-time feedback and no post-selection in a linear trapped-ion chain model with all-to-all connectivity.
AI.result: The two best-performing codes, [[20,4,4]] and [[16,4,4]], achieve break-even at two-qubit gate infidelities of 0.22% and 0.26%, respectively, matching the performance of Shor-style error correction with bivariate bicycle codes using weight-5 measurements.
AI.conclusion: Small high-rate 2D color codes offer a competitive, experimentally realistic route to multi-logical-qubit quantum error correction, with proven-optimal rates and performance on par with more complex bivariate bicycle code schemes.

title: Compute Before You Digitize: ADC-less Mixed-Signal Processing for Scalable Cryogenic Qubit Readout
summary: We introduce DIRAC, an ADC-less in-cryostat qubit readout architecture that uses analog computing to redraw the analog-digital boundary. Directly operating on the front-end's analog output, passive complex mixers perform the equivalent of digital demodulation, ping-pong active-RC integrators average their outputs into down-sampled per-qubit traces, and a time-domain stage digitizes them, eliminating Nyquist-rate ADCs. A TX-RX co-design derives the mixers' local oscillators from the readout transmitter's baseband rather than per-tone PLLs. A per-line calibration flow trains the matched filter jointly with the neural network, improving fidelity and enabling low-bit-width, low-voltage digital processing. Designed in 22 nm FD-SOI and evaluated at 4 K on 1.12M experimental shots, DIRAC matches the fidelity of a floating-point (FP32) digital pipeline for readout windows down to 750 ns, at 31.6$\times$ and 238$\times$ lower energy than the fixed-point (FxP) and FP32 pipelines. It cuts the total 4 K power per physical qubit by 50.4% and 68.6% relative to FxP and room-temperature flex cables, respectively. At a fixed logical-qubit count and 4 K budget, this yields, against FxP, a code distance larger by 2 to 6 and a 1.6-7.3$\times$ (Willow) and 4.9-204$\times$ (SI1000, $p = 10^{-3}$) lower logical error rate.

AI.tldr: DIRAC is an ADC-less, in-cryostat qubit readout architecture that performs analog demodulation, integration, and down-sampling before digitizing short time-domain traces, matching FP32 fidelity while cutting readout energy by 31.6×/238× versus fixed-point/FP32 pipelines.
AI.motivation: Conventional qubit readout relies on Nyquist-rate ADCs and power-hungry digital demodulation pipelines at 4 K, which dominate cryostat thermal budget and limit scalability of superconducting quantum systems.
AI.method: The architecture redraws the analog-digital boundary using analog computing: passive complex mixers mimic digital demodulation on front-end analog output, ping-pong active-RC integrators average and down-sample into per-qubit traces, and a time-domain stage digitizes the reduced traces, eliminating Nyquist-rate ADCs. A TX-RX co-design derives mixer LOs from the transmitter baseband instead of per-tone PLLs. A per-line calibration jointly trains the matched filter with a neural network, enabling low-bit-width, low-voltage digital processing. Implemented in 22 nm FD-SOI, evaluated at 4 K on 1.12M experimental shots.
AI.result: DIRAC matches FP32 digital pipeline fidelity for readout windows down to 750 ns, with 31.6× and 238× lower energy than fixed-point and FP32 pipelines. It reduces total 4 K power per physical qubit by 50.4% and 68.6% versus FxP and room-temperature flex cables. At fixed logical-qubit count and 4 K budget, it enables 2-6 larger code distance and 1.6-7.3× (Willow) and 4.9-204× (SI1000, p=10⁻³) lower logical error rate versus FxP.
AI.conclusion: Analog-computing-based in-cryostat readout that eliminates Nyquist-rate ADCs is a viable path to dramatically lower 4 K power and energy while preserving high fidelity, translating into substantial improvements in code distance and logical error rate for scalable quantum error correction.

title: Quantum Monge-Kantorovich optimal transport in spacetime through spatiotemporal Kirkwood-Dirac distributions and spatiotemporal states
summary: Monge-Kantorovich optimal transport is a mathematical framework that determines the most efficient way to transform one probability distribution into another while minimizing a given cost function. Its central constructions include the Wasserstein distances, which quantify the space of probability distributions, and dual formulations that link to convex analysis. Its standard quantum generalization replaces probability distributions with density operators and cost function with positive semidefinite cost operator, which should be regarded as spatial quantum optimal transport. In this work, we propose the quantum optimal transport problem in spacetime through the spatiotemporal phase-space Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability distribution and spatiotemporal states and through spatiotemporal state. We show that the two formalisms are equivalent and related via spatiotemporal operator frames. In the Kirkwood-Dirac phase-space formalism, the spatiotemporal distribution and the cost function are complex-valued, and the spatiotemporal couplings are Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability distributions that yield the correct marginals for the local states. In the spatiotemporal state formalism, the cost operators are generally non-Hermitian, and the spatiotemporal couplings are generally non-Hermitian and yield the correct reduced local states. The Margenau-Hill phase-space distribution gives rise to a real-valued optimal transport in spatiotemporal phase space; in the spatiotemporal state formalism, this corresponds to a Hermitian spatiotemporal coupling state. We give a rigorous definitions and a careful discussion of its duality. We also introduce a spatiotemporal quantum Wasserstein metric based on a metric in spatiotemporal phase spaces and show that it satisfies the metric axioms.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates quantum optimal transport in spacetime using spatiotemporal Kirkwood-Dirac (KD) quasiprobability distributions and spatiotemporal states, shows the two formalisms are equivalent via spatiotemporal operator frames, develops duality, and introduces a metric-axiom-satisfying spatiotemporal quantum Wasserstein distance.
AI.motivation: Standard quantum optimal transport is spatial, replacing distributions with density operators and costs with positive semidefinite operators. The paper aims to extend optimal transport to the spacetime setting, where quantum states live across time and space.
AI.method: Two equivalent formalisms: (1) a spatiotemporal phase-space approach via Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability distributions with complex-valued distributions/costs and KD couplings yielding correct local marginals; (2) a spatiotemporal state approach with generally non-Hermitian cost operators and non-Hermitian couplings giving correct reduced local states. Equivalence is established through spatiotemporal operator frames. The Margenau-Hill distribution yields a real-valued transport corresponding to Hermitian coupling states. Rigorous definitions and duality are provided.
AI.result: The two formalisms are proven equivalent and linked by operator frames. A spatiotemporal quantum Wasserstein metric based on a phase-space metric is introduced and shown to satisfy the metric axioms.
AI.conclusion: Quantum optimal transport can be consistently generalized from space to spacetime, unifying phase-space and state-based formulations, with a well-defined dual theory and a valid Wasserstein metric.

title: QCCDCert: Formally Verified Compilation for QCCD Co-Design
summary: Quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) architectures enable scalable trapped-ion quantum computing by dynamically shuttling ions between specialized processing and storage zones. A QCCD can be built with many trap sizes and layouts. Comparing them requires compiling every program under each design's transport, capacity and control constraints, and trusting the target code of each compilation. We present a co-design framework built on one Lean-verified compiler. The hardware description and its operating rules are compiler inputs, so a single theorem covers every candidate design: the target code of every compilation preserves its program's behavior and obeys the hardware rules. Across 75 benchmark programs of 11 to 130 qubits, the best design found takes 66% less modeled execution time on average than the worst design of equal capacity. An AI agent that proposes devices based on our compiler's checked results beats the fastest of these designs on 71 of 75 programs. Our verified compiler provably avoids the 11 defects that we report in three previous compilers. It scales to hundreds of qubits, compiling 512-qubit programs for a 38-trap device in 1 to 29 minutes.

AI.tldr: A co-design framework built on a single Lean-verified compiler lets one theorem cover all QCCD trap designs; the best of 75 tested designs is 66% faster on average than the worst, and an AI agent beats the fastest designs on 71/75 programs, while the compiler provably avoids 11 defects found in three prior compilers.
AI.motivation: QCCD architectures can be built with many trap sizes and layouts, but comparing them requires compiling every program under each design's transport, capacity, and control constraints and trusting the correctness of each compilation. This uniformity and trust burden motivates a verified, reusable compilation approach.
AI.method: The hardware description and its operating rules are made compiler inputs to one Lean-verified compiler. This yields a single theorem covering every candidate design: the target code of every compilation preserves program behavior and obeys the hardware rules. The framework is evaluated on 75 benchmark programs of 11 to 130 qubits, and an AI agent proposes devices based on the compiler's checked results.
AI.result: The best design found requires 66% less modeled execution time on average than the worst design of equal capacity. The AI agent beats the fastest of these designs on 71 of 75 programs. The verified compiler provably avoids 11 defects reported in three previous compilers and scales to hundreds of qubits, compiling 512-qubit programs for a 38-trap device in 1 to 29 minutes.
AI.conclusion: A single formally verified compiler can serve as the foundation for QCCD hardware co-design, giving design-wide correctness guarantees, meaningful performance differentiation among layouts, and scalability to large qubit counts.

title: Degree and normalization frontiers for bounded QSVT inversion
comment: 22 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. The Supplemental Material (82 pages) and a public verification set are ancillary files
summary: Quantum singular value transformation (QSVT) implements matrix inversion using bounded polynomials. Increasing polynomial degree can improve normalization and reduce amplified query cost, with savings that depend on the error criterion. However, existing bounded methods either fix the normalization or work far below the condition numbers of fault-tolerant resource estimates. We therefore analyze this trade-off for absolute reciprocal error, which controls inverse-operator accuracy, and for residual error, which suffices for normalized linear solves. For absolute reciprocal error, we establish a scaling limit to a constrained least-norm problem for entire functions and characterize its high-accuracy frontier using elliptic integrals. Constructions built from near-optimal limiting functions achieve certified query-cost savings over the rescaled minimax baseline of at least 11.8 percent at condition number ten thousand with error one millionth, and at least 22.8 percent at one million with error one ten-billionth. A simpler two-term rule also has certified savings, and its phase factors at condition number ten thousand pass numerical checks at selected points. For residual error, a sparse Chebyshev construction achieves certified savings over the residual-minimax baseline of at least 8.7 percent at condition number ten thousand with normalized-state error at most one hundred-millionth, and at least 13.1 percent at one million with error at most one ten-billionth. These results quantify the saving that a joint choice of degree and normalization gives beyond the minimax baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the degree-normalization trade-off in QSVT-based matrix inversion under two error criteria and provides certified query-cost savings over rescaled minimax baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing bounded-polynomial QSVT methods either fix the normalization or operate far below the condition numbers used in fault-tolerant resource estimates, leaving the degree-normalization trade-off for relevant error criteria unquantified.
AI.method: The authors analyze absolute reciprocal error (inverse-operator accuracy) and residual error (normalized linear solves). For absolute reciprocal error they derive a scaling limit to a constrained least-norm problem over entire functions and characterize its high-accuracy frontier via elliptic integrals; constructions from near-optimal limiting functions and a simpler two-term rule are proposed. For residual error, a sparse Chebyshev construction is introduced.
AI.result: Absolute reciprocal error: certified query-cost savings of at least 11.8% at condition number 10^4 with error 10^-6 and at least 22.8% at 10^6 with error 10^-10 versus the rescaled minimax baseline; the two-term rule also certifies savings and its phase factors pass numerical checks at selected points at condition number 10^4. Residual error: certified savings of at least 8.7% at condition number 10^4 with normalized-state error 10^-8 and at least 13.1% at 10^6 with error 10^-10 versus the residual-minimax baseline.
AI.conclusion: Jointly choosing polynomial degree and normalization yields quantifiable query-cost savings beyond standard minimax baselines, with the magnitude depending on the error criterion and condition number.

title: Singlet flags: using native entanglement to restore the circuit distance of shuttled qLDPC codes in silicon
summary: High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes could greatly reduce the qubit count of silicon spin-qubit processors, but their checks are long-range and of high weight. Shuttling one ancilla electron through every data qubit of a check measures such checks, but a single fault on the ancilla spreads to several data qubits, so the circuit distance can fall far below the code distance. We make the mobile ancilla one half of a spin singlet whose partner stays at home; a Bell measurement at the end of the check provides a flag for isolated bit-flip faults acquired during the walk. Using new distance-6 codes with check weights 8, 10 and 12, and exact circuit distances from two independent solvers, we show that without the flag the circuit distance falls as check weight grows, to 1 at weight 12, while with it every weight-8 and weight-10 code recovers circuit distance 5 or 6 and corrects as many faults as the code. For codes of distance 8 to 12 the flag raises the circuit distance by one to four, and the Gross code [[144,12,12]] rises from 7 to 10. In circuit-level simulations of shuttled spin qubits, the flag lowers logical error rates by typically 2-10x across bivariate-bicycle, circulant-permutation and surface codes, and the gain survives percent-level flag-readout errors and bit flips on the singlet's electrons. BP+OSD does not reach the full circuit distance of the flagged circuits, so our flagged logical error rates are upper bounds: decoding the same shots exactly raises the flag's gain on the distance-6 codes from 3-7x to 5-17x for the weight-6 BB code, and from 1-12x to 5-90x at weights 8 and 10 for p >= 2.5x10^-4.

AI.tldr: A spin-singlet mobile ancilla provides a Bell-measurement flag that suppresses fault spreading in shuttled-ancilla syndrome extraction of high-weight qLDPC checks, restoring circuit distance (e.g., 5-6 at weights 8-10, never 1) and cutting logical error rates 2-10x.
AI.motivation: High-rate qLDPC codes reduce qubit overhead for silicon spin qubits but need long-range, high-weight checks. Shuttling a single ancilla electron through the data qubits measures such checks, yet a single ancilla fault spreads to multiple data qubits, collapsing the circuit distance well below the code distance.
AI.method: The mobile ancilla is entangled as one half of a spin singlet whose partner remains stationary; a Bell measurement at the end of the check acts as a flag detecting isolated bit-flip faults incurred during the walk. The authors construct distance-6 codes with check weights 8, 10, 12 and compute exact circuit distances with two independent solvers, then run circuit-level simulations of shuttled spin qubits with BP+OSD decoding on bivariate-bicycle, circulant-permutation, and surface codes.
AI.result: Without the flag, circuit distance degrades with check weight, dropping to 1 at weight 12; with it, all weight-8 and weight-10 codes recover circuit distance 5 or 6 and correct as many faults as the code. For distance-8 to 12 codes the flag raises circuit distance by 1-4; Gross code [[144,12,12]] rises from 7 to 10. Flagged circuits show 2-10x lower logical error rates, robust to percent-level flag-readout errors and bit flips on the singlet electrons. Exact decoding of the same shots raises gains to 5-17x (weight-6 BB) and 5-90x at weights 8-10 for p >= 2.5x10^-4.
AI.conclusion: Bell-pair flagging of a shuttled ancilla is an effective, hardware-compatible remedy for fault spreading in high-weight qLDPC checks on spin qubits, restoring circuit distance and yielding substantial logical-error-rate reductions; since BP+OSD does not attain full circuit distance, the reported rates are upper bounds and true gains are larger.

title: Fe$^{2+}$:forsterite Qubit System
comment: Keywords: Qubit, forsterite, quantum gates, Fe$^{2+}$, zero-field splitting (ZFS), two-level system
summary: Quantum Computing uses quantum mechanical phenomena, such as superposition and entanglement of quantum bits (qubits), to represent and manipulate information in multidimensional state spaces. This approach allows complex mathematical functions to be executed simultaneously rather than sequentially, making them much more efficient than classical computers. However, current quantum computers suffer from quantum decoherence, where small changes to their environment, such as thermal fluctuations and vibrations, affect the systems' fragile states. The goal of this study is to discuss the functionality of a proposed Fe$^{2+}$:forsterite qubit system by solving the unitary time-evolution of a quantum state vector for the system's Hamiltonian, using known axial and traverse anisotropy terms at temperatures up to 10 K. The system can effectively transfer population between its two lowest states at rates predicted by the Rabi half-period, with 99.9% fidelity. Additionally, it can hold the population at a desired state without docohering. The results remained consistent for temperatures up to 10 K, meaning, unlike many common qubit systems, the proposed qubit system could function without a dilution fridge and is not fragile to thermal noise.

AI.tldr: A Fe²⁺:forsterite qubit system is analyzed via unitary time-evolution of its Hamiltonian; it achieves 99.9% population transfer fidelity and coherent state-holding at temperatures up to 10 K, suggesting operation without a dilution fridge.
AI.motivation: Quantum computers exploit superposition and entanglement for parallel evaluation of complex functions, but quantum decoherence from thermal fluctuations and vibrations degrades fragile qubit states. The study aims to demonstrate that a Fe²⁺:forsterite qubit can resist such thermal noise.
AI.method: The unitary time-evolution of a quantum state vector is solved for the system's Hamiltonian, incorporating known axial and transverse anisotropy terms at temperatures up to 10 K.
AI.result: The system transfers population between its two lowest states at rates matching the Rabi half-period, with 99.9% fidelity, and can hold population in a desired state without decohering. Results are consistent up to 10 K.
AI.conclusion: Unlike many common qubit systems, the proposed Fe²⁺:forsterite qubit could function without a dilution fridge and is not fragile to thermal noise.

title: Spectral Disks for Quantum Markov Generators
summary: Spectral bounds for Markov generators require a choice of time scale. In quantum dynamics, a rate read off from a jump representation, the escape rate from a pure state and the smallest spectral disk need not agree. We prove that the spectrum of every GKLS generator written without a Hamiltonian lies in a disk tangent to the imaginary axis, with radius given by the norm of the operator $Φ^\dagger(I)$ built from the jump map $Φ$. This settles the first two scaling conjectures of "Corralling spectra of generators of time-continuous Markov evolution (both classical and quantum)", J. Phys. A: Math. Theor. {59}, 175202 (2026). The third, escape-rate conjecture fails for a qutrit with a single normal jump. Nevertheless, twice the escape rate bounds every decay rate of any positive trace-preserving semigroup For GKLS generators with vanishing canonical Hamiltonian, four times the escape rate always supplies a spectral disk, and the factor four is optimal uniformly in dimension. We compare these bounds with classical Cassini ovals and thermodynamic ellipses, explain the obstacles to their quantum extensions, and formulate optimization over completely positive jump-map representations as a semidefinite program.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that the spectrum of any GKLS generator without a Hamiltonian lies in a disk tangent to the imaginary axis with radius ||Φ†(I)||, resolving two scaling conjectures (and refuting the third), and shows that four times the escape rate gives an optimal spectral disk bound.
AI.motivation: Spectral bounds for Markov generators depend on the choice of time scale: the rate read off from a jump representation, the escape rate from a pure state, and the smallest spectral disk need not coincide. The authors aim to settle scaling conjectures from a prior work on corralling spectra of GKLS generators.
AI.method: They analyze GKLS generators written without a Hamiltonian, characterizing the spectrum via the jump map Φ and the operator Φ†(I). They compare resulting bounds with classical Cassini ovals and thermodynamic ellipses, and formulate optimization over completely positive jump-map representations as a semidefinite program.
AI.result: The spectrum of every Hamiltonian-free GKLS generator lies in a disk tangent to the imaginary axis with radius ||Φ†(I)||, settling the first two scaling conjectures. The third (escape-rate) conjecture fails for a qutrit with a single normal jump. Twice the escape rate bounds every decay rate of any positive trace-preserving semigroup; for vanishing canonical Hamiltonian, four times the escape rate always yields a spectral disk, and the factor four is optimal uniformly in dimension.
AI.conclusion: The spectral disk bound with radius ||Φ†(I)|| resolves two conjectures and gives a sharp, dimension-independent escape-rate-based bound (factor four) for Hamiltonian-free GKLS generators; the escape-rate conjecture itself is false, and jump-map optimization is cast as a semidefinite program.

title: Instrument indeterminacy: separating uncertainty in POVM effects and its neutrosophic reading
summary: Neutrosophic annotation frameworks for quantum measurement attach an external triple $(t,i,f)$ to each Born probability, and explicitly leave open how indeterminacy could be defined operationally. We show that indeterminacy cannot be recovered from outcome probabilities, but can be computed from the pair (state, effect). For a binary POVM $\{A, I-A\}$ we define the instrument indeterminacy $\mathcal{I}_ρ(A) = 4 \mathrm{Tr}(ρ(A-A^2))$, which vanishes exactly when the state only sees the sharp part of the effect. The normalized Gini index of the outcome splits as $4TF = \mathcal{I}_ρ(A) + 4 \mathrm{Var}_ρ(A)$, a law of total variance that separates the instrument contribution from the state contribution; the identity is a special case of Massar's POVM uncertainty operator, and our contribution is its neutrosophic reading. Moving the system-apparatus cut to a Naimark dilation transfers exactly $\mathcal{I}_ρ(A)$ from indeterminacy to variance, which yields the missing operational definition. We extend the decomposition to $m$-outcome POVMs, relate the minimum indeterminacy of two incompatible unbiased qubit observables to their commutator through Busch's joint-measurability criterion, and show that $\mathcal{I}_ρ(A)$ equals twice the disagreement probability of a repeated Lüders measurement. The resulting estimator needs neither the state nor the effect and, in simulation, requires 2.5 to 6 times fewer shots than detector tomography for the same error.

AI.tldr: The paper gives an operational definition of neutrosophic indeterminacy for quantum measurements, showing it is computable from the (state, effect) pair—not from outcome probabilities—via an instrument indeterminacy functional that splits the Gini index of outcomes into indeterminacy plus variance.
AI.motivation: Neutrosophic annotation frameworks attach an external triple (t,i,f) to each Born probability but leave open how the indeterminacy component could be defined operationally; the paper aims to supply that missing operational definition.
AI.method: Defines instrument indeterminacy I_ρ(A) = 4 Tr(ρ(A − A²)) for binary POVMs {A, I−A}; proves a law of total variance decomposing the normalized Gini index of outcomes as 4TF = I_ρ(A) + 4 Var_ρ(A); shows the identity is a special case of Massar's POVM uncertainty operator; uses Naimark dilation (shifting the system–apparatus cut) to transfer I_ρ(A) from indeterminacy to variance; extends to m-outcome POVMs, links minimal indeterminacy of two incompatible unbiased qubit observables to their commutator via Busch's joint-measurability criterion, and identifies I_ρ(A) with twice the disagreement probability of a repeated Lüders measurement.
AI.result: I_ρ(A) vanishes exactly when the state only sees the sharp part of the effect; the Gini index splits cleanly into instrument and state contributions; Naimark dilation yields the missing operational definition; and the derived estimator requires neither state nor effect and, in simulation, needs 2.5–6× fewer shots than detector tomography for equal error.
AI.conclusion: Indeterminacy is recoverable from the (state, effect) pair rather than from outcome probabilities alone, providing a consistent neutrosophic reading of Massar's POVM uncertainty operator and a practical, shot-efficient estimator.

title: Perspectives on the hidden subgroup problem over unitriangular groups
summary: We investigate the quantum Hidden Subgroup Problem (HSP) over the upper unitriangular group $U_n(\mathbb{F}_p)$. While efficient quantum algorithms were discovered for some families of non abelian groups and nil-2 $p$-groups, no efficient algorithms are known for groups of nilpotency class higher than 2. The only techniques known for such groups scale exponentially in the size of the input. We first study the group $U_4(\mathbb{F}_p)$, the smallest upper unitriangular group exhibiting nilpotency class three. We analyze the application of the Pretty Good Measurement approach used for Heisenberg groups and show its limits. We then focus on the more general case $U_n(\mathbb{F}_p)$ to adapt existing techniques to this particular structure. In particular, we derive an algorithm for cyclic subgroups as a subroutine for a general algorithm, although it is not efficient in the size of the group. Our results highlight the difficulties introduced by the increasing nilpotency class and suggests some directions for an efficient quantum algorithm for the HSP over $U_n(\mathbb{F}_p)$.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the quantum Hidden Subgroup Problem over upper unitriangular groups U_n(F_p), focusing on U_4(F_p) (nilpotency class 3), shows limits of the Pretty Good Measurement approach, and derives a (not group-efficient) cyclic-subgroup subroutine.
AI.motivation: Efficient quantum HSP algorithms exist for some families of non-abelian and nil-2 p-groups, but none are known for nilpotency class higher than 2; existing techniques for such groups scale exponentially in input size. U_n(F_p) naturally exhibits growing nilpotency class and thus serves as a testbed for understanding the added difficulty.
AI.method: First analyzes U_4(F_p), the smallest unitriangular group with nilpotency class three, by applying the Pretty Good Measurement (PGM) approach previously used for Heisenberg groups and characterizing its limitations. Then generalizes to U_n(F_p), adapting existing techniques to this structure and deriving an algorithm for cyclic subgroups intended as a subroutine of a general algorithm.
AI.result: The PGM approach is shown to have limits beyond nilpotency class two. A cyclic-subgroup algorithm is obtained as a subroutine, but it is not efficient in the size of the group.
AI.conclusion: Increasing nilpotency class introduces substantial obstacles for the quantum HSP over U_n(F_p); the findings delineate these difficulties and suggest directions toward an efficient quantum algorithm.

title: Uniformly Convergent Perturbation Theory for Open Quantum Systems at, near, and away from Exceptional Points
summary: Near a Liouvillian exceptional point, spectral perturbation theory becomes ill-conditioned, yet the observable dynamics of a finite-dimensional open system remains regular in the perturbation. Using a Dyson expansion, which requires no diagonalization of the perturbed generator, we analyze the scaling, stability, and convergence of the perturbative corrections at, near and away from exceptional points. We derive scaling laws showing that nonperipheral Jordan blocks raise the degree of the polynomial-in-time factors multiplying decaying exponentials, which are present for any generator as resonances, and we quantify this excess. We further establish a uniform-in-time error estimate for the perturbative series, valid for any relaxing finite-dimensional Lindbladian and controlled by a parameter $q = |\varepsilon|R$, where $\varepsilon$ is the perturbation strength and $R$ is a constant built from unperturbed data. All constants of the bound remain continuous through an exceptional point when the coalescing eigenvalues are kept in one spectral cluster. The estimate extends to the frequency domain via the Laplace transform, and to time-dependent perturbations. We test it in a driven two-level system with a Liouvillian exceptional point, including perturbations that break its symmetry.

AI.tldr: Dyson-expansion perturbation theory for Liouvillian exceptional points yields scaling laws and a uniform-in-time error bound controlled by q = |ε|R that stays continuous through the exceptional point.
AI.motivation: Spectral perturbation theory becomes ill-conditioned near Liouvillian exceptional points even though the observable dynamics of finite-dimensional open systems stays regular under perturbation; a non-diagonalizing framework is needed to quantify scaling, stability, and convergence of perturbative corrections.
AI.method: A Dyson expansion requiring no diagonalization of the perturbed generator is used to analyze perturbative corrections at, near, and away from exceptional points. Scaling laws are derived relating nonperipheral Jordan blocks to the degree of polynomial-in-time factors multiplying decaying exponentials. A uniform-in-time error estimate is established for relaxing finite-dimensional Lindbladians, controlled by q = |ε|R with R built from unperturbed data, and extended to the Laplace/frequency domain and to time-dependent perturbations. Validation uses a driven two-level system with a Liouvillian exceptional point, including symmetry-breaking perturbations.
AI.result: Nonperipheral Jordan blocks are shown to raise the polynomial degree of the time-dependent prefactors on decaying exponentials (resonances present for any generator), and this excess is quantified. The uniform-in-time error bound holds for any relaxing finite-dimensional Lindbladian, with all constants remaining continuous through the exceptional point when coalescing eigenvalues are kept in one spectral cluster.
AI.conclusion: Dyson-expansion perturbation theory provides a well-conditioned, uniform-in-time description of Liouvillian dynamics through exceptional points, with error controlled by q = |ε|R and constants continuous across the EP, extending to frequency-domain and time-dependent settings.

title: Renormalization and exact Bloch bands: the trigonometric Rosen-Morse model
summary: We study the trigonometric Rosen-Morse potential as an isolated singular well and as an exactly solvable periodic lattice. The potential combines inverse-square singularities with Coulomb terms of opposite signs. In the strongly attractive regime, independent renormalization at the two endpoints gives a two-parameter family of spectra. Deep negative-energy levels form two asymptotic sequences with the same Efimov-like scaling and opposite first-order Coulomb corrections. In the weak-medium regime, self-adjoint matching conditions allow transmission between neighboring cells. We obtain the exact Bloch dispersion relation and determine the band widths, gaps, and electron and hole effective masses. At fixed band index, the bandwidth becomes exponentially small in the limit of large Coulomb coupling.

AI.tldr: The trigonometric Rosen-Morse potential with competing inverse-square singularities and opposite-sign Coulomb terms is solved exactly, both as an isolated singular well (giving a two-parameter Efimov-like spectrum) and as a periodic lattice (giving an exact Bloch dispersion relation with band widths, gaps and effective masses).
AI.motivation: To characterize a confining potential that combines inverse-square singularities with Coulomb terms of opposite signs, which admits exact treatment both as a single singular well and as a solvable periodic lattice, and to understand how strong Coulomb coupling controls the resulting spectral and band structure.
AI.method: Exact analytical solution of the trigonometric Rosen-Morse potential. In the strongly attractive regime, independent renormalization is performed at the two endpoints, yielding a two-parameter family of spectra. In the weak-medium regime, self-adjoint matching conditions are imposed to allow transmission between neighboring cells, from which the exact Bloch dispersion relation is derived and used to extract band widths, gaps and carrier effective masses.
AI.result: Deep negative-energy levels organize into two asymptotic sequences sharing the same Efimov-like scaling but with opposite first-order Coulomb corrections. The exact Bloch dispersion relation is obtained, along with band widths, gaps, and electron and hole effective masses.
