At fixed band index, the bandwidth becomes exponentially small in the limit of large Coulomb coupling.
AI.conclusion: The trigonometric Rosen-Morse potential provides a rare exactly solvable setting in which singular-well (few-body-like, Efimov-scaling) physics and periodic-lattice band physics are unified; strong Coulomb coupling drives exponentially narrow bands at fixed band index.

title: Separating QMA from the QCMA Hierarchy via a Switching Lemma for Polynomials
summary: We construct a classical oracle relative to which QMA is not contained in the QCMA hierarchy. Our main technical contribution is a switching lemma for bounded polynomials, which provides a new conceptual viewpoint on earlier sampler-based arguments separating QMA and QCMA. Crucially, the parameters of this switching lemma are independent of the number of input variables. The separation builds on the code intersection subset size problem of Bostanci, Huang, and Vaikuntanathan (FOCS 2026). We also construct a classical oracle relative to which QCMA collapses to P but QMA does not, and another relative to which QMA collapses to P but PP does not.

AI.tldr: A classical oracle is constructed relative to which QMA ⊄ QCMA-hierarchy, using a new switching lemma for bounded polynomials whose parameters are independent of the number of input variables.
AI.motivation: Previous separations of QMA and QCMA relied on sampler-based arguments. The paper seeks a new conceptual viewpoint for these separations and strengthens them to hierarchies and collapse regimes via relativized oracle constructions.
AI.method: Main technical tool: a switching lemma for bounded polynomials with parameters independent of the number of input variables. The separation builds on the code intersection subset size problem (Bostanci–Huang–Vaikuntanathan, FOCS 2026).
AI.result: Existence of a classical oracle relative to which QMA is not contained in the QCMA hierarchy. Additionally, oracles are constructed making QCMA collapse to P while QMA does not, and making QMA collapse to P while PP does not.
AI.conclusion: These constructions establish stronger relativized separations among QMA, QCMA, and classical classes, and introduce a dimension-independent switching lemma as a new lens on QMA vs. QCMA separation techniques.

title: Chirp-stabilized charging of a two-level quantum battery
summary: Resonantly driven two-level quantum batteries (QBs) suffer from strong pulse-area dependence and energy backflow inherent to Rabi oscillations. To address this limitation, we propose charging of a two-level QB with chirped pulses. We investigate four charging protocols formed by pairing hyperbolic secant (sech) or Gaussian pulse envelopes with linear or hyperbolic-tangent (tanh) frequency sweeps. We show that sufficiently strong chirp modulation converts the charging mechanism from pulse-area-governed Rabi rotation to adiabatic rapid passage. We analyze the underlying adiabatic dynamics and derive the criteria for robust chirped charging, which incorporate the sweep bandwidth, nonadiabatic transitions, and dissipative effects. Under strong chirp modulation, the final stored energy and ergotropy converge to stable plateaus that are nearly insensitive to the pulse area across an extended parameter window. Of the four schemes, the sech pulse with tanh chirp delivers the widest ergotropy plateau and the weakest pulse area sensitivity. Compared with counterdiabatic driving, the sech tanh protocol attains stable charging performance without demanding an extra drive quadrature. Furthermore, this chirp-enabled charging is resilient to static detuning and weak-to-moderate dissipation. This work establishes a practical route toward robust charging of quantum batteries using chirped pulse control.

AI.tldr: Chirped-pulse charging converts a two-level quantum battery from pulse-area-sensitive Rabi rotation into adiabatic rapid passage, yielding stable energy and ergotropy plateaus; the sech envelope with tanh chirp performs best.
AI.motivation: Resonantly driven two-level quantum batteries suffer strong pulse-area dependence and energy backflow due to Rabi oscillations, which undermines robust charging. The authors seek a charging scheme that removes this sensitivity.
AI.method: Four chirped charging protocols are constructed by pairing sech or Gaussian envelopes with linear or tanh frequency sweeps. The adiabatic dynamics are analyzed, and criteria for robust chirped charging are derived accounting for sweep bandwidth, nonadiabatic transitions, and dissipation. The protocols are benchmarked against counterdiabatic driving and tested under static detuning and dissipation.
AI.result: Sufficiently strong chirp converts charging from pulse-area-governed Rabi rotation to adiabatic rapid passage. Under strong chirp modulation, final stored energy and ergotropy converge to plateaus nearly insensitive to pulse area over an extended parameter window. The sech-tanh scheme gives the widest ergotropy plateau and weakest pulse-area sensitivity, matches counterdiabatic driving performance without an extra drive quadrature, and is resilient to static detuning and weak-to-moderate dissipation.
AI.conclusion: Chirped pulse control offers a practical route to robust quantum battery charging, with sech-tanh chirping as the optimal protocol among those studied.

title: Hierarchical coupling in tripartite van der Waals cavity magnonics for a low-loss and tunable coupled-mode Hamiltonian
summary: One of the greatest merits of cavity magnonics (CM) is the ability to explore rich coupled-mode physics, driven by the large \textit{in situ} flux tunability of magnonic resonances and magnon--photon coupling. Meanwhile, van der Waals (vdW) magnets offer an ultra-compact and highly integrated implementation of CM without complex fabrication processes. Nonetheless, the substantial magnon losses significantly hinder the combination of all these advantages. Here, we realize a hierarchical anti-crossing structure in a tripartite vdW CM with CrCl3 and realize an effective coupled-dual-mode Hamiltonian. We achieve an order-of-magnitude reduction in loss while maintaining a strong coupling condition. Additionally, we theoretically confirm the feasibility of simultaneous and \textit{in situ} tuning of both loss and coupling by varying the magnetic field direction and strength. Featuring a micrometer-scale thickness and a width of a few millimeters, our device is significantly smaller than those based on bulk crystals or crystal arrays. Our results establish vdW cavity magnonics as versatile platform for investigating intriguing phenomena predicted in coupled-mode systems.

AI.tldr: A tripartite van der Waals cavity magnonic system based on CrCl3 realizes a hierarchical anti-crossing structure and an effective coupled-dual-mode Hamiltonian, cutting magnon loss by an order of magnitude while preserving strong coupling.
AI.motivation: Cavity magnonics benefits from large in situ flux tunability of magnonic resonances and magnon–photon coupling, and van der Waals (vdW) magnets enable ultra-compact, highly integrated implementations without complex fabrication. However, substantial magnon losses prevent combining these advantages.
AI.method: The authors construct a tripartite vdW cavity magnonic device using CrCl3, in which they engineer a hierarchical anti-crossing structure described by an effective coupled-dual-mode Hamiltonian. They further analyze theoretically the in situ tuning of loss and coupling via the direction and strength of the applied magnetic field.
AI.result: Loss is reduced by roughly one order of magnitude while strong coupling is maintained. Theory confirms that both loss and coupling can be tuned simultaneously and in situ through magnetic field orientation and magnitude. The device, with micrometer-scale thickness and millimeter-scale width, is considerably smaller than bulk-crystal or crystal-array-based counterparts.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes vdW cavity magnonics as a versatile platform for exploring phenomena predicted in coupled-mode systems, combining compactness, integrability, and strong coupling with low loss.

title: Parity Push Post-Selection with Soft Parity Constraints for Quantum LDPC Codes
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables; Supplementary Information: 9 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables
summary: Post-selection lowers the logical error rate of a quantum error-correcting code by rejecting unreliable shots. For a code with $K$ logical observables, the logical gap, a standard post-selection criterion, involves $2^K$ logical classes, and existing approximations to it suffer from a non-convergence error floor or a shielding effect. We introduce a decoder-agnostic post-selection strategy for quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes, called parity push post-selection (PPPS), which re-decodes a shot once per logical observable with a push toward the opposite parity. Each push adds one check node and one variable node to the Tanner graph of the detector error model, and we accept a shot only when every re-decoding returns a solution in the original logical class. We show that, with degenerate maximum-likelihood decoding, PPPS accepts a shot exactly when the logical gap exceeds the push strength $λ$. Applied with the Relay-BP decoder to the [[72,12,6]] bivariate bicycle code at $p=10^{-3}$ and the [[144,12,12]] code at $p=3\times10^{-3}$ under circuit-level depolarizing noise, PPPS lowers the logical error rate by factors of about 50 and 75, respectively, at rejection rates near 1%. We observe that PPPS rejects failures that prior post-selection strategies cannot reject, and thus shows improved performance.

AI.tldr: The authors propose parity push post-selection (PPPS), a decoder-agnostic post-selection strategy for quantum LDPC codes that re-decodes each shot once per logical observable with a parity push, accepting only when all re-decodings remain in the original logical class; it reduces logical error rates by ~50x and ~75x at ~1% rejection on [[72,12,6]] and [[144,12,12]] bivariate bicycle codes.
AI.motivation: Standard logical-gap post-selection requires evaluating $2^K$ logical classes and existing approximations suffer from a non-convergence error floor or a shielding effect, limiting their effectiveness for codes with many logical observables.
AI.method: PPPS re-decodes each shot once per logical observable, applying a push toward the opposite parity by adding one check node and one variable node to the Tanner graph of the detector error model; a shot is accepted only if every re-decoding returns a solution in the original logical class. It is analyzed theoretically under degenerate maximum-likelihood decoding and applied practically with the Relay-BP decoder to bivariate bicycle codes under circuit-level depolarizing noise.
AI.result: With degenerate maximum-likelihood decoding, PPPS provably accepts a shot exactly when the logical gap exceeds the push strength $\lambda$. Applied to the [[72,12,6]] code at $p=10^{-3}$ and the [[144,12,12]] code at $p=3\times10^{-3}$, PPPS lowers the logical error rate by factors of about 50 and 75 respectively, at rejection rates near 1%, rejecting failures that prior strategies cannot.
AI.conclusion: PPPS provides a decoder-agnostic, scalable post-selection criterion that avoids the error floor and shielding issues of existing logical-gap approximations, delivering substantial logical error rate reductions at low rejection cost and outperforming prior post-selection strategies.

title: Addressable transversal CCZ gates on almost good quantum LDPC codes and nearly optimal magic state protocols
summary: Assuming uniform subfield product expansion, we construct quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes with distances $Ω_ε(N/\log^2N)$ and at least $N^{1-ε}$ individually addressable logical CCZ gates on pairwise disjoint triples of logical qubits, for every fixed $0<ε<1$. With all logical qubits outside these triples initialized to $|0\rangle$, any subset of the corresponding logical CCZ gates can be implemented with a transversal physical CCZ circuit. As applications, we obtain two nearly optimal magic state protocols: CCZ distillation with arbitrarily small overhead exponent $γ\rightarrow 0$ and error suppression of nearly linear order, and a magic state fountain that directly prepares $N^{1-ε}$ encoded CCZ magic states with nearly linear distance $Ω_ε(N/\log^2N)$. The construction uses balanced products of expanding graph covers. The assumption concerns Reed--Solomon codes on three subfields of characteristic two and pairwise coprime extension degrees, a local hypothesis studied in a companion manuscript. We design the expanding graph covers to admit many common classical codewords, which yield logical operators whose pairings select the logical CCZ gates independently. Without the product expansion assumption, the graph covers also yield classical LDPC codes over a fixed field with almost linear dimension and linear distance that satisfy a multiplication property: the coordinatewise product of any three codewords lies in a second LDPC code of linear distance.

AI.tldr: Assuming uniform subfield product expansion, the authors construct qLDPC codes with distance Ω_ε(N/log²N) and N^{1−ε} individually addressable logical CCZ gates on disjoint logical-qubit triples, enabling transversal physical CCZ implementation and two nearly optimal magic-state protocols.
AI.motivation: Quantum low-density parity-check codes that support many addressable logical non-Clifford gates (CCZ) are key to fault-tolerant magic-state injection with low overhead; existing constructions do not simultaneously achieve nearly linear distance and a large number of independently selectable logical CCZ gates.
AI.method: The construction uses balanced products of expanding graph covers, with the assumption being Reed–Solomon codes over three characteristic-two subfields with pairwise coprime extension degrees (a local hypothesis from a companion manuscript). Graph covers are designed to admit many common classical codewords, giving logical operators whose pairings select logical CCZ gates independently.
AI.result: For every fixed 0<ε<1, the codes have distance Ω_ε(N/log²N) and at least N^{1−ε} pairwise disjoint logical triples supporting individually addressable CCZ gates, which are implementable via a transversal physical CCZ circuit when other logical qubits are initialized to |0⟩. Applications include CCZ distillation with overhead exponent γ→0 and nearly linear-order error suppression, and a magic-state fountain directly preparing N^{1−ε} encoded CCZ magic states with distance Ω_ε(N/log²N).
AI.conclusion: The work yields nearly optimal magic-state protocols grounded in explicit qLDPC constructions under a local product-expansion assumption. Even without this assumption, the graph covers give classical LDPC codes over a fixed field with almost linear dimension and linear distance satisfying a multiplication property (coordinatewise product of any three codewords lies in a second LDPC code of linear distance).

title: Subsystem evolution in the history state formalism
summary: We present a relational framework for characterizing the evolution of quantum composite systems, based on the correlations within a history state describing the whole evolution relative to a quantum reference clock. While total system-clock entanglement entropy consistently measures the unitary evolution of the closed global system, a different picture emerges for the reduced state of an open subsystem, whose evolution is generally non-unitary due to environmental coupling. We introduce a general formalism that quantifies open-subsystem dynamics using a subsystem-clock mutual information derived from the history state. We demonstrate that this quantity serves as a consistent quantifier of subsystem evolution with respect to a given clock basis, can be applied to arbitrary dynamics, and reduces to system-time entanglement entropy in the global limit. Furthermore, maximizing this measure over all clock bases yields a basis-independent bound on the maximum evolution achievable relative to the clock, directly linked to the difference between the subsystem's entanglement with the rest of the history state and its entanglement with the environment. Finally, we derive analytical expressions for qubit clocks, illustrate our results using spin 1/2 and spin 1 quantum walks, and present a full matrix formalism of Kraus operators for describing the most general subsystem evolution.

AI.tldr: A relational framework quantifies the evolution of open quantum subsystems relative to a quantum clock using subsystem-clock mutual information from a history state, with a basis-independent bound linked to entanglement.
AI.motivation: Total system-clock entanglement entropy works only for closed global systems; for open subsystems undergoing non-unitary dynamics due to environmental coupling, a new consistent quantifier of evolution relative to a clock is needed.
AI.method: Constructs a history state describing the full evolution relative to a quantum reference clock and introduces subsystem-clock mutual information to quantify open-subsystem dynamics with respect to a given clock basis. Maximizes this measure over all clock bases and derives analytical expressions for qubit clocks, plus a full Kraus-operator matrix formalism.
AI.result: The subsystem-clock mutual information is a consistent quantifier for arbitrary dynamics, reducing to system-time entanglement entropy in the global limit; its basis-maximized value gives a basis-independent bound tied to the difference between the subsystem's entanglement with the rest of the history state and its entanglement with the environment. Results are illustrated with spin-1/2 and spin-1 quantum walks.
AI.conclusion: The framework extends relational evolution quantification from closed to open subsystems, providing a general, basis-independent and analytically tractable tool for characterizing quantum composite systems relative to a clock.

title: QWeaver: Quantum Circuit Cut Workflow with MLIR-based Compiler, Runtime, and Weaver Hybrid Tasks
comment: This is the pre-print version of the article to appear in SN Computer Science. Code will be released once manuscript is published
summary: Quantum computers available today are constrained by limited qubit counts and high noise levels, making the direct execution of large quantum circuits infeasible on a single device, and while quantum circuit cutting addresses this by partitioning a large circuit into smaller subcircuits for independent execution, orchestrating the full end-to-end workflow remains a significant programming challenge. In this paper, we present QWeaver, a task-graph-based programming and orchestration workflow framework for quantum circuit cutting that accepts OpenQASM quantum circuits as input and constructs a directed acyclic task graph. In this graph, the Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR)-based circuit cut is the first task, responsible for analyzing and partitioning the input circuit into executable fragment representations; the generated fragments are then handed to a set of quantum circuit execution tasks that depend on the cut task and can be dispatched concurrently across available quantum backends via the Quantum Intelligent Runtime System (Q-IRIS). Finally, a weaving task, dependent on all execution tasks, performs classical post-processing that applies quasi-probability reconstruction techniques to combine the sampled measurement outcomes of all fragments and recover an accurate approximation of the original circuit's output distribution. We describe the architecture of QWeaver, its integration with Q-IRIS and the execution engine for the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR-EE), validate end-to-end reconstruction on GHZ and Harris-Ross instances, and evaluate systems and width trade-offs on structured GHZ simulator workloads.

AI.tldr: QWeaver is a task-graph-based programming and orchestration framework that automates the end-to-end quantum circuit cutting workflow, from OpenQASM input through MLIR-based partitioning, concurrent fragment execution via Q-IRIS, to quasi-probability reconstruction of the original circuit's output distribution.
AI.motivation: Current quantum devices have limited qubit counts and high noise, making direct execution of large circuits infeasible on a single device. Quantum circuit cutting partitions large circuits into smaller subcircuits, but orchestrating the full end-to-end workflow remains a significant programming challenge.
AI.method: QWeaver takes OpenQASM circuits as input and constructs a directed acyclic task graph. The first task is an MLIR-based circuit cut that analyzes and partitions the circuit into executable fragments. Dependent execution tasks dispatch fragments concurrently across quantum backends via the Quantum Intelligent Runtime System (Q-IRIS). A final weaving task, dependent on all execution tasks, performs classical post-processing using quasi-probability reconstruction to combine sampled fragment outcomes.
AI.result: The work describes QWeaver's architecture and its integration with Q-IRIS and the QIR-EE execution engine, validates end-to-end reconstruction on GHZ and Harris-Ross instances, and evaluates systems and width trade-offs on structured GHZ simulator workloads.
AI.conclusion: QWeaver provides a unified, task-graph-based orchestration workflow that simplifies and automates the full quantum circuit cutting pipeline, enabling scalable execution of large circuits across distributed backends with accurate output reconstruction.

title: Spectral Engineering of Charge Localization and Work Reliability in Collective Quantum Batteries
summary: The performance of a quantum battery depends not only on how much energy it stores, but also on how rapidly useful charge can be restored after work extraction. We show how engineering the reservoir spectrum connects these properties in an interacting collective-spin battery. Interactions separate the Dicke transition frequencies, allowing frequency-selective pumping and loss to control where excitation accumulates and how populations move along the ladder. Analytical results relate the pump-to-loss ratio to charge localization, fluctuations, and extractable work. Two reservoirs producing the same mean charge can nevertheless exhibit markedly different localization and charging times. Under repeated extraction, finite-time recharging also generates correlations between successive work outputs. At matched mean work, these correlations can reverse the ordering of single-cycle and long-time fluctuations: a protocol with larger fluctuations in individual strokes can deliver more reliable accumulated work. An exact counting relation connects these statistics to net charging-energy transfer, while relaxation modes distinguish recovery of the stationary state from recovery of useful work. Finally, local dephasing redistributes population among collective-spin sectors, leading to an exact stationary symmetry-dilution law and a finite operating window for work extraction under a collective transverse controller.

AI.tldr: Engineering the reservoir (bath) spectrum in an interacting collective-spin quantum battery lets frequency-selective pumping/loss control charge localization, fluctuations, and extractable work; recharging dynamics create inter-cycle correlations that can reverse the ordering of single-cycle versus long-time work fluctuations, and local dephasing dilutes collective-spin symmetry via an exact stationary law.
AI.motivation: Quantum battery performance is usually judged by stored energy, but practical operation also requires fast restoration of useful charge after work extraction. The paper aims to connect energy capacity with the speed and reliability of recharging (and the shot-to-shot statistics of work output) in an interacting collective-spin battery.
AI.method: Analytical treatment of an interacting collective-spin (Dicke-type) battery coupled to engineered reservoirs. Interactions split the Dicke transition frequencies, enabling frequency-selective pump and loss to control where excitation accumulates and how populations move along the collective-spin ladder. Analytical relations link the pump-to-loss ratio to charge localization, fluctuations, and extractable work. Repeated finite-time extraction cycles are analyzed for correlations between successive work outputs, an exact counting relation ties these statistics to net charging-energy transfer, and relaxation modes are used to separate recovery of the stationary state from recovery of useful work. Local dephasing is treated to derive the stationary symmetry-dilution law and the operating window under a collective transverse controller.
AI.result: Two reservoirs with identical mean charge can yield markedly different charge localization and charging times. Finite-time recharging produces correlations between successive work outputs; at matched mean work these correlations can reverse the ordering of single-cycle versus long-time fluctuations, so a protocol with larger per-stroke fluctuations can deliver more reliable accumulated work. An exact counting relation connects the work statistics to net charging-energy transfer, and distinct relaxation modes separate stationary-state recovery from useful-work recovery. Local dephasing redistributes population among collective-spin sectors, giving an exact stationary symmetry-dilution law and a finite operating window for work extraction.
AI.conclusion: In an interacting collective-spin quantum battery, the reservoir spectrum—not just mean charge—governs localization, charging speed, and work-output reliability. Inter-cycle correlations from finite-time recharging can make nominally noisier single strokes more reliable in accumulated work, and dephasing sets an exact symmetry-dilution law that bounds the usable operating window for collective work extraction.

title: Stationary Quantum Time Series: Spectral Theory of Process Memory and Measurement Records
summary: Classical time series analysis converts temporal dependence into structure that can be learned from a single observed trajectory, through stationarity, ergodicity, spectral representation, and finite-memory models. Quantum experiments are naturally time series: every run is a sequence of interventions and outcomes, and the memory of an open system is written in its temporal statistics. However, the classical foundation cannot be translated directly: measuring a process and forgetting the outcome differs from not measuring at all, so no single family of joint probability distributions describes a quantum process. We develop a process-tensor framework for stationary quantum time series and establish its first structural theorems. For stationary combs of finite quantum Markov order l relative to a fixed informationally complete causal break, we construct a finite-dimensional causal transfer map of dimension at most d^{4l}, where d bounds the system Hilbert-space dimension at each step. ... These results supply the stationary foundation on which quantum spectral analysis, model identification, and single-trajectory inference can be built.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a process-tensor framework for stationary quantum time series and proves structural theorems, giving a finite-dimensional causal transfer map for stationary combs with finite quantum Markov order.
AI.motivation: Classical time series analysis turns temporal dependence into learnable structure via stationarity, ergodicity, spectral representation, and finite-memory models. Quantum experiments are intrinsically time series, but the classical foundation cannot be transplanted because measuring and forgetting an outcome differs from not measuring at all — so no single family of joint distributions characterizes a quantum process.
AI.method: A process-tensor framework for stationary quantum time series with structural theorems. For stationary combs of finite quantum Markov order l relative to a fixed informationally complete causal break, a finite-dimensional causal transfer map of dimension at most d^{4l} is constructed, where d bounds the per-step system Hilbert-space dimension.
AI.result: A finite-dimensional causal transfer-map representation, of dimension at most d^{4l}, is established for stationary combs with finite quantum Markov order under an informationally complete causal break.
AI.conclusion: The work provides the stationary foundation on which quantum spectral analysis, model identification, and single-trajectory inference can be built.

title: Covering the Pauli Observables: Sampling Thresholds and the Design Effect of a Measurement Setting
summary: Quantum state tomography and shadow-based estimation rely on measuring Pauli observables. An experiment does not measure them one at a time: it chooses a measurement setting that assigns one of the bases X, Y or Z to each qubit, and a single run in that setting yields estimates of every Pauli observable compatible with it. We say that the setting covers those observables. We determine how many random settings cover a prescribed fraction of all Pauli observables. As the number of settings grows exponentially with the number of qubits, the covered fraction has a sharp threshold at a growth rate of $3^{3/4}$ per qubit, set by the rate-distortion function of covering at zero distortion. We give an explicit expression for the number of settings needed to reach a target fraction, accurate up to a remainder that reduces to a small oscillation for many qubits, and show that random sampling is asymptotically optimal up to a factor of less than 1.69. Coverage does not determine what a setting contributes to an estimator. Observables covered by one setting are estimated from the same outcomes, so their estimates are correlated. We quantify this correlation through the design effect of a setting, which equals the squared Pauli expectation that the setting captures and depends on the target state. We derive its mean over settings in closed form for every state and show that it can be estimated without bias from the measurement data. In simulations on six qubits, measuring settings needs 7.6 to 38 times fewer circuit runs than measuring the same number of observables independently. At high coverage, fitting the outcome histograms instead of averaged estimates roughly halves the reconstruction error, mainly because the fit counts how many settings cover each observable. The correlation itself costs such a fit about a factor of two, and a larger design effect signals more to gain from modeling it.

AI.tldr: Random measurement settings cover Pauli observables with a sharp coverage threshold at growth rate 3^{3/4} per qubit; the authors give explicit coverage formulas, quantify inter-observable correlation via a setting's "design effect," and show fitting outcome histograms substantially outperforms independent estimation.
AI.motivation: Shadow-based estimation and quantum state tomography measure Pauli observables, but experiments measure a whole basis setting (assigning X, Y, or Z per qubit) that simultaneously covers many compatible observables. Prior work lacked a precise characterization of how many random settings are needed to cover a target fraction of observables, and ignored that observables covered by the same setting are estimated from shared outcomes, inducing correlations that affect estimator quality.
AI.method: The paper analyzes random measurement settings as covering the set of all Pauli observables. It derives the covered fraction's sharp threshold via the rate-distortion function of covering at zero distortion, giving an explicit counting expression accurate up to a small remainder, and shows random sampling is asymptotically optimal within a factor below 1.69. It introduces a per-setting "design effect" — the squared Pauli expectation the setting captures — computes its mean over settings in closed form for any state, and provides an unbiased estimator from measurement data. Simulations on six qubits compare circuit-run counts and histogram fitting versus averaged estimates.
AI.result: Coverage has a sharp threshold at growth rate 3^{3/4} per qubit. Measuring settings requires 7.6 to 38 times fewer circuit runs than measuring the same number of observables independently. At high coverage, fitting outcome histograms roughly halves reconstruction error versus averaged estimates, largely because the fit accounts for how many settings cover each observable. The estimation correlation itself costs such fits about a factor of two, and a larger design effect indicates more gain from modeling it.
AI.conclusion: Random settings are near-optimal for covering Pauli observables, and coverage-based histogram fitting exploits shared outcomes to substantially reduce measurement cost. The design effect provides a state-dependent, unbiasedly estimable diagnostic of when correlation modeling is worthwhile.

title: Aharonov-Bohm blockade of complete reversal in coupled Rabi cavities
summary: When a common bias reverses two bistable fields, the system can pass through either of two single-reversal configurations on its way to the favored state. We show that interference between these two orders of reversal can block the final step. In a dimer of coupled quantum Rabi cavities, the four field configurations form a loop, and a complex photon-hopping amplitude threads it with an Aharonov-Bohm flux. Near half a flux quantum, the two paths to complete reversal interfere destructively: in microscopic simulations, a slow uniform sweep reverses one field with probability 0.998, although the final bias favors reversing both. A four-state model calibrated at zero bias predicts how the window of this Aharonov-Bohm blockade narrows with sweep time. The blocked state remains coherent. A differential pulse followed by a return sweep converts the relative phase of the two single-reversal configurations into a fringe in the joint field signs, with contrast 0.95. In a trimer, a phase gradient imprinted between sweeps determines whether the next sweep adds or removes a reversed field: reversing the second of two gradients changes the most probable outcome from three reversed fields to one.

AI.tldr: A geometric (Aharonov–Bohm) phase from complex photon hopping between reversal paths causes destructive interference that blocks the final step of a bias-driven double-field reversal in coupled quantum Rabi cavities, and this blockade can be used to read out relative phase information.
AI.motivation: When a common bias reverses two bistable fields, the system can transiently pass through either of two single-reversal configurations. Extension to a trimer with imprinted phase gradients, plus a differential-pulse/return-sweep protocol.

The four-state model (calibrated at zero bias) predicts how the blockade window narrows with sweep time; the blocked state remains coherent. A differential pulse followed by a return sweep converts the relative phase of the two single-reversal configurations into a fringe in the joint field signs with contrast 0.95. In a trimer, a phase gradient imprinted between sweeps determines whether the next sweep adds or removes a reversed field—reversing the second of two gradients shifts the most probable outcome from three reversed fields to one.
AI.conclusion: Interference between alternative reversal orders constitutes a controllable Aharonov–Bohm blockade of a bias-favored final transition, yielding a coherent, phase-sensitive mechanism for steering and reading out multibit field configurations; in few-cavity lattices, imprinted phase gradients program which fields reverse.

title: Imaging chiral snake states in a qubit array with programmable gauge fields
comment: 22 pages, 12 figures (4 main-text figures and 8 Extended Data figures), and 1 Extended Data table
summary: Spatially varying magnetic fields steer charged particles along directed paths. Where a field reverses sign, particles follow snake-like orbits along the reversal line, in a direction set by both the field orientation and the sign of their energy. Transport measurements have detected such snake states, but imaging their dynamics in a reprogrammable field landscape remains challenging. Here we digitally simulate the Harper--Hofstadter model with programmable synthetic magnetic fields on a 49-qubit superconducting processor. In each Trotter step, every hopping term is one native fractional-iSWAP gate, and single-qubit $Z$ rotations set all 36 plaquette fluxes independently, without additional entangling gates. Uniform, random, and stepped flux landscapes reveal Aharonov--Bohm suppression of diagonal propagation, disorder-induced slowing, and magnetic reflection. At a field reversal, bonding and antibonding initial states, which carry opposite energy biases, propagate in opposite directions, and both directions reverse when the field is inverted. A symmetry analysis of these reversals yields a chiral displacement of nearly one lattice spacing after ten Trotter rounds, with symmetry-breaking residuals below 0.05 lattice spacings. Bond-resolved flux programming with site-resolved imaging thus provides a quantitative tool for synthetic gauge fields and a route to time-dependent gauge fields and interacting particles.

AI.tldr: A 49-qubit superconducting processor digitally simulates the Harper–Hofstadter model with individually programmable plaquette fluxes to resolve directional snake-state transport at field reversals.
AI.motivation: Snake orbits at magnetic field reversal lines have been detected in transport measurements, but their dynamics in a reprogrammable flux landscape is hard to image. The authors aim to build a controllable synthetic gauge-field platform to quantitatively study these chiral, direction-selective dynamics.
AI.method: Trotterized digital simulation of the Harper–Hofstadter model on 49 superconducting qubits. Each hopping term maps to one native fractional-iSWAP gate, while single-qubit Z rotations set all 36 plaquette fluxes independently with no extra entangling gates. Uniform, random, and stepped flux landscapes are imposed, and site-resolved imaging tracks particle propagation from bonding and antibonding initial states of opposite energy bias.
AI.result: Uniform, random, and stepped flux landscapes reproduce Aharonov–Bohm suppression of diagonal propagation, disorder-induced slowing, and magnetic reflection. At a flux reversal, bonding and antibonding states propagate in opposite directions, and both directions reverse upon field inversion. Symmetry analysis gives a chiral displacement of nearly one lattice spacing after ten Trotter rounds, with symmetry-breaking residuals below 0.05 lattice spacings.
AI.conclusion: Bond-resolved flux programming combined with site-resolved imaging provides a quantitative tool for synthetic gauge fields and a route toward time-dependent gauge fields and interacting particles.

title: Fault-tolerant quantum processor with minimal external control
comment: Reader's guide included at the end of section 1
summary: Contemporary classical information processors integrate tens of billions of transistors printed on a chip, yet are fully controlled through comparatively few external wires. This is possible because data flows through hard-coded operations in step with a global clock and is steered by external instructions. Today's solid-state quantum processors are different -- every qubit receives instructions from outside the chip via its own dedicated control line, and error correction adds a further torrent of syndrome data that is transported off-chip. Here we show that the external control of a quantum chip can be greatly simplified. We propose a fault-tolerant architecture for universal quantum computation, inspired by modern classical processors, in which quantum information flows through a fixed, clocked device, propelled by local gates in a planar array. Our quantum processor receives an input stream of classical instructions via a small, constant number of external wires, each attached to a single qubit. Except for those few qubits coupled to external wires, all qubits evolve under a periodically-applied geometrically-local depth-3 circuit, which is fixed at the time the device is fabricated. Assuming a noiseless global clock (so that every operation is applied on schedule, though imperfectly), we establish an accuracy threshold theorem: For physical noise below a universal threshold -- afflicting every gate, measurement, and wire -- a chip with $n$ physical qubits can run any quantum algorithm that uses~$n/{\sf polylog}(n/ε)$ logical qubits, where $ε$ is the error rate per logical gate. Each logical gate takes time~$n/{\sf polylog}(n/ε)$; an alternative design, in which quantum operations remain strictly local and noisy, but on-chip wires broadcast noiseless classical signals instantaneously, reduces the time per logical gate to ${\sf polylog}(n/ε)$.

AI.tldr: The authors propose a fault-tolerant quantum computing architecture in which a fixed, clocked planar array of qubits is driven by only a constant number of external classical instruction wires, achieving a universal accuracy threshold theorem.
AI.motivation: Solid-state classical processors use few external wires because data flows through hard-coded operations paced by a global clock, whereas current quantum processors require a dedicated control line per qubit plus off-chip syndrome transport. The motivation is to simplify external control of quantum chips by borrowing the classical processor paradigm while retaining fault tolerance.
AI.method: Design a fault-tolerant architecture for universal quantum computation where quantum information flows through a fixed, clocked device propelled by local gates in a planar array. The chip receives a classical instruction stream via a small, constant number of external wires, each attached to a single qubit; all other qubits evolve under a periodically applied, geometrically-local depth-3 circuit fixed at fabrication time. Analysis assumes a noiseless global clock (operations applied on schedule but imperfectly).
AI.result: An accuracy threshold theorem is established: for physical noise below a universal threshold afflicting every gate, measurement, and wire, an n-qubit chip can run any quantum algorithm using n/polylog(n/ε) logical qubits, where ε is the error rate per logical gate. Each logical gate takes time n/polylog(n/ε); an alternative design with strictly local, noisy quantum operations but instantaneous noiseless classical on-chip broadcast reduces time per logical gate to polylog(n/ε).
AI.conclusion: External control of quantum chips can be greatly simplified: a constant number of instruction wires suffices for universal, fault-tolerant quantum computation in a fixed clocked planar architecture, at the cost of favorable polylogarithmic overheads, with near-constant depth per logical gate when fast classical on-chip signaling is available.

title: General Noise Channels and Mid-Circuit Measurements for Pre-Trajectory Sampling with Batched Execution
comment: 25 pages, 8 figures (4 in the main text, 4 in the Supplementary Information)
summary: Many studies of quantum protocols require fast sampling of large amounts of measurement data from noisy quantum circuits, such as for training machine-learning decoders for quantum error correction. Exact simulation of realistic noise is expensive, while stabilizer-based simulators are fast but approximate, for example through Pauli twirling, which generally alters the output statistics. Pre-trajectory sampling with batched execution (PTSBE) accelerates exact trajectory simulation by sampling noise before state evolution. This method requires the outcome probability of every stochastic event to be independent of the state, which excludes mid-circuit measurements and general Kraus channels. We present a generalization of PTSBE to measurement and Kraus operators without approximation. Each event is partially pre-sampled, while deferred outcomes are drawn during grouped execution via multinomial branching and cached-state reuse. We implement the method for GPUs as an extension of CUDA-Q. On distance-3 topological code memories under amplitude damping, it is up to 24x faster than conventional trajectory sampling in CUDA-Q. On 30-qubit random circuits with mid-circuit measurements, it is up to 83x faster and outperforms the near-Clifford simulator Clifft when more than about 25% of the gates are non-Clifford. With repeated sampling of each final state, its sampling rate per trajectory exceeds that of CUDA-Q by nearly five orders of magnitude. Our method also allows us to compare exact amplitude damping with its Pauli-twirled channel on a surface-code memory, revealing that twirling overestimates the detection rate by 21% and raises the logical error rate of a lookup decoder by 8%. This work makes exact, high-throughput simulation practical for general noisy circuits, from data generation for training decoders to studying measurement-based fault-tolerant protocols under realistic noise.

AI.tldr: The authors generalize pre-trajectory sampling with batched execution (PTSBE) to handle mid-circuit measurements and general Kraus channels without approximation, achieving up to 83x speedups over conventional trajectory sampling and revealing that Pauli twirling misestimates surface-code error statistics.
AI.motivation: Fast sampling of large volumes of noisy measurement data is needed for tasks like training ML decoders for quantum error correction. Exact noise simulation is expensive, while stabilizer-based simulators (e.g., Pauli twirling) are fast but alter output statistics. Existing PTSBE speeds up exact trajectory simulation but requires event probabilities to be state-independent, which excludes mid-circuit measurements and general Kraus channels.
AI.method: The authors generalize PTSBE by partially pre-sampling each stochastic event and deferring outcomes that are state-dependent, drawing them during grouped execution via multinomial branching and cached-state reuse. The method is implemented on GPUs as an extension of CUDA-Q.
AI.result: On distance-3 topological code memories under amplitude damping, it is up to 24x faster than conventional trajectory sampling in CUDA-Q. On 30-qubit random circuits with mid-circuit measurements, it is up to 83x faster and outperforms Clifft when more than ~25% of gates are non-Clifford. For repeated sampling of each final state, sampling rate per trajectory exceeds CUDA-Q by nearly five orders of magnitude. Comparing exact amplitude damping with its Pauli-twirled channel on a surface-code memory shows twirling overestimates detection rate by 21% and raises lookup-decoder logical error rate by 8%.
AI.conclusion: The generalized PTSBE makes exact, high-throughput simulation practical for general noisy circuits, enabling data generation for decoder training and study of measurement-based fault-tolerant protocols under realistic noise, while also quantifying the inaccuracy introduced by Pauli twirling.

title: Faster than square-root run-time in adiabatic quantum algorithms for Exact Cover 3
summary: By intertwining ideas from sequential and adiabatic quantum computing, we propose a quantum algorithm for the problem class Exact Cover 3, which is a sub-class of 3-satisfiability (3-SAT) problems and NP (nondeterministic polynomial time) complete. We find a quantum run-time which is significantly faster than the square-root run-time $N\to N^{1/2}$ of the Grover algorithm. Depending on the structure of the problem (e.g., connectivity of clauses), the run-time scaling may range from approximately third root $N\to N^{1/3}$ to nearly fourth root $N\to N^{1/4}$, possibly even faster.

AI.tldr: The authors combine sequential and adiabatic quantum computing to build a quantum algorithm for Exact Cover 3 (an NP-complete 3-SAT subclass), achieving run-times from about N^(1/3) to N^(1/4), faster than Grover's N^(1/2).
AI.motivation: Grover's algorithm gives a square-root speedup (N^1/2) for unstructured search, and the authors seek a faster quantum run-time for the structured NP-complete problem Exact Cover 3 by exploiting problem structure.
AI.method: Intertwine ideas from sequential quantum computing and adiabatic quantum computing to construct a quantum algorithm for Exact Cover 3, a subclass of 3-SAT.
AI.result: The quantum run-time is significantly faster than Grover's N^1/2; depending on problem structure (e.g., clause connectivity), scaling ranges from roughly N^1/3 to nearly N^1/4, possibly even faster.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting instance structure via a hybrid sequential-adiabatic approach yields sub-Grover scaling for Exact Cover 3, with the run-time exponent depending on clause connectivity.

title: Analysis of a Homodyne-Like Measurement Scheme Using Photon Counters and Weak Local Oscillator
summary: In standard homodyne detection, an unknown optical signal state is combined with a local oscillator (LO) at a beam splitter (BS), and the appropriately integrated intensities at the two outputs of the BS are subtracted to obtain an approximate quadrature measurement. Accurate quadrature measurements require a high-amplitude LO and high-efficiency detectors. By varying the LO phase, the optical state in the mode matching the LO can be reconstructed. In many practical settings, a high-intensity LO is not desirable, which has led to the exploration of homodyne-like measurement schemes that replace photodiodes with photon-counting detectors and use an LO with a low average photon number. In this paper, we investigate what features of the unknown state can be determined by counting the total-photon number in one or both outgoing paths after the BS, keeping the mode of the LO fixed but adjusting its phase and magnitude. We find that it is possible to determine the unknown optical state in the mode matching the LO conditional on the number of photons in the orthogonal modes on the same path. If both the phase and the intensity of the LO can be varied, the statistics of just one of the detectors is sufficient to infer these parameters, but both detectors are required when the LO has a fixed intensity. Our analysis is carried out in the infinite-data limit, assuming access to the full photon-number distribution from one or both detectors.

AI.tldr: Replacing a strong local oscillator and photodiodes with low-photon-number LO and photon-counting detectors, the authors show which features of an unknown optical state can be reconstructed from post-beam-splitter photon-counting statistics, varying LO phase and magnitude.
AI.motivation: Standard homodyne detection demands a high-amplitude LO and high-efficiency detectors, which is undesirable in many practical settings; hence homodyne-like schemes using photon counting and weak LOs need a characterization of what state information remains accessible.
AI.method: The signal is combined with an LO at a beam splitter; total photon numbers are counted in one or both output paths while the LO phase and magnitude are tuned. Analysis is conducted in the infinite-data limit, assuming access to the full photon-number distribution.
AI.result: The unknown state in the LO-matched mode can be determined conditionally on the photon number in the orthogonal modes on the same path. With variable LO phase and intensity, one detector's statistics suffice; with fixed LO intensity, both detectors are required.
AI.conclusion: Photon-counting homodyne-like detection with a weak LO can recover the LO-matched mode's state, with detector requirements depending on whether LO intensity is tunable—establishing a viable alternative to high-amplitude homodyne detection.

title: Quantum Mpemba effect in a driven-dissipative atom-waveguide coupled system
summary: The quantum Mpemba effect (QME) describes the counterintuitive phenomenon in which a more strongly perturbed quantum system relaxes toward its steady state faster than a less perturbed one. Here, we investigate the QME in a weakly driven-dissipative atomic array coupled to a one-dimensional chiral waveguide. Starting from the steady state, we introduce a local quench by resetting a single atom to its ground state and examine the subsequent relaxation dynamics. We find that quenching atoms near the array boundaries induces faster initial relaxation through enhanced coupling to superradiant modes and direct photon emission into the waveguide, giving rise to an edge-enhanced QME. Strong directional decay further amplifies this effect by promoting the spatial accumulation of superradiant modes near the preferred boundary, leading to a skin-enhanced QME. At later times, relaxation is increasingly governed by long-lived subradiant modes localized predominantly in the bulk of the array. By coupling two atomic arrays with different interparticle spacings, we further demonstrate an interface-induced QME, where quenching an atom near the interface makes the system relax more slowly at early times but approach its steady state faster at later times, owing to weak participation in both superradiant and subradiant modes. Our findings reveal how the spatial structure of collective decay modes and directional dissipation jointly govern anomalous quantum relaxation, offering potential routes toward accelerated steady-state preparation in waveguide QED systems.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the quantum Mpemba effect (QME) in a weakly driven-dissipative atomic array coupled to a chiral 1D waveguide, showing that local quenching near boundaries (edge-enhanced QME), under strong directional decay (skin-enhanced QME), or near an interface between arrays of different spacing (interface-induced QME) yields anomalous relaxation, governed jointly by spatial structure of collective decay modes and directional dissipation.
AI.motivation: The QME—where a more strongly perturbed system relaxes faster than a weakly perturbed one—is counterintuitive and its manifestations in structured, dissipative photonic settings remain underexplored. The authors aim to understand how collective decay modes and chiral (directional) dissipation in waveguide QED govern anomalous relaxation, with a view toward accelerated steady-state preparation.
AI.method: A weakly driven-dissipative atomic array is coupled to a 1D chiral waveguide. Starting from the steady state, a local quench is applied by resetting a single atom to its ground state, and the subsequent relaxation dynamics are analyzed, examining the roles of superradiant vs. subradiant modes, directional decay, and array geometry (single array, strong asymmetry, and two arrays with different interparticle spacings forming an interface).
AI.result: Three regimes are identified: (i) edge-enhanced QME — quenching atoms near boundaries gives faster initial relaxation via enhanced coupling to superradiant modes and direct photon emission into the waveguide; (ii) skin-enhanced QME — strong directional decay amplifies this by accumulating superradiant modes near the preferred boundary; (iii) interface-induced QME — quenching near the interface relaxes more slowly at early times but approaches steady state faster at later times due to weak participation in both superradiant and subradiant modes. Later-time relaxation is dominated by long-lived subradiant modes localized mainly in the bulk.
AI.conclusion: The spatial structure of collective decay modes and directional dissipation jointly govern anomalous quantum relaxation in chiral waveguide QED. These findings clarify the mechanisms of the QME and suggest routes toward accelerated steady-state preparation in waveguide QED systems.

title: Topological Origin of Directional Amplification in Arbitrary-Dimensional Non-Hermitian Lattices
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, with Supplemental Material (11 pages, 1 figure)
summary: In non-Hermitian lattices, combinations of gain, loss and nonreciprocal couplings can generate exponentially growing directional amplification with applications in signal processing and precision measurement. An intriguing question is whether such amplification has a universal topological origin in arbitrary dimensions. Here we establish a dimension-independent framework to uncover the topological origin of directional amplification based on the concept of amoeba, which is the logarithmic image of the singularities of the response generating function. The complement of the amoeba in the logarithmic parameter space consists of connected components, each carrying a distinct and discrete topological label. We show that the asymptotic response is governed by the component extending toward negative infinity. When the origin of the logarithmic parameter space is outside this component and not on its boundary, there must exist some directions in which the response is exponentially amplified. Otherwise, there is no directional amplification in any direction. Our results provide a general topological criterion for classifying the responses in arbitrary-dimensional non-Hermitian lattices.

AI.tldr: Amoeba-based topological framework explains exponentially growing directional amplification in arbitrary-dimensional non-Hermitian lattices, independent of dimension.
AI.motivation: Gain, loss, and nonreciprocal couplings in non-Hermitian lattices can produce exponential directional amplification useful for signal processing and precision measurement. The open question is whether such amplification has a universal, dimension-independent topological origin.
AI.method: The authors build a dimension-independent framework using the "amoeba"—the logarithmic image of the singularities of the response generating function. The complement of the amoeba in logarithmic parameter space decomposes into connected components, each with a distinct discrete topological label. The asymptotic response is shown to be controlled by the component extending toward negative infinity.
AI.result: If the origin of logarithmic parameter space lies outside this component (and not on its boundary), exponentially amplified directions must exist; if the origin lies inside, no directional amplification occurs in any direction. This yields a general topological criterion.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a general, dimension-independent topological criterion for classifying responses in arbitrary-dimensional non-Hermitian lattices, tying directional amplification to amoeba topology.

title: Topological Quantum Reservoir Computing
summary: Scaling universal quantum computation and implementing quantum machine learning with protected logical qubits remain challenging. To harness the computational potential of existing fault-tolerant quantum platforms, we introduce topological quantum reservoir computing, a novel approach using protected degrees of freedom for storage and the host system's intrinsic dynamics for information processing. Using a one-dimensional Kitaev chain, we show how long-lived Majorana edge modes and fast bulk responses support these complementary functions within the same many-body system. We identify the tradeoffs governing access to protected memory and show how matched interfaces enable programmable writing and interactions enable autonomous information consolidation from the bulk to the edge. These mechanisms improve performance on tasks requiring long-term retention of temporal information. Our results establish topology as a new resource for quantum reservoir computing and open a route toward near-term quantum computing and quantum machine learning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces topological quantum reservoir computing, using long-lived Majorana edge modes in a 1D Kitaev chain for protected memory while exploiting fast bulk dynamics for computation, showing this topology-enabled division of labor improves temporal information processing.
AI.motivation: Universal quantum computation and quantum machine learning with protected logical qubits remain hard to scale, so the authors seek to exploit the intrinsic dynamics of existing fault-tolerant platforms rather than build full universal processors.
AI.method: Uses a one-dimensional Kitaev chain as a quantum reservoir: long-lived Majorana edge modes serve as protected memory while fast bulk responses perform information processing. Characterizes tradeoffs in accessing protected memory, designs matched interfaces for programmable writing and bulk-edge interactions for autonomous information consolidation.
AI.result: Identifies tradeoffs governing access to protected memory and demonstrates that matched interfaces and edge-bulk interactions enable programmable writing and autonomous consolidation, improving performance on tasks requiring long-term retention of temporal information.
AI.conclusion: Topology is established as a new resource for quantum reservoir computing, opening a route toward near-term quantum computing and quantum machine learning.

title: Distinguishing Conserved Quantum Sectors via Measurement Record Features
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, with 23 pages of Supplemental Material
summary: Conservation laws partition the Hilbert space of a quantum system into invariant sectors that are often difficult to identify directly. Repeated measurements on an ancillary probe, however, generate a measurement record that provides information about the occupied sector. Here we develop a framework for identifying conserved sectors using a $(K+1)$-dimensional feature vector of record statistics, comprising the average outcome frequency and pair-outcome correlations up to $K$ measurement cycles apart. For fixed $K$, the feature vector can be evaluated at a cost linear in record length. In quantum non-demolition measurement models, the average outcome frequency suffices for accurate sector identification. For an interacting spin bath with nontrivial dynamics within each sector, incorporating temporal correlations between successive and more widely separated measurements into the record feature vector substantially improves classification fidelity. Our framework provides an efficient approach to conserved-sector identification and demonstrates the importance of temporal correlations in distinguishing the underlying sector dynamics.

AI.tldr: A $(K+1)$-dimensional feature vector built from ancilla-probe measurement records—average outcome frequency plus pair-outcome correlations up to $K$ cycles apart—identifies conserved Hilbert-space sectors at cost linear in record length, with temporal correlations proving essential for interacting spin baths.
AI.motivation: Conservation laws partition a quantum system's Hilbert space into invariant sectors that are typically hard to identify directly. Repeated measurements on an ancillary probe yield a record carrying information about which sector is occupied, but a systematic, efficient framework for extracting that sector label from the record is lacking.
AI.method: Constructs a $(K+1)$-dimensional feature vector from record statistics: the average outcome frequency plus pair-outcome correlations at lags up to $K$ measurement cycles. For fixed $K$ the vector is computed in time linear in record length. The classifier is benchmarked on quantum non-demolition measurement models and on an interacting spin bath exhibiting nontrivial intra-sector dynamics.
AI.result: In quantum non-demolition models the average outcome frequency alone achieves accurate sector identification. For the interacting spin bath, adding temporal correlations between successive and widely separated measurements into the feature vector substantially improves classification fidelity over frequency-only features.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers an efficient, scalable approach to conserved-sector identification, and demonstrates that temporal correlations in the measurement record are key to distinguishing underlying sector dynamics when intra-sector evolution is nontrivial.

title: Vanilla Adiabatic Quantum Optimization Can Have Subexponential Advantage
summary: We construct a family of objective functions $f \colon \{0,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ for which vanilla adiabatic quantum optimization along $H(s) = -(1-s)\sum_{i=1}^n X_i + s\sum_x f(x)\lvert x\rangle\!\langle x\rvert$ finds the global minimizer in $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ time, whereas any classical algorithm requires $\exp(n^{Ω(1)})$ time to do so in the black-box model. Our result is achieved by replacing the linearization technique in an earlier work of Leng et al. (arXiv:2504.14841), which establishes a similar subexponential quantum speedup using a transverse field Ising mixer rather than $-\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$.

AI.tldr: Constructs objective functions where vanilla adiabatic quantum optimization finds the global minimizer in poly(n) time under a simple transverse-field driver, while any black-box classical algorithm needs exp(n^Ω(1)) time, improving the mixer and linearization approach of Leng et al.
AI.motivation: Earlier work (Leng et al., arXiv:2504.14841) established a subexponential quantum speedup for adiabatic optimization but relied on a transverse-field Ising mixer and a linearization technique. The authors aim to show a stronger separation using the standard/vanilla adiabatic Hamiltonian with the simple driver -sum X_i, avoiding the more elaborate mixer.
AI.method: Design a family of objective functions f: {0,1}^n -> R and analyze the adiabatic evolution under H(s) = -(1-s) sum_i X_i + s sum_x f(x)|x><x|. The construction replaces the linearization technique used by Leng et al. to control the spectral gap and guarantee the runtime, adapting the analysis to the plain transverse-field driver.
AI.result: For the constructed instances, vanilla adiabatic quantum optimization reaches the global minimizer in poly(n) time, whereas any classical black-box algorithm requires exp(n^Ω(1)) time. This yields an exponential (super-polynomial) quantum speedup over black-box classical optimization.
AI.conclusion: Vanilla adiabatic quantum optimization with the standard driver -sum X_i can provably outperform all black-box classical algorithms exponentially on tailored objective functions, strengthening the earlier subexponential result. This clarifies that even the simplest adiabatic schedule suffices for strong separations, with the key technical advance being a new construction replacing the prior linearization approach.

title: Accelerating Quantum Error Correction Simulations under Coherent Noise with Compiled Clifford-Augmented Matrix Product States
comment: Main text (8 pages, 6 figures), supplement (16 pages, 7 figures)
summary: Reliable assessment of quantum error correction requires understanding how coherent errors affect logical performance. Although tensor networks naturally capture coherent interference, entanglement growth and large qubit counts make repeated sampling costly. Here we develop a compiled Clifford-Augmented Matrix Product State (CAMPS) framework that reuses Clifford transformations across shots, recycles qubits released by measurements, evolves a compressed residual state, and accelerates sampling through rotation fusion and compilation tailored to the MPS layout. Surface-code benchmarks under fixed-sign coherent noise yield accurate logical error estimates at small bond dimensions, while random-sign simulations up to distance $d=9$ and on the $[[72,12,6]]$ bivariate bicycle code match the Pauli-twirling approximation results. Compared with uncompiled CAMPS, compiled CAMPS converges at smaller bond dimensions and achieves order-of-magnitude sampling speedups at equal bond dimension, opening a scalable route to studying coherent error propagation in larger fault-tolerant circuits.

AI.tldr: Compiled CAMPS framework enables accurate, scalable simulation of coherent errors in quantum error correction by reusing Clifford transformations and accelerating MPS sampling.
AI.motivation: Reliable assessment of quantum error correction requires understanding how coherent errors affect logical performance. Tensor networks naturally capture coherent interference, but entanglement growth and large qubit counts make repeated sampling costly.
AI.method: A compiled Clifford-Augmented Matrix Product State (CAMPS) framework that reuses Clifford transformations across shots, recycles qubits released by measurements, evolves a compressed residual state, and accelerates sampling via rotation fusion and compilation tailored to the MPS layout.
AI.result: Surface-code benchmarks under fixed-sign coherent noise yield accurate logical error estimates at small bond dimensions; random-sign simulations up to distance d=9 and on the [[72,12,6]] bivariate bicycle code match the Pauli-twirling approximation. Compared with uncompiled CAMPS, compiled CAMPS converges at smaller bond dimensions and achieves order-of-magnitude sampling speedups at equal bond dimension.
AI.conclusion: The compiled CAMPS framework opens a scalable route to studying coherent error propagation in larger fault-tolerant circuits.

title: Odd-Even Effects on Liouvillian Spectra and Relaxation Dynamics in Boundary-Driven Spin Chains
summary: We investigate odd-even effects on Liouvillian spectra and relaxation dynamics in boundary-driven XY and cluster chains. With the bulk couplings and boundary dissipation rule fixed, the parity of chain length determines whether non-decaying oscillatory modes exist. Consequently, odd- and even-sized chains exhibit qualitatively different dynamical behaviors. We trace this mechanism to the coupling between bulk Majorana paths and the boundary jump operators. An isolated path supports undamped modes, and products of an even number of its Majorana operators span a non?decaying subspace of even operators. This structure yields nonzero purely imaginary eigenvalues of the Liouvillian and persistent contributions to bond correlations or magnetization after preparation in product states. The mechanism extends to cluster interactions of even range under a fixed boundary dissipation rule. The existence and frequencies of the persistent modes are independent of the magnitudes of the positive boundary dissipation rates. Our results unveil how chain parity controls the existence of persistent dynamics.

AI.tldr: Chain parity in boundary-driven XY and cluster chains dictates whether non-decaying oscillatory modes exist in the Liouvillian spectrum, producing qualitatively distinct relaxation dynamics for odd versus even lengths.
AI.motivation: To understand what controls the existence of persistent (undamped) dynamics in boundary-driven open quantum chains, the authors examine how the parity of chain length affects Liouvillian spectra and relaxation.
AI.method: The study analyzes Liouvillian spectra and relaxation dynamics of boundary-driven XY and cluster chains with fixed bulk couplings and boundary dissipation, tracing the mechanism to coupling between bulk Majorana paths and boundary jump operators. The mechanism is extended to cluster interactions of even range.
AI.result: Parity determines existence of non-decaying oscillatory modes: isolated Majorana paths support undamped modes, and products of an even number of Majorana operators span a non-decaying subspace of even operators. This yields nonzero purely imaginary Liouvillian eigenvalues and persistent contributions to bond correlations or magnetization after product-state preparation; existence and frequencies are independent of the magnitudes of positive boundary dissipation rates.
AI.conclusion: Chain parity controls the existence of persistent dynamics in these boundary-driven chains, revealing a structural mechanism linking Majorana paths and boundary dissipation to undamped modes.

title: Reliability of quantum communication over erasure channels
summary: Quantum information can be reliably transmitted at rates below the quantum capacity with an error that vanishes as the number of channel uses grows. The reliability function characterizes the optimal exponential decay rate of this error. For quantum erasure channels with a prime input dimension, we determine the reliability function exactly at all positive communication rates below capacity that meet or exceed an explicit critical rate. Notably, stabilizer coding strategies attain this optimal reliability throughout this regime.

AI.tldr: For quantum erasure channels with prime input dimension, the reliability function is determined exactly at all rates between an explicit critical rate and the quantum capacity, and stabilizer codes are shown to attain this optimal error exponent.
AI.motivation: Quantum information can be transmitted reliably below the quantum capacity with vanishing error, but the optimal exponential decay rate of that error (the reliability function) is largely unknown for quantum channels. Prior work lacked an exact characterization for a natural channel family.
AI.method: The authors analyze quantum erasure channels with prime input dimension and derive the reliability function in closed form for the rate regime from an explicit critical rate up to capacity. They construct stabilizer coding strategies and analyze their error exponents to establish achievability matching the converse bound.
AI.result: The reliability function is exactly determined at all communication rates below capacity that meet or exceed an explicit critical rate. Stabilizer codes are shown to achieve the optimal exponential error decay throughout this rate regime.
AI.conclusion: Stabilizer coding suffices to attain the optimal reliability of prime-dimensional quantum erasure channels above the critical rate, yielding an exact reliability function for this regime.

title: CCZ gate beyond the strong Rydberg-blockade regime
summary: We present a protocol for implementing a controlled-controlled-Z (CCZ) gate on a neutral-atom platform, employing three individually addressable atoms confined in a linear array of optical tweezers and operating under finite Rydberg-Rydberg interaction (RRI). The protocol combines successive excitation of the Rydberg atoms with analytically determined pulses and uses two Rydberg levels to access opposite-sign interaction shifts. We show two different paths to get the conditional phase in the target atom: a pair of target pulses with opposite phases and a single detuned target pulse followed by a local phase correction. We derive analytical expressions for the time-integrated Rydberg populations to calculate the associated decay errors and also evaluate gate performance through master-equation simulations. Numerical comparisons with a fast Rydberg-antiblockade (RAB)-based CCZ protocol show improved gate performance at larger interatomic separations within the parameter regime considered. Monte Carlo sampling further quantifies the sensitivity to thermally induced position fluctuations. These results identify the tradeoffs between gate duration, Rydberg-state exposure, and interaction sensitivity, providing an analytically specified route to native three-qubit phase gates beyond the strong-blockade regime.

AI.tldr: A protocol for a native controlled-controlled-Z gate on neutral atoms in a linear tweezer array, using two Rydberg levels under finite Rydberg-Rydberg interaction with analytically designed pulses, is analyzed and shown to outperform a fast antiblockade-based CCZ at larger separations.
AI.motivation: Native three-qubit gates avoid decomposition into two-qubit gates, but strong-blockade Rydberg schemes are limited; the authors seek an analytically tractable CCZ route that works in the finite (non-strong-blockade) interaction regime and clarifies tradeoffs among speed, Rydberg exposure, and interaction sensitivity.
AI.method: Three individually addressable atoms in a linear optical-tweezer array are driven with analytically determined pulses, using two Rydberg levels that access opposite-sign interaction shifts. Two variants realize the conditional phase on the target atom: (i) a pair of target pulses with opposite phases, and (ii) a single detuned target pulse plus local phase correction. Time-integrated Rydberg populations give analytical decay-error estimates, and master-equation simulations assess gate performance, with numerical comparison against a fast Rydberg-antiblockade CCZ and Monte Carlo sampling of thermal position fluctuations.
AI.result: The protocol yields improved gate performance relative to the fast RAB-based CCZ at larger interatomic separations within the studied parameter regime; analytical decay-error expressions agree with master-equation results, and Monte Carlo sampling quantifies sensitivity to thermally induced position fluctuations.
AI.conclusion: The work provides an analytically specified native three-qubit phase gate beyond the strong-blockade regime and identifies tradeoffs between gate duration, Rydberg-state exposure, and interaction sensitivity.

title: Quantum Parallel Algorithm for Multivariate Trace Estimation with Applications
summary: Estimating multivariate traces Tr(A1A2......Ak) is a fundamental task arising across diverse fields. In this paper, We develop a quantum algorithm for this problem tailored to near-term quantum devices. We access matrices by preparing their vectorized states. This access mode yields a tensor-network representation of the multivariate trace, which in turn guides the design of a parallel algorithm. The resulting circuit has depth dominated solely by that of the input oracle and independent of the number of matrices k, at the cost of a qubit count scaling as Θ(k)-a trade-off between circuit depth and circuit size. Moreover, the circuit exhibits a simple modular structure that allows explicit distribution over O(k) devices. We further establish efficient preparation circuits for a broad range of matrix classes, demonstrating the wide applicability of our approach. we present two applications: spectral sum estimation and a quantum implementation of the classical Lanczos method. Both reduce the target problem to sums of multivariate traces, thereby avoiding the construction of matrix polynomial transformations and achieving two levels of parallelism. For certain matrix classes, the resulting algorithms reduce circuit depth by a factor equal to the degree of the approximating polynomial. The shallow circuit depth and distributed implementation make our algorithms particularly suitable for near-term devices.

AI.tldr: The authors propose a shallow, parallel quantum algorithm for estimating multivariate traces Tr(A1...Ak) using a vectorized-state access model, yielding a tensor-network circuit whose depth depends only on the input oracle and is independent of k, at the cost of Θ(k) qubits, with applications to spectral-sum estimation and a quantum Lanczos method.
AI.motivation: Multivariate trace estimation is a fundamental primitive across many fields, yet existing quantum approaches are ill-suited to near-term hardware because circuit depth typically grows with the number of matrices k and with polynomial-transformation overheads. The goal is a resource-efficient, hardware-friendly algorithm.
AI.method: Matrices are accessed by preparing their vectorized states, which induces a tensor-network representation of the multivariate trace that directly guides a parallel circuit design. The circuit has a simple modular structure enabling distribution over O(k) devices, and the authors construct explicit efficient state-preparation circuits for a broad range of matrix classes. The primitive is then applied by reducing spectral-sum estimation and a quantum Lanczos method to sums of multivariate traces, avoiding explicit matrix-polynomial transformations.
