AI.result: The circuit depth is dominated solely by the input-oracle depth and is independent of k, at the cost of Θ(k) qubits—an explicit depth-versus-width trade-off—and admits distribution across O(k) devices. For certain matrix classes, the resulting spectral-sum and Lanczos algorithms reduce circuit depth by a factor equal to the degree of the approximating polynomial, achieving two levels of parallelism.
AI.conclusion: The shallow depth, modularity, and distributed implementability make the approach well suited to near-term quantum devices, while the vectorized-state tensor-network framework offers a general and broadly applicable route to multivariate trace estimation.

title: Gradient Blindness in Adaptive Architecture Search for IQP Born Machines
summary: Instantaneous quantum polynomial (IQP) Born machines learn a probability distribution from data with a circuit of commuting gates that a classical computer trains at hundreds of qubits. Adaptive algorithms grow a sparse circuit from a small seed by adding in every round the candidate gates with the largest loss gradient. Such algorithms never add a candidate whose gradient vanishes, so the choice of seed decides which circuits they can reach. Here we show that a candidate gate has a nonzero gradient for some angles of the circuit exactly when its generator is the sum of an odd number of linearly independent generators already in the circuit. The common seed of one-qubit gates therefore never adds a gate on an even number of qubits, which exact gradients on 12 qubits confirm. A seed of one-qubit gates plus the edges of the Chow-Liu tree sees every candidate, and its circuits match the full circuits on 12 and 16 qubits with 10 to 13 percent of their parameters. At 484 qubits, a heredity pool keeps the search over higher-order gates feasible, and the circuits grown from this seed reach a lower test loss than the dense two-body circuit with 6 percent of its parameters, although the higher-order gates add no gain.

AI.tldr: Adaptive IQP Born machine training can only ever add a gate whose generator is the sum of an odd number of linearly independent generators already present, so the standard one-qubit seed can never add even-qubit gates; an edge-augmented (Chow-Liu tree) seed sees every candidate and reaches full-circuit performance with only 10–13% of parameters, and up to 484 qubits with a heredity pool.
AI.motivation: Adaptive circuit-growing algorithms for IQP Born machines pick, each round, the candidate gates with the largest loss gradient, so vanishing-gradient candidates are never added and the choice of seed silently restricts the reachable circuit space. The paper aims to characterize exactly what a given seed can and cannot reach.
AI.method: A theoretical characterization relating nonzero gradient of a candidate gate (at some circuit angles) to its generator being the sum of an odd number of linearly independent generators already in the circuit. This is validated by exact gradient computations on 12 qubits, and exploited to design a seed of one-qubit gates plus the edges of the Chow-Liu tree. A heredity pool restricts the higher-order gate search for scalability.
AI.result: The one-qubit-gate seed can never add a gate acting on an even number of qubits, confirmed by exact gradients on 12 qubits. The Chow-Liu-edge seed sees every candidate; its grown circuits match full circuits on 12 and 16 qubits using 10–13% of parameters. At 484 qubits, circuits grown from this seed with a heredity pool reach lower test loss than the dense two-body circuit using 6% of its parameters, though higher-order gates yield no additional benefit.
AI.conclusion: Seed choice provably determines reachability in adaptive IQP Born-machine training; a small, physically motivated seed (single-qubit gates + Chow-Liu tree edges) suffices for universality of candidate access and yields highly parameter-efficient, scalable circuits, while higher-order gates appear unnecessary in practice.

title: In-memory measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution
summary: Quantum memories offer to significantly extend the performance of quantum networks, but their complexity and limited performance at telecommunication wavelengths have so far hindered practical deployment. We propose a new memory-assisted measurement device independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) protocol based on in-memory interference. Our approach leverages progress in atomic ensemble memories that enable the interference of a stationary matter qubit and a travelling photonic qubit inside a single quantum memory. We quantitatively evaluate the performance of this scheme against memoryless MDI-QKD and existing two-memory architectures, showing that it not only achieves superior secret key rates and surpasses the memoryless bound at substantially shorter distances, but also reduces hardware requirements by halving the number of memories and detectors. Our results further indicate that off resonant cascaded absorption (ORCA) memories are a particularly promising platform for implementing this protocol, and we outline a concrete design compatible with their capabilities. These findings demonstrate that in-memory interference provides a higher performance, and resource efficient route toward near term memory enhanced quantum secure communications.

AI.tldr: A new memory-assisted MDI-QKD protocol uses in-memory interference between a stationary matter qubit and a travelling photonic qubit within a single atomic ensemble memory, achieving higher secret-key rates, shorter crossover distance to surpass the memoryless bound, and halved hardware (memories and detectors) versus two-memory architectures; ORCA memories are identified as the most promising platform.
AI.motivation: Quantum memories can substantially extend quantum network performance, but their complexity and limited performance at telecom wavelengths have hindered practical deployment. Existing two-memory MDI-QKD architectures also impose heavy hardware demands.
AI.method: Propose a memory-assisted MDI-QKD protocol based on in-memory interference, exploiting atomic ensemble memories that allow interference between a stationary matter qubit and a travelling photonic qubit inside a single quantum memory. Quantitatively benchmark the scheme against memoryless MDI-QKD and existing two-memory architectures, and outline a concrete design compatible with off-resonant cascaded absorption (ORCA) memories.
AI.result: The scheme achieves superior secret-key rates, surpasses the memoryless bound at substantially shorter distances, and halves the number of required memories and detectors. ORCA memories emerge as a particularly promising implementation platform.
AI.conclusion: In-memory interference offers a higher-performance, resource-efficient route toward near-term memory-enhanced quantum secure communications.

title: Quantifying extractable imaginarity with qubit triangles
summary: Two qubit states with the same robustness of imaginarity can differ in the robustness attainable by real filtering on a successful outcome. We represent the input robustness $R$ and the largest conditional robustness $κ$ by the base of a right triangle and the slope of its hypotenuse, respectively. Twice the area, $R^2κ$, defines a faithful, convex measure that is monotone on average under real instruments. In arbitrary finite dimensions, maximizing the mean normalized area of the extracted qubits gives the pointwise smallest strongly monotone extension of the qubit measure. We derive computable bounds on this area by determining the maximum mean squared robustness of the output qubits. This maximum equals the Bures quantum $χ^2$ divergence between the input and its real part. A projection onto orthogonal real subspaces attains the maximum and, when its outcome is retained, preserves the quantum Fisher information at the midpoint of a mixture of the input and its complex conjugate. We obtain exact areas for states with commuting real and imaginary parts and for pure states mixed with white noise. Two eight-dimensional states have identical $R$, $κ$, and optimal mean squared robustness, yet their different areas rule out deterministic conversion by real operations in one direction.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce a geometric "area" measure of imaginarity for qubit states, framed as R²κ (twice the triangle area with base R and hypotenuse slope κ), prove it is a faithful convex monotone under real instruments, extend it to arbitrary dimensions as the pointwise smallest strongly monotone extension, and give computable bounds via the Bures quantum χ² divergence.
AI.motivation: Two qubit states sharing the same robustness of imaginarity R can differ in the conditional robustness κ achievable after real filtering on a successful outcome, so R alone is insufficient to characterize imaginarity. A refined, faithful, and operationally meaningful quantifier—and a way to extend it beyond qubits—is needed.
AI.method: Represent the input robustness R as the base of a right triangle and the largest conditional robustness κ as the slope of its hypotenuse; define twice the area, R²κ, as the measure. Prove monotonicity on average under real instruments. In finite dimensions, maximize the mean normalized area of extracted qubits to obtain the pointwise smallest strongly monotone extension. Bound the area by computing the maximum mean squared robustness of output qubits, showing it equals the Bures quantum χ² divergence between the input and its real part; identify the projection onto orthogonal real subspaces as the optimizer, and analyze quantum Fisher information preservation at the mixture midpoint of the input and its complex conjugate.
AI.result: R²κ is faithful and convex and monotone on average under real instruments; the maximization yields the pointwise smallest strongly monotone extension of the qubit measure. The maximum mean squared robustness equals the Bures quantum χ² divergence to the real part, is attained by projection onto orthogonal real subspaces, and—when that outcome is retained—preserves quantum Fisher information at the midpoint of the input and its complex conjugate. Exact areas are derived for states with commuting real and imaginary parts and for pure states mixed with white noise. Two eight-dimensional states with identical R, κ, and optimal mean squared robustness have different areas, ruling out deterministic conversion by real operations in one direction.
AI.conclusion: The area measure R²κ constitutes a faithful, convex, on-average monotone quantification of imaginarity that refines the robustness, admits a canonical strongly monotone multidimensional extension, and is operationally powerful: it certifies the impossibility of deterministic real-operation conversion between higher-dimensional states that are indistinguishable under R, κ, and optimal mean squared robustness.

title: A Convex-Roof Affinity-Square Measure of Quantum Imaginarity
summary: Quantum imaginarity characterizes the part of a quantum state that cannot be represented by real density matrices in a fixed reference basis. We study an affinity-square measure of imaginarity for pure states and its convex-roof extension to mixed states. The pure state quantity is defined by minimizing the affinity-square measure over the convex set of real states. This optimization admits a closed expression determined by the modulus of the conjugation overlap between a state and its complex conjugate. The measure vanishes precisely when the state is real up to a global phase. We prove that the convex-roof extension is faithful, convex, monotone under real operations, and nonincreasing on average under selective real operations. For arbitrary single-qubit mixed states, we evaluate the convex roof exactly and express it in terms of the imaginary component of the off-diagonal density-matrix element. We also compare pure-state imaginarity with an auxiliary affinity-square coherence functional and give the corresponding phase weights.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces and analyzes an affinity-square measure of quantum imaginarity for pure states, with a closed-form expression via the conjugation overlap, and extends it to mixed states via convex roof, proving required resource-theoretic properties and deriving exact results for qubits.
AI.motivation: Quantum imaginarity quantifies the part of a quantum state that cannot be described by real density matrices in a fixed reference basis. There is a need for a well-behaved, computable imaginarity measure with rigorous resource-theoretic properties and tractable evaluations.
AI.method: Define a pure-state affinity-square imaginarity measure as the minimum of the affinity-square functional over the convex set of real states, yielding a closed form determined by the modulus of the conjugation overlap between the state and its complex conjugate. Extend to mixed states via the convex-roof construction.
AI.result: The closed-form pure-state measure vanishes exactly when the state is real up to a global phase. The convex-roof extension is proven faithful, convex, monotone under real operations, and nonincreasing on average under selective real operations. For arbitrary single-qubit mixed states the convex roof is computed exactly in terms of the imaginary part of the off-diagonal density-matrix element. Pure-state imaginarity is also compared with an auxiliary affinity-square coherence functional, providing corresponding phase weights.
AI.conclusion: The affinity-square imaginarity measure, both in pure form and via convex roof, is a valid and computable imaginarity quantifier satisfying key resource-theoretic monotonicity properties, with exact qubit expressions and a clear relationship to coherence functionals.

title: QuFrame: Pauli Frame Tracking for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Control
summary:
Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires continuous quantum error correction (QEC) to suppress physical noise. While Clifford-only workloads can defer corrections to software post-processing, universal computation breaks this paradigm: executing non-Clifford gates via magic-state gadgets introduces hard, real-time control-flow dependencies on error-corrected measurements. Consequently, the controller must extract syndromes, decode them, and update the Pauli frame in real time, closing the entire QEC loop within a strict $1\,μ\text{s}$ cycle. However, prior proposals on Pauli frame tracking remain largely theoretical, leaving the microarchitectural bottlenecks of tracking, resolving, and synchronizing frame updates across distributed control pipelines unaddressed.
  To this end, we present QuFrame, a control microarchitecture for real-time Pauli frame tracking that closes the QEC loop within $1\,μ\text{s}$ while sustaining QPU-rate throughput. By introducing QuFrameISA, we cleanly decouple instruction execution from continuous Pauli frame management. Execution is distributed across per-qubit Instruction Resolution Engines (IREs) that resolve instructions against the frame via a single table lookup, while a Pauli Frame Management Unit enables independent, lock-free concurrent commits. To strictly guarantee the $1\,μ\text{s}$ deadline, QuFrame pairs an asynchronous primary decoder with an on-chip fallback decoder that resolves in $144\,\text{ns}$, natively reconciling divergent updates in hardware without degrading logical error rates.

AI.tldr: QuFrame is a control microarchitecture that achieves real-time Pauli frame tracking, closing the full quantum error correction loop within a strict 1 μs cycle at QPU-rate throughput, using a dedicated ISA, per-qubit resolution engines, and a dual-decoder design.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing needs continuous QEC. Clifford-only workloads can defer corrections to software post-processing, but universal computation with non-Clifford gates via magic-state gadgets introduces hard real-time control-flow dependencies on error-corrected measurements, requiring the controller to extract syndromes, decode, and update the Pauli frame within 1 μs. Prior Pauli frame tracking proposals are largely theoretical and leave microarchitectural bottlenecks of tracking, resolving, and synchronizing frame updates across distributed pipelines unaddressed.
AI.method: QuFrame introduces QuFrameISA to cleanly decouple instruction execution from continuous Pauli frame management. Execution is distributed across per-qubit Instruction Resolution Engines (IREs) that resolve instructions against the frame via a single table lookup, while a Pauli Frame Management Unit enables independent, lock-free concurrent commits. To guarantee the 1 μs deadline, QuFrame pairs an asynchronous primary decoder with an on-chip fallback decoder resolving in 144 ns, natively reconciling divergent updates in hardware.
AI.result: QuFrame closes the QEC loop within 1 μs while sustaining QPU-rate throughput. The fallback decoder resolves in 144 ns and reconciles divergent updates in hardware without degrading logical error rates.
AI.conclusion: QuFrame demonstrates a practical control microarchitecture for real-time Pauli frame tracking, addressing the microarchitectural bottlenecks left open by prior theoretical proposals and enabling the hard real-time loop required for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: Doppler effect on dual-downlink time-bin quantum key distribution and a proposed ephemeris-assisted witness-field correction
summary: Time-bin entanglement is promising for satellite Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) due to its compatibility with telecom fiber networks, but its phase-sensitive measurements are vulnerable to Doppler effects induced by satellite motion. We present a spectral-temporal framework for time-bin-entangled photon pairs generated onboard a satellite via Spontaneous Parametric Down Conversion (SPDC) and distributed to two Optical Ground Stations (OGSs) over independent downlinks with distinct Doppler shifts. Each OGS is equipped with an Unbalanced Mach-Zehnder Interferometer (UMZI) used to perform Bennett-Brassard-Mermin 1992 (BBM92) entangled-photon QKD. In a simulated Low Earth Orbit (LEO) pass with matched 400 ps analyzer delays, the received time-bin separation changes by at most 8.8 fs per link, while the combined carrier phase shifts by about 38 rad, which primarily degrades phase-basis correlations. After zero-Doppler calibration, this phase separates into independent signal-and idler-link contributions, allowing each station to correct its link Doppler phase shift locally, without real-time phase exchange between the stations. We propose an ephemeris-assisted feed-forward architecture, in which an auxiliary interferometer analyzes a co-propagating classical witness field to reconstruct the local Doppler-induced phase, which a phase modulator then compensates on the quantum channel. In a noise-free model, a 1 Hz sample-and-hold correction rate keeps the phase-basis Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) below 2% and retains 93% of the ideal asymptotic key yield. After 18 accumulated passes, the corrected finite secret key reaches 95% of its ideal length, whereas relabeling the parity from the ephemeris without optical correction reaches only about 8%.

AI.tldr: A spectral-temporal framework models time-bin-entangled SPDC photon pairs generated onboard a satellite and measured at two optical ground stations under distinct Doppler shifts; a local ephemeris-assisted feed-forward optical phase correction restores phase-basis correlations without real-time inter-station phase exchange.
AI.motivation: Time-bin entanglement suits satellite QKD for telecom-fiber compatibility, but its phase-sensitive BBM92 measurements are degraded by satellite-motion-induced Doppler shifts on independent downlinks, which alter both the time-bin separation and the accumulated carrier phase and thus raise phase-basis QBER.
AI.method: Source-in-space SPDC time-bin pairs distributed to two OGSs, each with a UMZI (400 ps matched analyzer delays) for BBM92 QKD, analyzed in a spectral-temporal model over a simulated LEO pass. After zero-Doppler calibration, the combined carrier phase decomposes into independent signal- and idler-link contributions, enabling purely local correction. An ephemeris-assisted feed-forward architecture uses an auxiliary interferometer to sense a co-propagating classical witness field, reconstructs the local Doppler phase, and applies compensation via a phase modulator on the quantum channel.
AI.result: Received time-bin separation changes by at most 8.8 fs per link, while the combined carrier phase shifts by ~38 rad over the pass, primarily degrading phase-basis correlations. In a noise-free model, a 1 Hz sample-and-hold correction keeps phase-basis QBER below 2% and retains 93% of ideal asymptotic key yield; after 18 accumulated passes the corrected finite secret key reaches 95% of its ideal length, versus ~8% for ephemeris-only parity relabeling without optical correction.
AI.conclusion: Local, witness-field-based feed-forward phase compensation makes onboard-generated time-bin entanglement viable for satellite BBM92 QKD across Doppler-shifted downlinks, removing the need for real-time phase exchange between ground stations while preserving near-ideal key rates and finite-key performance.

title: Long-distance continuous variable entanglement distribution over deployed fibre
summary: Continuous-variable (CV) entanglement offers deterministic generation and room-temperature coherent detection for quantum networks, but distributing it over deployed fibre has been hindered by the need to stabilise optical phase, polarisation, and timing at remote receivers. Here we demonstrate, to our knowledge, the first distribution of CV entanglement over deployed metropolitan fibre using independent coherent receivers. The two modes of a two-mode squeezed vacuum state are delivered to remote nodes through 23 km ($\approx 7$ dB loss) and 450 m ($\approx 1$ dB loss) deployed fibre links. Each node uses its own free-running laser and polarisation-diverse coherent receiver. Co-propagating pilot tones enable digital recovery of timing, phase and polarisation, while inter-mode correlations fix the quadrature alignment. We certify entanglement with a Simon-Duan value of $1.915\pm 0.013$, below the separability bound of 2 and a logarithmic negativity of $0.067\pm0.011$. By replacing optical stabilisation with digital reconstruction, our approach offers a practical route towards scalable CV quantum networks.

AI.tldr: First distribution of continuous-variable (CV) entanglement over deployed metropolitan fibre using independent, free-running coherent receivers at remote nodes, with digital recovery of timing, phase, and polarisation replacing optical stabilisation.
AI.motivation: CV entanglement offers deterministic generation and room-temperature coherent detection for quantum networks, but field distribution over deployed fibre has been hindered by the need to stabilise optical phase, polarisation, and timing at remote receivers.
AI.method: Two modes of a two-mode squeezed vacuum state are delivered to remote nodes over 23 km (≈7 dB) and 450 m (≈1 dB) deployed fibre links. Each node uses its own free-running laser and polarisation-diverse coherent receiver. Co-propagating pilot tones enable digital recovery of timing, phase, and polarisation, while inter-mode correlations fix the quadrature alignment.
AI.result: Entanglement is certified with a Simon-Duan value of 1.915±0.013 (below the separability bound of 2) and a logarithmic negativity of 0.067±0.011, confirming successful CV entanglement distribution.
AI.conclusion: Replacing optical stabilisation with digital reconstruction offers a practical route towards scalable CV quantum networks.

title: Efficient simulation of variational quantum circuits: representation, accuracy and CPU/GPU allocation
summary: Classical circuit simulation supports quantum software development and verification and provides a baseline for assessing quantum advantage. We compare gate-based statevector simulation, direct Pauli evolution and matrix product states for molecular and spin Variational Hamiltonian Ansatze and hardware-efficient ansatze on CPU/GPU systems, varying width, depth, precision and resource allocation. In the tested implementations, direct Pauli evolution benefits complex molecular VHA, whereas GPUs accelerate wider spin and hardware efficient circuits. Matrix product state is useful when limited entanglement permits accurate compression; corrected CPU FP32 can meet the tested tolerance while costing more than FP64. Workload size, startup, worker memory and task-specific profiling can change the preferred allocation. Matched NumPy Pauli updates accelerate two-layer full LiH by 3.45-fold; the GPU gives approximately 30-fold acceleration over 18-thread Aer for 28-qubit, four-layer TFIM, both in FP64. We provide a procedure for choosing representation, precision and worker allocation jointly, comparing the cost of complete energy evaluations under accuracy, memory and core constraints.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks classical quantum circuit simulation methods (gate-based statevector, direct Pauli evolution, matrix product states) for Variational Hamiltonian Ansätze and hardware-efficient ansätze on CPU/GPU, and provides a procedure for jointly selecting representation, precision, and worker allocation under accuracy, memory, and core constraints.
AI.motivation: Classical circuit simulation underpins quantum software development and verification and serves as a baseline for assessing quantum advantage, yet practitioners lack guidance on which simulation representation, numerical precision, and hardware allocation to choose for molecular and spin variational ansätze.
AI.method: Compares gate-based statevector simulation, direct Pauli evolution, and matrix product states across CPU/GPU systems, varying circuit width, depth, precision (FP32/FP64), and resource allocation, using molecular VHA and hardware-efficient ansätze; includes matched NumPy Pauli updates and profiling of startup, worker memory, and task-specific behavior.
AI.result: Direct Pauli evolution benefits complex molecular VHA, while GPUs accelerate wider spin and hardware-efficient circuits; MPS is useful when limited entanglement permits accurate compression; corrected CPU FP32 meets tested tolerance but costs more than FP64. Matched NumPy Pauli updates accelerate two-layer full LiH by 3.45-fold, and the GPU achieves ~30-fold speedup over 18-thread Aer for 28-qubit, four-layer TFIM (both FP64).
AI.conclusion: Representation, precision, and worker allocation should be chosen jointly, since workload size, startup, worker memory, and task-specific profiling affect the preferred configuration; the paper supplies a procedure comparing the cost of complete energy evaluations under accuracy, memory, and core constraints.

title: A unified approach to the time-dependent quantum harmonic oscillator via point transformations and Lie symmetries
summary: We revisit the time-dependent harmonic oscillator (TDHO) in quantum mechanics based on the notion of equivalence transformations and Lie point symmetries. Within this framework, we give the most general point transformations depending on seven parameters which map from the TDHO to the usual harmonic oscillator (HO) and the other way around. As a byproduct we reconstruct the Schrödinger propagator (Mehler's kernel) for the time-independent harmonic oscillator. We demonstrate, without recourse to the Lewis--Riesenwert (LR) invariant, how Lie algebraic methods enable alternative derivation of the normalized wave functions of the TDHO by constructing solutions invariant under some specific subgroup of $\SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ combined with the gauge group. We further show that, on the relevant $\SL(2,\mathbb{R})$-invariant solution family, the Lewis--Riesenfeld operator defines a compatible second-order differential constraint, thereby clarifying its relation to the Lie symmetry structure of the TDHO.

AI.tldr: The paper derives the most general seven-parameter point transformations mapping the time-dependent harmonic oscillator (TDHO) to the standard harmonic oscillator and back, reconstructs Mehler's propagator as a byproduct, and shows that Lie algebraic methods (without invoking the Lewis–Riesenfeld invariant) yield the normalized TDHO wave functions; it also shows the LR operator acts as a compatible second-order differential constraint on the relevant SL(2,R)-invariant solution family.
AI.motivation: Standard treatments of the TDHO rely heavily on the Lewis–Riesenfeld invariant without clarifying its connection to the symmetry structure. The authors seek an equivalence-transformation/Lie-symmetry based understanding that is self-contained and that explains the LR invariant's role relative to the Lie symmetry algebra.
AI.method: Equivalence transformations and Lie point symmetry analysis. A general seven-parameter family of point transformations connecting TDHO and HO is constructed. Normalized TDHO wave functions are obtained by building solutions invariant under specific subgroups of SL(2,R) combined with the gauge group. The LR operator is then examined as a differential constraint on the SL(2,R)-invariant solution family.
AI.result: A seven-parameter point transformation relating TDHO and HO is given. Mehler's kernel for the time-independent oscillator is rederived as a byproduct. The normalized TDHO wave functions are recovered via Lie algebraic methods without the LR invariant. On the SL(2,R)-invariant solution family, the Lewis–Riesenfeld operator is shown to define a compatible second-order differential constraint.
AI.conclusion: Lie symmetry and equivalence-transformation techniques provide an alternative, invariant-free route to the TDHO solution and clarify the LR operator as a second-order constraint compatible with the SL(2,R) symmetry algebra, situating the LR invariant within the Lie symmetry structure of the TDHO.

title: Virtual Autopurification in Translationally Invariant Quantum States
summary: We introduce virtual autopurification (VAP), a protocol for virtual purification that operates entirely within a single translationally invariant system. Virtual purification suppresses thermal fluctuations and decoherence noise by amplifying the dominant pure component of a mixed state, but its standard implementation requires multiple copies of the state and global entangled measurements. VAP avoids the multiple-copy overhead by constructing virtual copies from spatially separated subregions and performing entangled measurements only between them. Assuming clustering of correlations, we show that VAP reproduces the expectation values of the standard virtual purification protocol, with discrepancies that decay exponentially in both the buffer length and the inter-subregion distance. Numerical simulations support the theoretical predictions and demonstrate accurate implementation of virtual cooling with reduced resource requirements. Our results establish VAP as a resource-efficient and scalable approach to quantum-state purification in near-term devices.

AI.tldr: VAP is a single-system protocol for virtual purification that uses spatially separated subregions as virtual copies, reproducing standard virtual purification with exponentially small error and reduced resources.
AI.motivation: Standard virtual purification amplifies the dominant pure component of a mixed state to suppress thermal and decoherence noise, but it requires multiple copies of the state and global entangled measurements—an expensive overhead for near-term devices.
AI.method: VAP constructs virtual copies of the state from spatially separated subregions of a single translationally invariant system and performs entangled measurements only between these subregions, avoiding multiple-copy overhead. Under an assumption of clustering of correlations, the authors bound the deviation from the standard protocol.
AI.result: VAP reproduces the expectation values of standard virtual purification, with discrepancies decaying exponentially in both the buffer length and the inter-subregion distance. Numerical simulations confirm the theoretical predictions and show accurate virtual cooling with reduced resource requirements.
AI.conclusion: VAP is a resource-efficient and scalable approach to quantum-state purification suited to near-term devices.

title: Linear-mode photon counting performance and intrinsic dark current in HgCdTe APDs for quantum optical applications
summary: The performance of HgCdTe APDs for single photon detection at T=80 K has been characterized using a hybrized Resistive Trans-Impedance Amplifier (RTIA) and a deported Capacitance Trans-impedance amplifier (CTIA). The single-photon detection capacity was characterized with the HgCdTe APDs operated in linear mode with high APD gain, M>400, and hybridized with the RTIA. The measurements revealed an external photon detection efficiency (PDE) of 42 % to 55 %, and a dark count rate (DCR) of 2.6 MHz to 17 MHz, for an amplitude threshold ranging from 2.5 to 4.5 times the rms noise of the amplifier. Taking into account the unity gain quantum efficiency, QE=63%, this corresponds to an internal PDE ranging from 66 % to 86 %. Using the deported CTIA, it was demonstrated that the high level of DCR is not the intrinsic limit of the APD technology. The CTIA approach enables direct measurement of the APD dark current, Idark, with gain-normalized dark current levels as low as Idark/M=10.9 fA at M = 450. This corresponds to a DCR of 150 Hz which is compatible with the requirements for most of the quantum photonics applications.

AI.tldr: HgCdTe APDs at 80 K are characterized for single-photon detection with two amplifiers; external PDE of 42–55% and DCR of 2.6–17 MHz are found, and a deported CTIA shows the high DCR is amplifier-limited, not intrinsic, with gain-normalized dark current down to 10.9 fA (DCR ≈ 150 Hz).
AI.motivation: Assess whether HgCdTe avalanche photodiodes (APDs) at T=80 K are viable for single-photon detection, and determine whether the observed dark count rate reflects an intrinsic limit of the APD technology or an artifact of the readout circuitry.
AI.method: HgCdTe APDs were operated in linear mode at high gain (M>400) and hybridized with a Resistive Trans-Impedance Amplifier (RTIA) for single-photon counting measurements at T=80 K. A deported Capacitance Trans-impedance Amplifier (CTIA) was used to measure the APD dark current directly, gain-normalized.
AI.result: With the RTIA, external PDE of 42–55% and DCR of 2.6–17 MHz were measured at thresholds of 2.5–4.5× the amplifier rms noise; relative to unity-gain QE = 63%, the internal PDE is 66–86%. With the CTIA, gain-normalized dark current as low as Idark/M = 10.9 fA at M = 450 was obtained, corresponding to DCR ≈ 150 Hz.
AI.conclusion: The elevated DCR measured with the RTIA is not the intrinsic limit of the HgCdTe APD technology but is governed by the readout/amplifier configuration. The CTIA-derived DCR of ~150 Hz satisfies the requirements of most quantum photonics applications, establishing HgCdTe APDs as a promising single-photon detection technology.

title: Bound entanglement as a trigonometric moment problem
summary: Entangled states that are positive under partial transposition (PPT) are the main obstruction to a simple description of entanglement. We study three basic questions about them within a class of multiqubit states, the mixtures, with real but possibly negative weights, of products of equatorial spin coherent states of several groups of qubits: which PPT entangled states belong to the class, how robust their entanglement is to white noise, and how small their rank can be. In this class each question becomes a question about a truncated trigonometric moment problem. Every such state is PPT across every bipartition, and it is fully separable exactly when an associated multi-level Toeplitz matrix is the moment matrix of a positive measure on the torus. We answer the three questions exactly in the following cases. For three qubits, every rank-four PPT entangled state with nonzero Lorentz invariant belongs to the class after invertible local operators, which proves a working hypothesis of Garberg, Irgens and Myrheim and yields a complete set of invariants for this seven-dimensional family; among the states with vanishing invariant, exactly a one-parameter family belongs to it. For every three-qubit state built from an unextendible product basis, the white-noise threshold for full separability is $λ^*=1-2/(1+\sqrt{1+s})$ with a local-unitary invariant $s\in(0,1]$, and $λ^*=3-2\sqrt2$ for the Shifts basis; a witness in closed form detects every entangled state of this family with eight local Pauli settings. For two groups of qubits we construct extremal states of minimal rank, and for three groups we determine the minimal rank of entanglement within the class in several configurations.

AI.tldr: PPT-entangled multiqubit states are recast as truncated trigonometric moment problems; this yields exact answers on membership, white-noise robustness, and minimal rank for equatorial-coherent-state mixtures.
AI.motivation: PPT entangled states obstruct a simple characterization of entanglement. The authors ask three basic questions about them (which PPT entangled states lie in the class, how robust the entanglement is to white noise, and how small the rank can be) inside a tractable family.
AI.method: They consider mixtures (real, possibly negative weights) of products of equatorial spin coherent states over several groups of qubits, reducing each question to a truncated trigonometric moment problem. Full separability is shown equivalent to an associated multilevel Toeplitz matrix being the moment matrix of a positive measure on the torus; they solve this exactly in specific cases.
AI.result: For three qubits, every rank-four PPT entangled state with nonzero Lorentz invariant lies in the class under invertible local operators (confirming a hypothesis of Garberg, Irgens and Myrheim) and a complete set of invariants is obtained for this seven-dimensional family; with vanishing invariant, exactly a one-parameter family belongs. For every three-qubit unextendible-product-basis state the white-noise threshold is λ* = 1 − 2/(1 + √(1+s)), s ∈ (0,1], with λ* = 3 − 2√2 for the Shifts basis, and a closed-form witness with eight local Pauli settings detects all entangled states of the family. For two groups of qubits extremal minimal-rank states are constructed, and for three groups the minimal entanglement rank is determined in several configurations.
AI.conclusion: The moment-problem reformulation gives exact, constructive answers to the three questions for equatorial-coherent-state mixtures, including a full invariant classification of three-qubit rank-four PPT states and closed-form entanglement witnesses.

title: From BBM92 Measurements to Secure Keys: Challenges in a Practical Implementation
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures. Published in Entropy Special Issue "Quantum Information" Celebrating Professor Gilles Brassard's 70th Birthday
summary: The protocol introduced by C. H. Bennett, G. Brassard and N. D. Mermin in 1992 (BBM92) is one of the most important and widely adopted quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols. As with any other QKD protocol, its practical security depends on satisfying the assumptions underlying its theoretical security proofs. Here, we examine two common implementations of BBM92: a conventional passive receiver and a time-multiplexed configuration that halves the number of detectors. We characterise the passive polarisation analysers common to both architectures and present experimental results obtained with the time-multiplexed receiver, employing a continuous-wave (CW) pumped spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) source of polarisation-entangled photon pairs and threshold detectors. We investigate the challenges encountered during post-processing when attempting to satisfy the requirements of existing security proofs and discuss the gap between theoretical security assumptions and the extraction of a provably secure cryptographic key.

AI.tldr: This work characterizes passive polarization analyzers in two BBM92 QKD receiver architectures (conventional passive and a time-multiplexed design halving detector count) and experimentally tests the time-multiplexed receiver with a CW-pumped SPDC polarization-entangled source and threshold detectors, highlighting post-processing challenges that create a gap between theoretical security assumptions and provably secure key extraction.
AI.motivation: BBM92 is a leading QKD protocol, but its practical security depends on satisfying the assumptions of its theoretical security proofs; real implementations may violate these assumptions, so the practical behavior of common receiver designs needs examination.
AI.method: Characterization of the passive polarization analyzers shared by both receiver architectures; experimental evaluation of a time-multiplexed receiver using a continuous-wave-pumped SPDC source of polarization-entangled photon pairs and threshold detectors; analysis of post-processing steps aimed at meeting security-proof requirements.
AI.result: Experimental results are reported for the time-multiplexed receiver, and post-processing is found to face challenges in satisfying the requirements of existing security proofs, exposing a discrepancy between theoretical assumptions and practical key extraction.
AI.conclusion: Practical BBM92 implementations, particularly the time-multiplexed receiver, do not straightforwardly meet the assumptions of existing security proofs; a gap remains between theoretical security and the extraction of a provably secure cryptographic key, motivating closer alignment of implementation and proof assumptions.

title: Sharp rank thresholds and cubic support in PPT extensions of completely symmetric states
summary: For completely symmetric states on $d\ge3$ parties of actual local rank $N\ge3$, the least rank of an entangled state passing any prescribed finite positive level of the PPT extension hierarchy is $3d+N-3$. At equality, the two- and three-party marginals recover a ternary plane cubic shared by every extension. On this cubic the hierarchy becomes exact at a finite level precisely when every singularity outside the zero locus of the contraction quadratic is a split real node. We give the first exact level or an exact feasibility test for it, independent of $d$. On a smooth cubic the thresholds along the specified paths to the square of a flex tangent reduce to elliptic division and have unique rank-two Gram matrices. On reflection-invariant paths we obtain a quartic formula and the leading asymptotic constant. The least rank for entanglement itself is $3d+N-5$, and we classify equality. An explicit rational rank-nine three-qutrit state on a smooth cubic passes the first extension level and fails the second.

title: A Relativistic Quantum Mechanical Formulation of Wu-Shaknov Entanglements
comment: Some further improvements upon the text have been made
summary: It is suggested that a spontaneous formation of quantum mechanical entanglements does actually occur between spin, helicity and polarization states involved in creation-annihilation processes. A framework built up earlier that presumably affords a unified relativistic quantum mechanical description of free particle-antiparticle pairs of any spin is used to propose a comprehensive formulation of Wu-Shaknov entanglements. Explicit relationships between amplitudes and Born-like probabilities associated to incoming and outgoing states are obtained thereafter on the basis of certain theoretical assumptions. The behaviours of these relationships under the action of a dynamical group which is taken to supply observational correlations for different frames in spacetime are then specified. It appears that a modified version of some of the conventional conservation laws may afford a set of general selection rules for the formation of relativistic entanglements.

AI.motivation: The abstract is motivated by the need for a unified relativistic quantum mechanical description of entanglement formation (Wu-Shaknov type) involving spin, helicity, and polarization states in creation-annihilation processes, extending a previously constructed framework to arbitrary spin.
AI.method: A previously built unified relativistic quantum-mechanical framework for free particle-antiparticle pairs of any spin is used to formulate Wu-Shaknov entanglements comprehensively. Explicit relations between amplitudes and Born-like probabilities for incoming and outgoing states are derived under stated theoretical assumptions, and their behavior under a dynamical group supplying observational correlations across spacetime frames is specified.
