AI.conclusion: Spontaneous entanglement formation among spin, helicity, and polarization states is argued to occur in creation-annihilation processes, and modified conservation laws may provide general selection rules governing relativistic entanglement formation.

title: On a local hidden-variable model for postselected EPR correlations
summary: A theoretical and numerical analysis of a Bell-type experiment is presented, where linear polarization measurements on nonmaximally entangled two-qubit states are modeled through a sigmoid-based threshold mechanism that violates the fair-sampling assumption required by the CHSH inequality. Numerical simulations characterize how closely this local construction can reproduce quantum-like correlations in the postselected detected sample, for both the |Phi_r> and |Psi_r> states over a range of entanglement parameters. For the tested configurations, the model produces CHSH-type violations only in the postselected detected sample through a setting-dependent detection mechanism, operating outside the assumptions of both the CHSH inequality and Mermin's 82.8% efficiency bound. The model is not in conflict with loophole-free Bell experiments, which specifically close the detection loophole exploited here. The CH--Eberhard analysis in the one-detector-per-side configuration yields J < 0 throughout the full range of entanglement parameters, as required for a strictly local model. The model is further extended with a local adaptive-threshold mechanism implementing one-sided memory. A paired comparison shows that this specific memory rule produces a systematic and reproducible shift in the CH--Eberhard parameter J relative to the fixed-threshold model, while leaving the CH--Eberhard analysis qualitatively unchanged under the tested conditions. The results characterize how a local, setting-dependent postselection mechanism shapes Bell-test statistics across a range of entanglement parameters, within the specific configurations and threshold rules tested.

AI.tldr: A local, setting-dependent sigmoid threshold model reproduces CHSH-type violations only in postselected samples (exploiting the detection loophole) for nonmaximally entangled |Phi_r> and |Psi_r> states, while the CH-Eberhard parameter stays J < 0; a one-sided memory adaptive threshold shifts J systematically without changing the qualitative analysis.
AI.motivation: To test whether a strictly local, fair-sampling-violating detection mechanism can mimic quantum-like Bell correlations, and to characterize how such postselection shapes Bell-test statistics across entanglement parameters without conflicting with loophole-free Bell experiments.
AI.method: Linear polarization measurements on nonmaximally entangled two-qubit states are modeled with a sigmoid-based threshold detection mechanism that is setting-dependent and violates the fair-sampling assumption. Numerical simulations compare CHSH statistics for |Phi_r> and |Psi_r> over a range of entanglement parameters, plus a CH-Eberhard analysis in the one-detector-per-side configuration and an extension with a local adaptive-threshold rule implementing one-sided memory.
AI.result: CHSH-type violations appear only in the postselected detected sample and only via the setting-dependent detection mechanism, operating outside both the CHSH assumptions and Mermin's 82.8% efficiency bound. CH-Eberhard analysis yields J < 0 across the full entanglement range, consistent with locality. The adaptive (memory) threshold produces a systematic, reproducible shift in J relative to fixed-threshold results while leaving the CH-Eberhard analysis qualitatively unchanged.
AI.conclusion: The work characterizes how a local, setting-dependent postselection mechanism shapes Bell-test statistics over a range of entanglement parameters within the tested configurations and threshold rules, and remains compatible with loophole-free Bell experiments that close the detection loophole.

title: Gutzwiller Quantum-Classical Embedding for Dynamics Simulations of Correlated Electron Systems
summary: Simulating the real-time dynamics of correlated electron systems requires a nonperturbative treatment of local correlations over long times, a challenge for classical methods. We present the time-dependent Gutzwiller quantum-classical embedding framework, t-GQCE, for generic multi-orbital lattice models with time-dependent Hamiltonians. Within the time-dependent ghost Gutzwiller approximation, the lattice dynamics is mapped onto a noninteracting quasiparticle lattice, propagated classically, coupled to finite interacting embedding models propagated on quantum processors. The two parts exchange only embedding Hamiltonian parameters and single-particle density matrices, and the framework is agnostic to the quantum dynamics solver. We demonstrate it with adaptive variational quantum dynamics simulations of interaction quenches in the Hubbard model on the Bethe lattice. Without ghost orbitals, the embedding problem reduces to a single qubit, simulated on IBM quantum hardware with two qubits, including an ancilla. With more ghost orbitals, t-GQCE suppresses the artificial undamped oscillations of the conventional Gutzwiller approximation and approaches nonequilibrium dynamical mean-field theory results for weak and strong quenches. Statevector simulations with 2, 4 and 6 ghost orbitals per spin, or 8, 12 and 16 qubits, give adaptive circuits that follow the embedding states with infidelities below $5\times10^{-4}$. Under trapped-ion noise models, circuit compression, measurements in rotated orbital bases with post-selection, and noise mitigation reduce the measurement errors severalfold. At one third of the error rates of a hardware-benchmarked noise model, they reach an accuracy of $0.01$ for the single-particle density matrix and the double occupancy with $10^5$ shots per time step, and the Quantinuum H2-Emulator gives similar accuracy.

AI.tldr: t-GQCE is a hybrid quantum-classical embedding framework that propagates a noninteracting quasiparticle lattice classically and finite interacting embedding models on quantum processors, enabling nonperturbative real-time dynamics of correlated multi-orbital lattice models.
AI.motivation: Simulating real-time dynamics of correlated electron systems requires nonperturbative treatment of local correlations over long times, which is challenging for classical methods. The authors seek a framework that offloads the hard local interacting problem to quantum hardware while keeping lattice-scale propagation classically tractable.
AI.method: Within the time-dependent ghost Gutzwiller approximation, the lattice maps onto a noninteracting quasiparticle lattice propagated classically, coupled to finite interacting embedding models solved on quantum processors. Only embedding Hamiltonian parameters and single-particle density matrices are exchanged, making the scheme solver-agnostic. They use adaptive variational quantum dynamics simulations of interaction quenches in the Hubbard model on the Bethe lattice, with 2, 4, 6 ghost orbitals per spin (8, 12, 16 qubits), plus a two-qubit IBM demonstration (one data qubit plus ancilla) in the no-ghost limit, and trapped-ion noise models with circuit compression, rotated-basis measurements with post-selection, and error mitigation.
AI.result: With more ghost orbitals, t-GQCE suppresses artificial undamped oscillations of conventional Gutzwiller and approaches nonequilibrium DMFT for weak and strong quenches. Statevector adaptive circuits track embedding states with infidelities below 5e-4. Under trapped-ion noise, compression, rotated-basis post-selection, and mitigation reduce measurement errors severalfold; at one third of hardware-benchmarked error rates they achieve 0.01 accuracy in the single-particle density matrix and double occupancy with 1e5 shots per step, and the Quantinuum H2-Emulator shows similar accuracy.
AI.conclusion: t-GQCE offers a modular, solver-agnostic quantum-classical route to long-time, nonperturbative dynamics of correlated lattice models, with demonstrated accuracy and noise robustness on near-term quantum hardware and emulators.

title: No-Go Theorems for Ordered Universal Entanglement Purification
summary: Entanglement purification is a fundamental tool for obtaining high-fidelity entangled states used in various quantum technologies. It aims to increase the fidelity of noisy shared entangled states with a fixed maximally entangled state through LOCC. In distributed quantum systems, such as networks employing quantum repeaters, limited memory, probabilistic entanglement generation, and unequal storage times can leave a finite collection of nonidentical pairs. Their states may remain incompletely characterized even when calibrated preparation and storage records establish their fidelity ordering. Recent work has investigated whether fidelity ordering permits nontrivial universal purification. A nontrivial universal $n$-to-1 protocol must, conditioned on success, never lower the highest input fidelity and strictly increase it for at least one allowed joint input. Although no-go results have been established for a restricted class of LOCC protocols, the corresponding question for general LOCC has remained unresolved. Here, we study ordered universal purification under separable operations. Specifically, for every fixed finite $n\ge2$, we prove that when independently prepared two-qubit pairs range over the full family of states above a fixed fidelity threshold $0\le F_*<1$, any separable success map that never lowers the highest input fidelity on the allowed ordered inputs must preserve that fidelity exactly whenever it succeeds. This excludes nontrivial universal LOCC purification even for arbitrarily high input fidelities, without imposing a positive lower bound on success probability. ...

AI.tldr: For any fixed finite n≥2, any separable operation that never lowers the highest input fidelity among ordered nonidentical two-qubit pairs (above threshold 0≤F*<1) must preserve that highest fidelity exactly on success, ruling out nontrivial universal LOCC entanglement purification even at arbitrarily high fidelities.
AI.motivation: In distributed quantum systems (quantum repeater networks), limited memory, probabilistic generation, and unequal storage times yield finite sets of nonidentical entangled pairs whose states may be incompletely characterized but whose fidelity ordering is known. Prior no-go results for ordered universal purification covered only a restricted class of LOCC protocols; the general LOCC question was open.
AI.method: A theoretical no-go proof under separable operations (a superset of LOCC). Taking independently prepared two-qubit pairs ranging over all states above a fixed fidelity threshold F*, the work analyzes separable success maps acting on ordered inputs and constrains their effect on the maximum input fidelity.
AI.result: Any separable success map that never lowers the highest input fidelity on allowed ordered inputs must preserve that fidelity exactly whenever it succeeds. This holds for every finite n≥2, every threshold 0≤F*<1, and without any positive lower bound on success probability.
AI.conclusion: Nontrivial universal LOCC entanglement purification of ordered nonidentical pairs is impossible, extending the no-go from restricted LOCC to general separable operations and showing the obstruction persists at arbitrarily high input fidelities.

title: Measurement-order dependence bounds uncertainty, contextuality, steering, and Bell nonlocality
summary: Two quantum measurements applied to the same input in opposite orders give two joint distributions of the same outcomes. For Lüders instruments we measure how far apart these order records can be, over all inputs, by their total-variation distance $\mathcal{T}$, their Jensen-Shannon divergence $\mathcal{J}$ (in bits), and their squared Hellinger distance. These order scores vanish exactly when the measurements commute, and $\mathcal{T}=\|[A,B]\|/4$ for two binary sharp observables. Some pairs of bases exceed mutually unbiased bases in squared Hellinger score, and in odd dimensions in $\mathcal{J}$, although their minimal entropy sum is smaller. For projective measurements, a Maassen-Uffink bound $q>0$ implies $\mathcal{T}\ge1-2^{-q}$ and a positive lower bound on $\mathcal{J}$. Measuring all observables of a scenario in sequence defines a joint distribution, so violations of noncontextuality, steering, and Bell inequalities are bounded by distances between order records. For correlation Bell inequalities with binary sharp observables, the squared Bell operator is a symmetrized (Jordan) part minus tensor products of local commutators. If one party has two settings, the violation is bounded bilinearly in the two parties' order scores; we conjecture this bound in general. On Clifford realizations it would follow from a Hilbert-Schmidt variant of Grothendieck's inequality, which we prove when one party has at most three settings. For three binary sharp measurements, the violation of Bell's original inequality by a maximally entangled state equals an order effect in three-measurement records of the maximally mixed state minus four times an alternation probability. For the rank-one Klyachko-Can-Binicioğlu-Shumovsky pentagon on a qutrit, the violation is at most the largest product of the order scores of two crossing diagonals, with equality at the maximal violation.

AI.tldr: The paper quantifies how far the "order records" of two quantum measurements applied in opposite orders can differ, using total-variation, Jensen-Shannon, and squared Hellinger distances, and shows these order scores bound violations of noncontextuality, steering, and Bell inequalities.
AI.motivation: Sequential measurements of the same observables in opposite orders produce different joint outcome distributions whenever the observables do not commute. The authors aim to turn this noncommutativity-induced order effect into a quantitative measure that vanishes exactly for commuting measurements and that controls—and thus explains—quantum correlation violations.
AI.method: They define three order scores (total-variation distance T, Jensen-Shannon divergence J in bits, squared Hellinger distance) between opposite-order joint distributions of Lüders instruments, maximized over inputs. They relate these to commutators (T = ||[A,B]||/4 for binary sharp observables), to Maassen-Uffink entropic uncertainty, and to Bell/steering/noncontextuality violations via the Bell operator's symmetrized (Jordan) part minus tensor products of local commutators, plus a Hilbert-Schmidt Grothendieck inequality for Clifford realizations.
AI.result: Order scores vanish iff measurements commute; T = ||[A,B]||/4 for two binary sharp observables. Some basis pairs exceed mutually unbiased bases in squared Hellinger score (and in J for odd dimensions) despite smaller minimal entropy sum. A Maassen-Uffink bound q>0 implies T ≥ 1-2^{-q} and a positive lower bound on J. Bell violations are bounded by order-score distances: bilinearly when one party has two settings (conjectured in general); for Clifford realizations the bound follows from a Hilbert-Schmidt Grothendieck inequality, proved when one party has at most three settings. For three binary sharp measurements, the Bell-inequality violation with a maximally entangled state equals an order effect on the maximally mixed state minus four times an alternation probability. For the rank-one KCBS pentagon on a qutrit, violation is at most the largest product of order scores of two crossing diagonals, with equality at maximal violation.
AI.conclusion: Order effects between oppositely ordered Lüders measurements provide a unifying, quantitatively tight measure of noncommutativity that directly bounds noncontextuality, steering, and Bell violations, offering a commutator-based account of quantum correlation strength.

title: Number-correlated photon entanglement with a quantum memory interferometer
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures. Supplementary Information appended to the manuscript
summary: Strong photon-photon interactions are central to quantum optical technologies yet remain challenging to realise at the single-photon level. Here, we show how embedding a quantum memory within a Mach-Zehnder interferometer enables a coherent transformation that converts single-mode photon states into number-correlated entangled states. Using an off-resonant ladder-type atomic interaction, storage and retrieval within a quantum memory maps a single-photon excitation onto a pair of photons across distinct optical modes via a driving control field. Embedding this within an interferometer deterministically produces an effective transformation in the photon number basis: $\sum_n a_n |n\rangle \to \sum_n a_n |n\rangle |n\rangle$ without relying on conventional optical nonlinearities. Measurement of one mode enables photonic non-demolition detection, state preparation, and frequency conversion as applications of the same underlying transformation. These results establish quantum memories embedded within an interferometric architecture as a platform for measurement-induced photon-photon interactions and the generation of Gaussian and non-Gaussian entangled states.

AI.tldr: Embedding a quantum memory in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer converts single-mode photon states into number-correlated entangled states via an off-resonant ladder-type atomic interaction, enabling deterministic photon-number-basis transformation without conventional optical nonlinearities.
AI.motivation: Strong photon-photon interactions are central to quantum optical technologies but remain hard to realize at the single-photon level. The work seeks a platform for measurement-induced photon-photon interactions that avoids relying on conventional optical nonlinearities.
AI.method: A quantum memory is embedded within a Mach-Zehnder interferometer. Using an off-resonant ladder-type atomic interaction, storage and retrieval with a driving control field maps a single-photon excitation onto a pair of photons in distinct optical modes. Interferometric embedding deterministically realizes the effective transformation sum_n a_n|n> -> sum_n a_n|n>|n> in the photon-number basis.
AI.result: The scheme deterministically produces the number-correlated transformation; measuring one mode yields photonic non-demolition detection, state preparation, and frequency conversion as applications of the same underlying transformation.
AI.conclusion: Quantum memories embedded in an interferometric architecture form a platform for measurement-induced photon-photon interactions and for generating Gaussian and non-Gaussian entangled states.

title: Instanton tunnelling as a verifiable benchmark for digital quantum simulation: circuit structure, classical simulability and hardware reproducibility
summary: We use instanton-mediated tunnelling in the quartic double well as a benchmark for digital quantum simulation that is checkable against an exact answer at every step. The instanton enters through the classical analysis; the hardware tests the dynamics of the lattice model. A unary (single-excitation) encoding maps N lattice sites to N qubits, with the single-excitation dynamics as a reference that remains classically cheap at any N. For a second-order Trotter circuit with adjacent, equal-angle XX/YY pairs on each bond, we prove that the Schmidt rank across any cut is at most four at every gate boundary and at most two after each pair, independently of N. Matrix-product-state simulations of this gate list reproduce the exact splitting up to N = 48. For this bond-wise formula the admissible Trotter step shrinks roughly as N^-2, so one tunnelling period costs about N^3.3 two-qubit gates; a kinetic/potential splitting keeps the step near 0.065 up to N=128, so this scaling belongs to splitting the kinetic term bond by bond. At a coarser, separately bounded step we measure the full transfer at N=8 on two superconducting processors, recovering the lattice splitting to a few percent and its dependence on the barrier height, which at this resolution is set by the lattice rather than by the instanton. Over 9 repetitions, runs taken minutes apart agree to shot noise, while runs hours to weeks apart differ by up to 6.1%, also on a fixed set of qubits; with sessions as the sampling unit, the processors differ in the damping, while a difference in the splitting is not established. Normalising by the measured single-excitation population extends the usable depth about 4-fold but does not improve the splitting. A Gaussian start state, which needs no diagonalisation, reproduces the splitting of the eigenvector-based start to within 1.6 percentage points.

AI.tldr: Instanton-mediated tunnelling in a quartic double well serves as a step-wise checkable benchmark for digital quantum simulation, validated via MPS numerics up to N=48 and superconducting-hardware transfer measured at N=8.
AI.motivation: A digital quantum simulation needs a benchmark whose exact answer is known at every step; the quartic double well with instanton-mediated tunnelling provides such a reference, while the unary single-excitation encoding keeps classical verification cheap at any lattice size N.
AI.method: A unary (single-excitation) encoding maps N lattice sites to N qubits. For a second-order Trotter circuit with adjacent equal-angle XX/YY pairs per bond, the authors bound the Schmidt rank across any cut (≤4 at gate boundaries, ≤2 after each pair, independent of N). Matrix-product-state simulations reproduce the exact splitting up to N=48; Trotter-step scaling is analysed for bond-wise versus kinetic/potential splittings; the full transfer at N=8 is measured on two superconducting processors with session-based sampling, normalization by single-excitation population, and Gaussian start states.
AI.result: The bond-wise formula requires a Trotter step shrinking as ~N^-2, costing ~N^3.3 two-qubit gates per tunnelling period, whereas kinetic/potential splitting keeps the step near 0.065 up to N=128. Hardware recovers the lattice splitting to a few percent and its barrier-height dependence. Over 9 repetitions, runs minutes apart agree to shot noise, while runs hours-to-weeks apart differ up to 6.1%; processors differ in damping but not in splitting. Normalization extends usable depth ~4-fold without improving the splitting; a Gaussian start reproduces the eigenvector-based splitting within 1.6 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: The instanton double well is a viable, exactly checkable digital-quantum-simulation benchmark; the bond-wise Trotter scheme has low-entanglement structure but poor step scaling, while kinetic/potential splitting is preferred, and current hardware achieves few-percent splitting accuracy with stability limited by long-timescale drift rather than shot noise.

title: A provably efficient classical algorithm for simulating OTOC$^{(1)}$ in 1D
summary: Out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) are quantities of broad interest in many-body physics due to their connection with information scrambling and quantum chaos. Recently, estimating higher-order OTOCs in random quantum circuits was proposed as a promising avenue for quantum advantage, yet the classical hardness of this task remains poorly understood. Even for first-order OTOCs, where growing evidence suggests classical tractability, no efficient classical algorithm with rigorous guarantees has been established to date. In this work, we introduce "window propagation," the first provably polynomial-time classical algorithm for approximating first-order OTOCs in 1D Haar-random brickwork circuits, at arbitrary depths and with inverse-polynomial mean-squared error. We also conduct numerical experiments comparing our simulation results to exact computation on up to $512$ qubits for Clifford circuits with $768$ $T$-gates and up to $22$ qubits for Haar-random circuits. We emphasize that our results do not directly apply to second-order OTOCs in 2D, which is the subject of recent quantum advantage proposals. Nevertheless, our work provides a rigorous step towards understanding the classical complexity of OTOC estimation and represents a family of non-trivial quantum circuits for which a provable, polynomial time algorithm is now known, establishing foundations for understanding these widely used diagnostics of quantum chaos.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "window propagation," the first provably polynomial-time classical algorithm for approximating first-order out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) in 1D Haar-random brickwork circuits at arbitrary depth with inverse-polynomial mean-squared error, and validates it numerically up to 512 qubits (Clifford+T) and 22 qubits (Haar-random).
AI.motivation: OTOCs are central to information scrambling and quantum chaos, and higher-order OTOC estimation in random circuits has been proposed as a route to quantum advantage. However, the classical hardness of even first-order OTOCs is poorly understood, and no efficient classical algorithm with rigorous guarantees has existed for this task.
AI.method: The authors propose "window propagation," a classical algorithm exploiting the local structure of 1D Haar-random brickwork circuits to propagate a bounded window of relevant correlations, yielding provable polynomial-time complexity at arbitrary circuit depth. They complement the analysis with numerical experiments: comparison against exact simulation for Clifford circuits with 768 T-gates on up to 512 qubits, and for Haar-random circuits on up to 22 qubits.
AI.result: Window propagation achieves an inverse-polynomial mean-squared approximation error in polynomial time, establishing rigorous classical tractability for first-order OTOCs in 1D Haar-random brickwork circuits. Numerical experiments confirm agreement with exact computation in both tested regimes. The authors explicitly note the results do not directly extend to second-order OTOCs in 2D, which underpin recent quantum advantage proposals.
AI.conclusion: The work delivers the first rigorous polynomial-time classical algorithm for estimating first-order OTOCs, identifies a non-trivial family of quantum circuits with provable classical simulability, and lays foundations for characterizing the classical complexity of OTOC-based diagnostics of quantum chaos.

title: On Reaction Depth and Fast Fault-Tolerant Boolean Logic
summary:
Reducing runtimes of quantum applications is critical for practical viability. On quantum computers, the runtime can depend both on the speed of quantum operations and on how often the program must wait for the classical coprocessor to determine adaptive operations. Some recent approaches to reducing this overhead have focused on minimizing the "reaction depth" of a computation, informally defined as the number of times the classical coprocessor must be consulted while running a quantum program.
  In this work, we formalize the notion of reaction depth. We find several subtleties in this theory. For example, we distinguish the reaction depth of a circuit from that of a circuit run, and show that the magic depth of a unitary can be higher than the reaction depth once compiled into Clifford computation and magic state injection.
  We then focus on the specific case of coherent Boolean logic, a common and expensive component in quantum algorithms. We use a natural gateset for fast operations with Low-Density Parity Check (LDPC) codes, which consists of homogeneous $Z$- and $X$-type Pauli Product Measurements (PPMs), alongside a supply of Toffoli states. We prove that, using this gateset, any Boolean arithmetic circuit can be implemented on a quantum computer with constant quantum depth and constant reaction depth, at the cost of exponential space and leaving some qubits "dirty". Using the same gateset we find two efficient AutoAND circuits that require only a Toffoli state and homogeneous PPMs. We then give efficient implementations of the quantum ripple-carry adder and quantum schoolbook multiplier, which require a low number of heterogeneous PPMs for uncomputation. We find implementations competitive with the state-of-the-art despite the restricted gateset.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes "reaction depth" as the number of times a quantum program must consult the classical coprocessor during execution, distinguishes it from magic depth, and shows that with a gateset of homogeneous PPMs plus Toffoli states, Boolean arithmetic circuits can be run at constant quantum and reaction depth (at exponential space cost), while giving efficient competitive implementations of ripple-carry adders and schoolbook multipliers.
AI.motivation: Practical quantum applications are bottlenecked by runtime, which depends both on quantum gate speed and on how often the control flow must wait for a classical coprocessor to resolve adaptive (feed-forward) operations. Prior work tried to reduce this classical-communication overhead via the informal notion of "reaction depth," but lacked a rigorous treatment of the concept and of its behavior under compilation and in realistic LDPC-code gatesets.
AI.method: The authors formalize reaction depth, distinguishing the reaction depth of a circuit from that of a circuit run, and analyze subtleties such as magic depth of a unitary exceeding its reaction depth once compiled into Clifford computation plus magic-state injection. They then target coherent Boolean logic using a gateset of homogeneous Z- and X-type Pauli Product Measurements (PPMs) with Toffoli-state supply, proving a constant-depth/constant-reaction-depth construction for arbitrary Boolean circuits and designing two efficient AutoAND circuits plus ripple-carry adder and schoolbook multiplier implementations requiring few heterogeneous PPMs for uncomputation.
AI.result: They establish a formal theory of reaction depth with several identified subtleties (circuit vs. run distinction; magic depth can exceed reaction depth after compilation). They prove any Boolean arithmetic circuit can be implemented with constant quantum depth and constant reaction depth using the LDPC-friendly gateset, at the cost of exponential space and dirty qubits. They also deliver two efficient AutoAND circuits using only a Toffoli state and homogeneous PPMs, and efficient ripple-carry adder and schoolbook multiplier implementations that are competitive with the state of the art despite the restricted gateset.
AI.conclusion: Reaction depth is a meaningful and formalizable resource for characterizing quantum runtime overhead, and it can be dramatically reduced—even held constant—for Boolean arithmetic under an LDPC-compatible PPM+Toffoli-state gateset. The results yield practical, state-of-the-art-competitive primitives (adders, multipliers) and clarify the relationship between reaction depth and magic depth, with space and dirty qubits as the principal trade-offs.

title: Coherent-Response and Thermal-Fluctuation Information in Cavity-Magnon Magnetometry
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures, Accepted by APL Quantum
summary: Magnetic sensing with cavity--magnon systems typically relies on the coherent response, while field-dependent fluctuations are treated as measurement noise. Here, we show that the variance of a measured microwave quadrature provides a distinct source of magnetic-field information. For repeated phase-sensitive measurements of a calibrated quadrature, we derive the Gaussian likelihood and show that its Fisher information separates exactly into two terms. The coherent-displacement term depends on the field derivative of the quadrature mean, and the thermal-fluctuation term depends on the field derivative of its variance. Both terms are accessible from the same measurement record, but their optimal operating conditions differ. For the amplitude quadrature, the dimensionless coherent response factor reaches its global maximum at cooperativity $C=2$, corresponding to a coupling strength $g=\sqrt{2κ_aκ_m}$, and at linewidth-normalized detunings $δ_a=δ_m=\pm 1$. In the near-resonance approximation, the reduced variance-information term is globally maximized at cavity--magnon frequency matching, $Δ_a=Δ_m$, and approaches a finite limit at large cooperativity. We map the relative contributions of the two terms across drive frequencies, drive strengths, and temperatures. Strong coherent driving favors displacement-based sensing, whereas at finite temperature the variance contribution can dominate under weak driving and remain finite even when the coherent-displacement contribution vanishes. These results establish a measurement-specific framework for cavity--magnon magnetometry and identify operating regimes for exploiting the quadrature mean, its variance, or both.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the variance of a measured microwave quadrature in a cavity–magnon system carries independent magnetic-field information, complementing the conventional coherent-displacement response, and maps the optimal operating regimes for each sensing channel.
AI.motivation: Cavity–magnon magnetic sensing is conventionally based on the coherent response, while field-dependent fluctuations are discarded as measurement noise, leaving a potentially useful information channel unexploited.
AI.method: For repeated phase-sensitive measurements of a calibrated quadrature, the authors derive the Gaussian likelihood and show its Fisher information separates exactly into a coherent-displacement term (from the field derivative of the quadrature mean) and a thermal-fluctuation term (from the field derivative of its variance). They optimize each term over cooperativity, detunings, and drive conditions, using a near-resonance approximation, and map relative contributions versus drive frequency, drive strength, and temperature.
AI.result: The dimensionless coherent response factor for the amplitude quadrature peaks globally at cooperativity C=2 (g=√(2κ_aκ_m)) and at linewidth-normalized detunings δ_a=δ_m=±1. The reduced variance-information term is globally maximized at cavity–magnon frequency matching (Δ_a=Δ_m) and approaches a finite limit at large cooperativity. Strong coherent driving favors displacement sensing, while at finite temperature the variance contribution can dominate under weak driving and stays finite where the displacement contribution vanishes.
AI.conclusion: A measurement-specific Fisher-information framework is established for cavity–magnon magnetometry, identifying operating regimes where the quadrature mean, its variance, or their combination provides the best field sensitivity.

title: The magical memory cost of entanglement spectrum compression
summary: How much quantum memory is needed to faithfully retain the entanglement spectrum of a bipartite pure state after separating out Bell pairs through local unitaries? We derive the exact tradeoff between Bell-pair yield, residual memory, and reconstruction fidelity under local unitaries, defining an operational measure of entanglement-spectrum complexity. Smoothed entanglement spread bounds this memory cost from below, while diverging nonlocal magic forces unbounded memory at any fixed positive fidelity. Chaotic circuit dynamics exhibit a transient memory peak whose height increases with system size, followed by declining cost despite continued entropy growth. A large typical Haar-random state requires only an accuracy-dependent memory, whereas stationary fermionic Gaussian states retain a growing cost with size. In the circuits studied, the multiscale spectral structure associated with entanglement catalysis also has a practical consequence for matrix product state compression, yielding a multiplicative overhead not captured by the conventional entropy-based bond dimension estimate.

AI.tldr: This work derives the exact tradeoff between Bell-pair yield, residual quantum memory, and reconstruction fidelity under local unitaries, defining an operational measure of entanglement-spectrum complexity. Smoothed entanglement spread gives a lower bound on memory cost, nonlocal magic forces unbounded memory, and chaotic/Haar-random/fermionic Gaussian states show distinct memory-scaling behaviors, with implications for MPS compression.
AI.motivation: To determine how much quantum memory is required to faithfully retain a bipartite pure state's entanglement spectrum after extracting Bell pairs via local unitaries, and to operationalize entanglement-spectrum complexity.
AI.method: Derive the exact tradeoff among Bell-pair yield, residual memory, and reconstruction fidelity under local unitaries; establish a lower bound via smoothed entanglement spread; analyze memory scaling for chaotic circuit dynamics, Haar-random states, stationary fermionic Gaussian states, and entanglement catalysis; assess consequences for matrix product state compression.
AI.result: Smoothed entanglement spread bounds memory cost from below; diverging nonlocal magic forces unbounded memory at any fixed positive fidelity; chaotic circuits show a transient memory peak growing with system size followed by declining cost despite entropy growth; typical Haar-random states need only accuracy-dependent memory, while stationary fermionic Gaussian states retain growing cost; catalysis-related multiscale spectral structure induces multiplicative overhead in MPS compression beyond entropy-based bond dimension estimates.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement-spectrum complexity is captured by an operational memory cost with sharp lower bounds, and the multiscale spectral structure has practical consequences for matrix product state compression not captured by conventional entropy-based estimates.

title: Squeezed Cooling and Lasing with Cold Atoms in Cavity-QED
comment: 27 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables. Main text with Methods, followed by Supplementary Information
summary: A squeezed laser undergoes a lasing transition into a squeezed cavity mode, where stimulated emission generates a bright coherent field with a laser-like coherence time while maintaining one field quadrature below the vacuum noise level. Here we propose an optical implementation that needs neither a nonlinear crystal nor injected squeezed light, based on engineered interactions between ensembles of rubidium atoms and a squeezed cavity mode via cavity-assisted Raman transitions. A first ensemble cools the cavity into a squeezed vacuum, a mechanism we term squeezed cooling, yielding up to 9 dB in the intracavity field, surpassing the 3 dB limit of optical parametric oscillators. Tuned for output instead, it reaches up to 18 dB of output squeezing. Incoherently pumping a second ensemble drives a lasing transition into the squeezed mode, emitting a bright beam with long coherence time and noise below vacuum spanning a megahertz-wide band, away from the sharp phase-diffusion peak of excess noise at the carrier frequency, and robust to relaxation oscillations. We characterize lasing thresholds, superradiant emission, and linewidth narrowing, and identify the experimentally accessible regime where the system exhibits the defining features of a squeezed laser.

AI.tldr: The authors propose an all-atomic optical realization of a squeezed laser based on cavity-assisted Raman transitions in two rubidium ensembles, without nonlinear crystals or injected squeezed light. A "squeezed cooling" stage prepares intracavity squeezing up to 9 dB (output up to 18 dB), and incoherent pumping of a second ensemble drives a lasing transition into the squeezed mode, producing a bright, long-coherence-time beam with sub-vacuum noise over a megahertz-wide band.
AI.motivation: A squeezed laser—lasing into a squeezed cavity mode—offers a bright coherent field with laser-like coherence while keeping one quadrature below the vacuum noise level, but existing implementations require nonlinear crystals or externally injected squeezed light, which limits practicality and achievable squeezing. The work seeks an alternative optical implementation avoiding these requirements.
AI.method: Engineered interactions between ensembles of rubidium atoms and a squeezed cavity mode via cavity-assisted Raman transitions. A first ensemble cools the cavity into a squeezed vacuum ("squeezed cooling"), which can be tuned for output coupling. A second ensemble, incoherently pumped, drives the lasing transition into the squeezed mode. The analysis characterizes lasing thresholds, superradiant emission, linewidth narrowing, and the experimentally accessible regime exhibiting squeezed-laser signatures.
AI.result: Squeezed cooling yields up to 9 dB of intracavity squeezing, exceeding the 3 dB limit of optical parametric oscillators; tuned for output, up to 18 dB of output squeezing is reached. The lasing transition emits a bright beam with long coherence time and noise below vacuum across a megahertz-wide band, aside from the sharp phase-diffusion excess-noise peak at the carrier, and is robust to relaxation oscillations. Thresholds, superradiant emission, and linewidth narrowing are characterized, and an experimentally accessible regime is identified.
AI.conclusion: A squeezed laser can be realized in an atomic platform using only cavity-assisted Raman interactions and incoherent pumping, circumventing nonlinear crystals and injected squeezed light, while surpassing parametric-oscillator squeezing limits and retaining laser-like coherence—providing a practical route to bright sub-shot-noise light sources.

title: Environment-assisted imaginary time evolution in feedback-based quantum algorithms
summary: The Feedback-based Algorithm for Quantum Optimization (FALQON) prepares ground states without classical parameter optimization, but requires deep circuits and can stagnate away from the ground state as a consequence of barren plateaus and symmetry protection. In order to avoid stagnation, imaginary time evolution (ITE) layers can be incorporated into FALQON layers, enhancing FALQON convergence. However, applying a non-unitary ITE layer in a closed quantum system is not possible, and approximations must be made to use ITE on real hardware; using an open quantum system formulation to incorporate ITE into FALQON represents a better approach. We describe ITE as a quantum operation induced by an environment, and combine it with the FALQON feedback law. In simulations of a frustrated Ising chain (ANNNI) and of MaxCut, the resulting algorithm prepares the ground state starting from any initial state, where FALQON can fail, and needs fewer layers on average when the initial state is fixed for the two investigated problems. The CITE-FALQON advantage strongly depends on the system phase for the ANNNI chain, and on the graph weights for the MaxCut problem.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CITE-FALQON, a hybrid algorithm that embeds imaginary time evolution (ITE) layers as environment-induced quantum operations into the feedback-based FALQON ansatz, avoiding stagnation and reducing circuit depth for ground-state preparation.
AI.motivation: FALQON prepares ground states without classical parameter optimization, but it requires deep circuits and can stagnate away from the ground state due to barren plateaus and symmetry protection. Naively adding ITE layers is impossible in closed quantum systems (non-unitary), so a physically realizable formulation is needed.
AI.method: The authors describe ITE as a quantum operation induced by an environment (open quantum system formulation) and combine it with the FALQON feedback law, yielding the CITE-FALQON algorithm. This enables approximate, hardware-compatible inclusion of ITE layers alongside FALQON layers.
AI.result: In simulations of a frustrated ANNNI Ising chain and of MaxCut, CITE-FALQON prepares the ground state from any initial state—including cases where FALQON fails—and on average requires fewer layers when the initial state is fixed. The advantage depends strongly on the system phase for ANNNI and on graph weights for MaxCut.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating environment-induced ITE into FALQON provides a viable, hardware-realizable route to enhanced convergence, though the benefit is problem- and regime-dependent.

title: Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Learning
summary: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has attracted increasing interest as a possible route to construct feature representations that are difficult to reproduce with classical models. However, near-term QML architectures based on trainable parametrized quantum circuits remain affected by limited hardware resources, noise, and severe optimization difficulties such as barren plateaus. In this work we propose Soft-MoQE, a Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts architecture that replaces variational quantum training with the input-dependent selection and combination of fixed quantum feature maps. The model is composed of a heterogeneous pool of non-trainable quantum circuits, each defining a distinct embedding, and a classical gating network that learns how to weight these embeddings for each data point. We benchmark Soft-MoQE on three PCA-reduced tasks: MNIST parity, MNIST 10-class, and FashionMNIST. Soft-MoQE outperforms the single best expert, the uniform average of all experts and a linear baseline, achieving task-dependent performance comparable to that of a trainable quantum neural network, without optimizing any quantum parameter and with a quantum training cost that is lower by orders of magnitude. The analysis of the class- conditioned expert usage shows that the learned routing combines a few experts for each input, with a selection that depends on the class. These results support the learned routing among fixed quantum circuits as a trainability-aware design principle for hybrid QML.

AI.tldr: Soft-MoQE replaces variational quantum training with input-dependent routing over a pool of fixed quantum feature maps, matching trainable QNN performance on PCA-reduced MNIST/FashionMNIST with orders-of-magnitude lower quantum training cost.
AI.motivation: Near-term QML with trainable parametrized quantum circuits suffers from limited hardware resources, noise, and severe optimization pathologies such as barren plateaus. The authors seek a trainability-aware design that avoids variational optimization of quantum parameters altogether.
AI.method: Soft-MoQE is a Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts: a heterogeneous pool of non-trainable quantum circuits, each defining a distinct embedding, combined by a classical gating network that learns input-dependent weights. The gating is trained classically, so no quantum parameters are optimized.
AI.result: On three PCA-reduced tasks (MNIST parity, MNIST 10-class, FashionMNIST), Soft-MoQE outperforms the single best expert, the uniform average of all experts, and a linear baseline, reaching task-dependent performance comparable to a trainable quantum neural network. Class-conditioned expert usage analysis shows that routing selects a few experts per input, with class-dependent selection patterns.
AI.conclusion: Learned routing among fixed quantum circuits is a viable trainability-aware design principle for hybrid QML, sidestepping barren plateaus and costly quantum optimization while retaining expressive quantum feature representations.

title: Shedding Light on Quantum Non-Classicality: Witnessing Wigner Negativity with Free Electrons
summary: Certifying quantum non-classicality like Wigner negativity typically demands full optical state tomography. This work introduces a noise-resilient framework for witnessing optical Wigner negativity using phase-resolved quantum photon-induced near-field electron microscopy (QPINEM). By mapping electron coherences directly to symmetrically ordered optical characteristic functions within a coupling-limited phase-space region, the protocol bypasses full optical reconstruction. A post-measurement witness matrix is constructed via Bochner's theorem from recorded electron spectra, where negative eigenvalues certify non-classicality. To ensure reliability under realistic experimental conditions, a noise-aware selection procedure decouples discovery from statistical validation. Benchmarked across various optical preparations-including vacuum-Fock superpositions, odd cat states, and GKP states-the protocol provides a statistically bounded pathway for probing quantum features with free electrons.

AI.tldr: A noise-resilient framework witnesses optical Wigner negativity via phase-resolved quantum photon-induced near-field electron microscopy (QPINEM), avoiding full state tomography by mapping electron coherences to symmetrically ordered characteristic functions and certifying non-classicality through a Bochner-theorem-based witness matrix.
AI.motivation: Certifying quantum non-classicality such as Wigner negativity conventionally requires full optical state tomography, which is demanding and fragile. The authors seek a noise-resilient alternative that bypasses full reconstruction.
AI.method: Phase-resolved QPINEM maps electron coherences directly onto symmetrically ordered optical characteristic functions within a coupling-limited phase-space region. From the recorded electron spectra, a post-measurement witness matrix is built via Bochner's theorem, where negative eigenvalues certify non-classicality. A noise-aware selection procedure decouples discovery from statistical validation to ensure reliability under realistic conditions.
AI.result: The protocol is benchmarked across multiple optical preparations—vacuum–Fock superpositions, odd cat states, and GKP states—and provides a statistically bounded pathway for probing quantum features with free electrons.
AI.conclusion: QPINEM-based phase-resolved electron spectroscopy offers a practical, noise-resilient route to witness Wigner negativity and quantum non-classicality without full optical tomography, with statistically validated certification demonstrated across several non-classical optical states.

title: The limits of magic-state cultivation
summary: Fault tolerance is understood through Pauli algebra, which fails at non-Clifford gates. Circuits such as magic-state cultivation, which checks an encoded T state with physical T gates, have therefore lacked an exact theory of which faults are harmful. We develop such a theory and show that, for any circuit that prepares a magic state with non-Clifford gates and postselection, one stabilizer code on the non-Clifford gates decides which faults are harmful. This ties cultivation to distillation, bounds its T-count from below and gives an exact test. For a single check on an ideally encoded state, the fault distance reduces to Pauli algebra on the code. As a use case, we analyze the S gates that have stood in for T gates in the design of cultivation. We show that this proxy can only overstate the fault distance of such a check, and that the checks in use, on color and surface codes, tolerate at most half as many faults as their code allows. The theory also yields nearest-neighbor checks that keep the full distance, certified up to code distance nine.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an exact theory of fault tolerance for non-Clifford circuits that prepare magic states with postselection, showing that a single stabilizer code on the non-Clifford gates decides which faults are harmful, and applies it to analyze S-gate proxies and nearest-neighbor cultivation checks.
AI.motivation: Fault tolerance is traditionally understood through Pauli algebra, which fails at non-Clifford gates. Circuits like magic-state cultivation (which check an encoded T state using physical T gates) therefore lacked an exact theory of which faults are harmful, leaving their fault distance and T-count poorly characterized.
AI.method: The authors construct a theory for circuits that prepare a magic state using non-Clifford gates plus postselection, identifying a single stabilizer code defined on the non-Clifford gates as the object that determines harmful faults. They tie cultivation to distillation, derive a lower bound on T-count, and give an exact test for harmful faults. For a single check on an ideally encoded state, the fault distance reduces to Pauli algebra on the relevant code. As a case study, they analyze the S gates used as proxies for T gates in cultivation design, and additionally construct nearest-neighbor checks.
AI.result: The S-gate proxy can only overstate the fault distance of such a check, and the checks in use on color and surface codes tolerate at most half as many faults as their code allows. The theory also yields nearest-neighbor checks that preserve the full distance, certified up to code distance nine.
AI.conclusion: An exact stabilizer-code-based framework characterizes harmful faults in non-Clifford magic-state preparation circuits, unifying cultivation and distillation, providing a T-count lower bound and exact fault-distance test, exposing a factor-of-two fault-tolerance gap in existing color/surface code checks, and offering distance-preserving nearest-neighbor check constructions.

title: Hurst Exponent Estimation with Quantum Wavelets
summary: How accurately can the Hurst exponent $H$ of fractional Brownian motion be estimated from repeated preparations of a single amplitude-encoded path, when every measurement interrogates the same realization? We extend the $ε$-decimated quantum nondecimated wavelet transform in three directions: we remove the endpoint jump of circular filtering, derive the sampling distribution of the estimator, and compare readouts at equal query budgets. A one-qubit mirror extension removes the jump and keeps every coefficient that straddles a fold of the same order as an interior coefficient, for any compactly supported filter and circular shift. The transform for any such filter is compiled from the paraunitary lattice of its filter bank, and the energy share of a level is the success probability of one multiply-controlled reflection, which is both the controlled unitary of a Hadamard test and the oracle of amplitude estimation. For filters with at least two vanishing moments we prove a root-$N$ central limit theorem for the log-energy contrasts, independent of the limiting path norm, so the studentized estimator is asymptotically standard normal for deterministic query budgets under which the success count at every level diverges. For sparse counts we give a working multinomial--lognormal likelihood, exact in its readout model for direct measurement, and check its coverage by simulation. For paths of length $512$, mirroring reduces RMSE by a factor of $3$--$10$ for $H\ge0.5$, and with exact shares the nondecimated db2 estimator is $6$--$14\%$ above the root Cramér--Rao bound. Hadamard level tests are less accurate than direct measurement of the leading qubits at every budget. At $H=0.9$ and $2^{20}$ queries, maximum-likelihood amplitude estimation attains RMSE $0.0347$, against $0.0451$ for direct measurement and $0.0295$ with exact shares.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how accurately the Hurst exponent H of fractional Brownian motion can be estimated from repeated preparations of a single amplitude-encoded path, extending the ε-decimated quantum nondecimated wavelet transform by removing an endpoint jump, deriving the estimator's sampling distribution, and comparing readout strategies at equal query budgets.
AI.motivation: Estimating the Hurst exponent from a single encoded realization raises the question of achievable accuracy when every measurement interrogates the same path; existing quantum nondecimated wavelet transform approaches suffer from an endpoint jump artifact and lack a sampling-distribution theory and fair readout comparison.
AI.method: The authors use a one-qubit mirror extension to eliminate the circular-filtering endpoint jump, preserving boundary-straddling coefficients at interior-coefficient order for any compactly supported filter and shift. The transform is compiled from the paraunitary lattice of the filter bank, with level energy share expressed as success probability of a multiply-controlled reflection (Hadamard-test controlled unitary / amplitude-estimation oracle). They prove a root-N central limit theorem for log-energy contrasts for filters with ≥2 vanishing moments, and develop a multinomial–lognormal likelihood for sparse counts, validated by simulation.
AI.result: For paths of length 512, mirroring reduces RMSE by a factor of 3–10 for H≥0.5. With exact shares, the nondecimated db2 estimator lies 6–14% above the root Cramér–Rao bound. Hadamard level tests are less accurate than direct measurement of leading qubits at all budgets. At H=0.9 and 2^20 queries, maximum-likelihood amplitude estimation attains RMSE 0.0347, versus 0.0451 for direct measurement and 0.0295 with exact shares.
AI.conclusion: The mirror extension substantially improves estimation accuracy, and the studentized estimator is asymptotically standard normal under diverging success counts, providing a rigorous statistical framework; maximum-likelihood amplitude estimation outperforms Hadamard-based level tests and approaches the exact-share benchmark.

title: Quantum Simulation of First-Quantised Chemistry with a Sum-of-Squares Representation
summary: Calculating molecular energies is expected to be an important application of quantum computers, but the most efficient algorithms to achieve this typically have significant space requirements. Scaling quantum processors to thousands of logical qubits is a daunting engineering challenge, so developing algorithms that run with reduced qubit requirements is of particular importance. Moreover, most algorithms are benchmarked on active spaces with about as many orbitals as electrons, missing dynamical correlation which is necessary to describe real chemistry. Capturing this correlation requires several times more orbitals than electrons, even in compact atomic-orbital basis sets. This low-filling regime favours first quantisation, where each electron is represented by a number of qubits that grows only logarithmically with the number of orbitals. Whether this approach translates into a practical advantage in orbital basis sets of realistic size, however, has been unclear. Here, we develop a first-quantised phase estimation algorithm for generic orbital basis sets, based on a non-convex sum-of-squares representation of the Hamiltonian and spectral-gap amplification. We compare it with the state-of-the-art second-quantised algorithm, compiling both with the same techniques at the logical level. For six molecules with 4 to 24 electrons in 5 to 14 times as many orbitals, our first-quantised method needs up to 16 times fewer Toffoli gates than the second-quantised algorithm in the low-qubit regime, where only a few hundred logical qubits are available. It stays cheaper up to between several hundred and about 1\,400 qubits, and its smallest qubit count is 1.4 to 2 times lower than in second quantisation. In the low-qubit and low-filling regime, our algorithm is therefore the method of choice for chemistry in orbital basis sets.

AI.tldr: A first-quantised phase-estimation algorithm for molecular energy estimation, using a non-convex sum-of-squares Hamiltonian representation and spectral-gap amplification, beats the state-of-the-art second-quantised approach by up to 16× in Toffoli gates in the low-qubit regime and reduces qubit counts 1.4–2×.
AI.motivation: Efficient molecular-energy algorithms for quantum computers demand many logical qubits, and scaling to thousands of logical qubits is a major engineering hurdle. Existing benchmarks also use near-full active spaces (orbitals ≈ electrons), ignoring dynamical correlation, which requires several times more orbitals than electrons and pushes the problem into a low-filling regime where first quantisation's logarithmic qubit-per-electron cost could pay off—but whether this gives a practical advantage at realistic basis-set sizes was unclear.
AI.method: The authors develop a first-quantised quantum phase estimation algorithm applicable to generic orbital basis sets, built on a non-convex sum-of-squares representation of the Hamiltonian plus spectral-gap amplification. They compile it and the state-of-the-art second-quantised algorithm with identical logical-level techniques to enable a fair resource comparison.
AI.result: Across six molecules with 4–24 electrons in 5–14 times as many orbitals, the first-quantised method requires up to 16× fewer Toffoli gates than second quantisation in the low-qubit regime (a few hundred logical qubits), remains cheaper up to roughly several hundred to ~1,400 qubits, and achieves 1.4–2× lower minimum qubit counts.
AI.conclusion: In the low-qubit, low-filling regime relevant to realistic chemistry in orbital basis sets, the proposed first-quantised algorithm is the method of choice, making it a practical path toward molecular-energy simulation on early fault-tolerant quantum hardware.

title: CREST: A Hardware-Aware GNN-Based Framework for High-Fidelity and Robust Superconducting Quantum Compilation
summary: Quantum compilation on superconducting processors requires selecting a connected execution region whose topology and calibrated properties suit the input circuit. This choice constrains subsequent routing and influences the noise encountered during execution, yet aggregate hardware-quality metrics alone may not reliably predict the execution fidelity of a given circuit. Calibration updates can also change region suitability and trigger the rebuilding of calibration-dependent resource structures. We present CREST, a graph neural network (GNN)-based framework that evaluates circuit-region compatibility before routing. It encodes gate dependencies and logical-qubit interactions alongside each candidate region's connectivity and current calibration attributes; bidirectional cross-graph attention relates the two representations, while real-device execution outcomes supervise candidate ranking. The trained scorer is reused with updated calibration attributes. Evaluations on 324 circuits from seven datasets on TianYan-176 show that CREST improves mean measurement-distribution fidelity by 19.03% over the strongest baseline and achieves the highest mean fidelity on every dataset. Furthermore, using updated calibration attributes, the same trained model maintains the highest overall mean fidelity across six measurement dates without retraining. With a unified model of circuit-region compatibility, CREST improves execution fidelity across diverse workloads and sustains that advantage as hardware calibration changes.

AI.tldr: CREST is a GNN-based framework that scores circuit–region compatibility before routing, using bidirectional cross-graph attention between circuit and hardware-region graphs, supervised by real-device outcomes. It raises mean measurement-distribution fidelity by 19.03% over the strongest baseline on TianYan-176 and keeps the highest mean fidelity across six calibration dates without retraining.
AI.motivation: On superconducting processors, choosing a connected execution region constrains routing and determines the noise a circuit meets, but aggregate hardware-quality metrics poorly predict per-circuit execution fidelity. Calibration drift further changes region suitability and forces rebuilding of calibration-dependent resource structures.
AI.method: CREST builds two graph representations: a circuit graph encoding gate dependencies and logical-qubit interactions, and a candidate-region graph encoding connectivity plus current calibration attributes. Bidirectional cross-graph attention relates the two, and real-device execution outcomes supervise candidate ranking; the trained scorer is reused with updated calibration attributes.
AI.result: On 324 circuits from seven datasets on TianYan-176, CREST improves mean measurement-distribution fidelity by 19.03% over the strongest baseline and attains the highest mean fidelity on every dataset. With updated calibration attributes, the same trained model retains the highest overall mean fidelity across six measurement dates without retraining.
AI.conclusion: A unified circuit–region compatibility model improves execution fidelity across diverse workloads and sustains the advantage as hardware calibration changes, avoiding per-calibration retraining.

title: Residual-Algebraic Design of Symmetry-Preserving Variational Quantum Circuits
summary: Symmetry-preserving (SP) variational quantum circuits restrict evolution to physically relevant sectors of Hilbert space, but symmetry preservation alone does not guarantee accessibility within those sectors. We show that a restricted generator set can possess a residual dynamical Lie algebra whose commutant further decomposes the target symmetry sector into invariant blocks. The associated block populations are conserved and impose a kinematic upper bound on the fidelity with a target state. We then invert this diagnostic into a circuit-design principle: candidate SP generators can be screened before variational optimization by asking whether they break the residual commutant, which invariant blocks they couple, and what adjoint module they generate under the residual algebra. For two orthogonal residual blocks we prove that a single elementary real inter-block rotation generates the full orthogonal algebra. We further derive a complex escape criterion: if the real and imaginary parts of an inter-block seed are independent over the residual intertwiner algebra, the generated module is the full complex coupling space and the enlarged algebra becomes special unitary. A connected residual-block graph yields a natural multi-block generalization and suggests minimum-cost spanning-tree circuit design. We demonstrate this design principle in the XXZ and Hubbard models, where residual-algebra screening identifies SP circuit extensions that remove the relevant accessibility obstructions. These examples establish a unified route from residual-symmetry diagnosis and fidelity bounds to predictive quantum circuit design.

AI.tldr: Symmetry-preserving variational circuits can still be trapped inside invariant blocks of the target symmetry sector determined by the commutant of the residual dynamical Lie algebra; these blocks impose kinematic fidelity bounds. The authors turn this diagnostic into a circuit-design principle: screen candidate generators by whether they break the residual commutant, which blocks they couple, and what adjoint module they generate, yielding proven criteria for achieving full orthogonal (real) or special-unitary (complex) coupling, plus a spanning-tree design for multi-block graphs, demonstrated on XXZ and Hubbard models.
AI.motivation: Symmetry-preserving (SP) ansätze are widely used to restrict evolution to physically relevant Hilbert-space sectors, but symmetry preservation is only a kinematic constraint and does not ensure that the target state is reachable within that sector. A restricted generator set can leave a residual dynamical Lie algebra whose commutant further decomposes the sector into invariant blocks, blocking accessibility. The paper aims to characterize this obstruction quantitatively and convert it into actionable design guidance for choosing generators before variational optimization.
AI.method: Diagnostic: analyze the residual dynamical Lie algebra generated by the chosen SP gates and its commutant, showing the commutant decomposes the target symmetry sector into invariant blocks with conserved populations that yield a kinematic fidelity upper bound. Inversion to design: screen candidate SP generators by (i) whether they break the residual commutant, (ii) which invariant blocks they couple, and (iii) what adjoint module they generate under the residual algebra. Proofs: for two orthogonal residual blocks, a single elementary real inter-block rotation generates the full orthogonal algebra; a complex escape criterion states that if the real and imaginary parts of an inter-block seed are independent over the residual intertwiner algebra, the generated module is the full complex coupling space and the enlarged algebra becomes special unitary. Multi-block extension via a connected residual-block graph with a minimum-cost spanning-tree circuit construction. Validation on the XXZ and Hubbard models.
AI.result: The commutant-based block decomposition quantitatively bounds achievable fidelity, explaining accessibility failures of purely symmetry-preserving circuits. The screening criteria are proven to be sufficient for algebra enlargement: one real inter-block rotation suffices for full orthogonality between two blocks, and intertwiner-independence of real/imaginary parts suffices for full complex coupling and an su-type algebra. Applied to XXZ and Hubbard models, residual-algebra screening identifies concrete SP circuit extensions that remove the relevant accessibility obstructions.
AI.conclusion: Symmetry preservation is necessary but not sufficient for accessibility; residual commutants and their invariant blocks are the controlling structure. Screening generators against the residual commutant, the inter-block coupling pattern, and the generated adjoint module provides a predictive, pre-optimization design route—from residual-symmetry diagnosis and fidelity bounds to systematically constructed circuits, including spanning-tree designs for multi-block residual-block graphs—establishing a unified framework for predictive SP quantum circuit design.

title: Dressed-State Quantum Information Processing Using a Multilayer Ion Trap Chip with an Integrated Radio Frequency Resonator
summary:
We present the experimental preparation of a radio frequency (RF)-dressed-state qubit, the coherent operation of a single RF-dressed qubit, and the selective readout of RF-dressed hyperfine states of $^{171}$Yb${^+}$ ions trapped using a novel microstructured ion trap chip. We demonstrate the individual addressing of RF-dressed-state qubits in a two-ion Coulomb crystal. To this end, we developed, manufactured, and characterized a trap chip specifcally designed for quantum information processing with RF-dressed-state qubits. The chip consists of multiple layers, one of which includes an integrated resonator that creates a gradient of the RF magnetic field amplitude along the axis of a linear ion crystal. This RF gradient enables the individual addressing of dressed qubit states as well as their coupling. We characterize the ion trap chip experimentally using the hyperfine states of the electronic ground state of laser cooled $^{171}$Yb${^+}$ ions and by applying a single, global, modulated RF field oscillating near 12.6 GHz that drives dressed-state resonances.
  We present a microfabricated multilayer ion trap chip specifically designed for quantum information processing based on dressed-state qubits. This ion trap chip consists of multiple layers, one of which includes an integrated radio frequency (RF) resonator, creating a gradient of the RF magnetic field amplitude that allows for individual qubit addressing and qubit-qubit coupling. We experimentally characterize this ion trap chip demonstrating dressed-qubit state preparation, coherent single dressed-qubit operation, and dressed-state-selective read-out using hyperfine states of the electronic ground state of $^{171}$Yb${^+}$. For this purpose, a global modulated RF driving field oscillating near 12.6 GHz is applied to the ions. In addition, we demonstrate individual addressing of dressed-state qubits in a two-ion Coulomb crystal.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a microfabricated multilayer ion trap chip with an integrated RF resonator that generates a magnetic-field-gradient, enabling preparation, coherent operation, selective readout, and individual addressing of RF-dressed-state qubits using $^{171}$Yb$^+$ hyperfine states driven near 12.6 GHz.
AI.motivation: Dressed-state qubits in trapped ions offer robustness, but individual addressing and qubit-qubit coupling require a spatially varying RF magnetic field amplitude, which conventional trap chips do not provide. The authors aim to realize a chip platform specifically engineered for RF-dressed-state qubit quantum information processing.
AI.method: A multilayer microfabricated ion trap chip is developed, manufactured, and characterized; one layer contains an integrated RF resonator producing a gradient of RF magnetic field amplitude along the linear ion crystal axis. Experiments use laser-cooled $^{171}$Yb$^+$ hyperfine ground states with a single global modulated RF field near 12.6 GHz driving dressed-state resonances, demonstrating state preparation, coherent single-qubit operation, dressed-state-selective readout, and individual addressing in a two-ion Coulomb crystal.
AI.result: The chip is experimentally characterized successfully: RF-dressed-state qubit preparation, coherent single dressed-qubit operation, and selective readout of dressed hyperfine states are demonstrated, and individual addressing of dressed-state qubits is achieved in a two-ion Coulomb crystal. The RF gradient also enables qubit-qubit coupling.
AI.conclusion: The integrated-resonator multilayer trap chip provides a viable hardware platform for RF-dressed-state qubit quantum information processing, supporting gradient-based individual addressing and coupling, with the demonstrated operations forming building blocks for scaled dressed-state ion-trap quantum processors.

title: A Nonsecular Quantum Master Equation with Detailed Balance and Second-order Error Bound
summary: An effective theory of open quantum systems should preserve the detailed balance structure inherited from microscopic reversibility and remain accurate throughout relaxation. Meeting both requirements is particularly challenging in quantum many-body systems, where dense spectra can invalidate the secular approximation even at weak coupling. Here we construct a nonsecular quantum master equation that satisfies time-reversal Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (TR-KMS) detailed balance. Under suitable conditions, we prove a time-uniform $O(λ^2)$ bound on the difference between the predicted and exact reduced density matrices, where $λ$ is the system-bath coupling strength. Our construction completes the Redfield generator by imposing detailed balance while matching its dissipative and coherent coefficients at resonance. In this approach, TR-KMS detailed balance is compatible with resonance matching, whereas its counterpart without time reversal is not. In a benchmark against the exact microscopic dynamics of two coupled oscillators, our equation maintains $O(λ^2)$ accuracy across secular and nonsecular regimes, outperforming the existing detailed-balance equations tested. These results provide a systematic route from microscopic models to thermodynamically consistent descriptions of open quantum dynamics beyond the secular approximation.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs a nonsecular quantum master equation satisfying time-reversal KMS detailed balance, proves a time-uniform O(λ²) accuracy bound, and shows it matches exact many-body dynamics across secular and nonsecular regimes.
AI.motivation: Effective theories of open quantum systems must both preserve the detailed balance structure inherited from microscopic reversibility and stay accurate throughout relaxation. In quantum many-body systems with dense spectra, the secular approximation breaks down even at weak coupling, making it hard to satisfy both requirements simultaneously.
AI.method: The authors build a nonsecular master equation that enforces time-reversal Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (TR-KMS) detailed balance. They complete the Redfield generator by imposing detailed balance while matching its dissipative and coherent coefficients at resonance; unlike its time-reversal-free counterpart, TR-KMS detailed balance is shown to be compatible with resonance matching. A rigorous time-uniform O(λ²) bound on the difference between predicted and exact reduced density matrices is proven under suitable conditions.
AI.result: The derived O(λ²) error bound holds uniformly in time. In a benchmark against exact microscopic dynamics of two coupled oscillators, the equation maintains O(λ²) accuracy in both secular and nonsecular regimes, outperforming existing detailed-balance equations tested.
AI.conclusion: The work offers a systematic route from microscopic models to thermodynamically consistent descriptions of open quantum dynamics beyond the secular approximation, reconciling detailed balance with nonsecular accuracy.
